title: Hedonic vs. Utilitarian Divide: How Emotional Valence and Arousal Moderate Attribute Effects on Repeat Purchase in Online Reviews
affiliations: , , ,  and

detail.title: Hedonic vs. Utilitarian Divide: How Emotional Valence and Arousal Moderate Attribute Effects on Repeat Purchase in Online Reviews

keywords.keywords: Repeat Purchase Product Attributes Emotional ValenceEmotional ArousalHedonic ProductsUtilitarian Products

detail.abstract: In highly competitive e-commerce markets, online reviews not only influence initial purchase decisions but also play a pivotal role in driving repeat purchases—a critical source of long-term profitability. Yet prior research has rarely examined how the interplay between product attributes and emotional cues in reviews shapes repurchase intentions across different product types. To address this gap, we analyze 976,483 Amazon reviews from six product categories using a two-stage research design that integrates machine learning and econometric modeling. In Study 1, Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) topic modeling and manual coding extract five core product attributes—performance, functionality, physical appearance, value for money, and customer service. Emotional valence and arousal are quantified using a lexicon-based approach. A random forest model identifies the most predictive attributes of repurchase intentions. In Study 2, logistic regression tests the moderating roles of valence and arousal in hedonic versus utilitarian products. Findings reveal striking asymmetries: in hedonic products, all attributes positively drive repurchase intentions, with arousal amplifying all the effects, while valence dampening certain effects; in utilitarian products, only value for money exerts a positive effect out of expectation, and valence consistently weakens all the effects, while arousal selectively strengthens attribute impacts. By integrating the Valence–Arousal–Dominance (VAD) emotion model with hedonic–utilitarian product theory, this study advances understanding of multi-attribute and emotional moderation mechanisms in repurchase behavior and offers actionable insights for leveraging review content to enhance customer retention strategies.

title: Managing Sales Agents and Product Returns While Guarding Against Fake Orders
affiliations: National University of Singapore (NUS) - Department of Information Systems and Analytics, Students, University of California, Berkeley - Haas School of Business and National University of Singapore (NUS) - Department of Information Systems and Analytics

detail.title: Managing Sales Agents and Product Returns While Guarding Against Fake Orders
detail.abstract: Managing a sales force and product returns poses a unique challenge. Generous return policies attract consumers, but can also create perverse incentives for an unscrupulous sales agent to place fake orders and subsequently return them to earn sales commissions. Our game-theoretic model shows that when the agent is scrupulous, the firm should pay the agent commissions on net sales (after returns) rather than gross sales (before returns) if return volumes are highly uncertain, but pair gross-sales commissions with free returns otherwise. Yet, such a combination would trigger fake orders from an unscrupulous agent. To guard against fakery, the firm can take one of the following three precautionary measures: (1) prohibiting product returns, (2) paying commissions on net sales, or (3) issuing partial refunds for returns. These precautions have nuanced implications for the firm's pricing and return policies. A higher salvage value from returns may induce a less generous return policy, whereas a higher consumer valuation of a matched product may compel a lower price. Finally, even when the agent can fully resolve consumers' pre-purchase match uncertainty at no cost and thus eliminate returns, the firm may still favor offering returns after purchase over having the agent inform consumers before purchase.

title: Return-freight insurance strategy and power structure selection for a live-streaming e-commerce supply chain
affiliations: Chongqing Technology and Business University,  and

detail.title: Return-freight insurance strategy and power structure selection for a live-streaming e-commerce supply chain
detail.abstract: Product returns exert significant pressure on the streamers and their partner firms. Crafting an optimal return-freight insurance strategy is vital. Meanwhile, the selection of power structure emerges as a crucial factor influencing the return-freight insurance strategy. Therefore, considering power structure and consumer bounded rationality, this study constructs game-theoretic models for two return-freight insurance strategies(complimentary and optional), under three power structures(Firm-Stackelberg, Vertical-Nash and Streamer-Stackelberg). By analyzing the optimal solutions derived from these game models, several conclusions are derived. Firstly, under Firm-Stackelberg, the streamer's optimal strategy is influenced by return-freight costs, streamer's commission, rational consumer proportion, and streamer’s influence; complimentary insurance is favorable only when all factors are high, whereas under Vertical-Nash and Streamer-Stackelberg, it is always unfavorable. Secondly, under the complimentary return-freight insurance strategy, when the streamer wields significant influence, Firm-Stackelberg structure is firm's optimal strategy, otherwise, Streamer-Stackelberg structure is; under the return-freight insurance option strategy,  Firm-Stackelberg structure is always  firm's optimal strategy. Finally, when all four factors are simultaneously high, the pure strategy Nash equilibrium is  { Complimentary return-freight insurance strategy, Firm-Stackelberg sturucure } , when any one of these four factor is relatively low, the pure strategy Nash equilibrium is { Return-freight insurance option strategy, Firm-Stackelberg structure } .

detail.abstract: Small businesses constitute over 90% of enterprises globally yet remain disproportionately vulnerable to cyber threats due to resource constraints, limited expertise, and cognitive biases regarding risk. This study addresses the paucity of cybersecurity research focused specifically on small businesses by conducting a systematic review of empirical literature. Searching the Semantic Scholar corpus and applying rigorous inclusion criteria, we identified 10 studies examining small business cybersecurity practices. Thematic analysis, guided by the Technology-Organization-Environment (TOE) framework and Risk Homeostasis Theory (RHT), revealed three interdependent pillars distinguishing robust from weak cybersecurity approaches: organizational culture, risk management strategy, and technology adoption. Integrating these theoretical perspectives, we developed the Integrated Cybersecurity Resilience Framework (ICRF), a practical, evidence-based model designed for resource-constrained implementation. The framework includes a phased 12-month roadmap, barriers-drivers matrix for strategic positioning, and curated free-to-low-cost tools. This study contributes theoretically by synthesizing TOE and RHT in the small business cybersecurity context and practically by providing actionable guidance tailored to small business realities.

detail.abstract: This study introduces and empirically validates a computer-implemented framework for proactive e-commerce, designed to reduce cognitive load in recurring B2B procurement. The proposed method termed the Symbiotic Assistant algorithmically synthesizes two previously unconnected data streams: (1) historical consumption data derived from e-commerce transactions and (2) external, non-transactional intent data sourced from booking and calendar APIs. The architecture combines an Event-Driven Demand Model (EDDM), which semantically maps upstream intent events to SKU-level consumption needs, with a Fusion Engine that reconciles historical and forward-looking signals to compute a Predicted Need Window (PNW). A Trust-by-Design, Human-in-theLoop (HITL) interface ensures user control through non-transactional draft orders and transparent reasoning for every recommendation. A 12-month randomized field experiment conducted within a live B2B platform (F.O.X Nails USA) shows significant commercial and behavioral effects: a 72.5% average acceptance rate for draft orders, a 44% increase in customer retention, and a 46% reduction in cognitive-toorder lead time relative to a passive control. These findings establish proactive commerce as a viable and scalable paradigm for digital markets. Theoretically, the study reframes online procurement as a cognitive coordination process between human and algorithmic agents. Practically, it offers a deployable blueprint for multi-tenant SaaS ecosystems seeking to balance automation efficiency with human trust and autonomy.

title: Inclusive and Equitable Urban Nature-based Solutions: A Practical Guide

detail.title: Inclusive and Equitable Urban Nature-based Solutions: A Practical Guide

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We have no conflict of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: Water Sensitive Cities Australia and the authors would like to thank The Resilient Urban Centres and Surrounds Program for funding this work.

detail.abstract:
This guide is developed in the context of the Resilient Urban Centres and Surrounds (RUCaS) which is being implemented across 4 Mekong countries—Cambodia, Lao PDR, Thailand, and Vietnam. Through local works on ground, the program demonstrates how nature-based solutions (NbS) can act as a catalyst to promote inclusive, climate-resilient urban areas through addressing local environmental, social and economic issues, and building resilient and adaptive capabilities that can be applied across the region. RUCaS is being implemented by Water Sensitive Cities Australia (WSCA) based at Monash University in partnership with the International Centre for Environmental Management (ICEM) and supported by the Australian Government. 

This guide is designed for a broad range of use cases. It can be used to plan and develop long-term programs for NbS in response to urban challenges that drive system transformation towards equity, fairness, and justice for those most in need. In this framing, GEDSI is not an add-on; it is central to achieving fair, inclusive, equitable, and sustainable urban change. 

Not every project that integrates GEDSI will deliver system change. Thus, the guide can also be used selectively and ad hoc for projects already underway to make components more GEDSI-sensitive and to improve the likelihood of equitable outcomes (e.g. developing accessible communication materials for people with disabilities).

Integrating GEDSI can seem overwhelming, but it can begin with recognising local actors’ rights, diverse needs and languages. For example, involve groups most affected by local flooding in planning and co-design so that solutions respond directly to their priorities; or co-design NbS such as a city park with diverse community groups so the result is a more inclusive public space.

With this in mind, the guide is not prescriptive. Rather than a detailed blueprint, it offers suggestions and principles to help NbS projects generate positive responses to urban challenges. The guide draws on examples and experiences from across the Mekong region and shows how diverse stakeholders can co-develop urban NbS designs that address common issues faced by cities in the region.

Our approach to mainstreaming GEDSI in NbS-related projects follows 4 interconnected phases. The activities proposed within these phases are indicative, not exhaustive, and should be flexibly adapted to the needs, languages, and context of specific projects.

title: The Designometric Perspective and the Psychometric Fallacy in Developing user Experience Rating Scales
affiliations: University of Twente, University of Twente and University of Twente

detail.title: The Designometric Perspective and the Psychometric Fallacy in Developing user Experience Rating Scales
detail.abstract: Rating scales are widely used in user experience (UX) research to compare and rank design alternatives, yet their development typically relies on psychometric procedures originally created for assessing human traits. We argue that this practice commits the psychometric fallacy: evaluating designometric instruments-tools intended to discriminate between designs-using person × item response matrices that exclude the essential third dimension of design. Because design evaluation inherently forms a design × person × item data structure, valid scale development requires samples of designs large enough to assess how well items rank design alternatives. We show that collapsing the data cube along persons yields a design × item matrix that allows psychometric tools to be applied meaningfully, whereas collapsing along designs yields misleading psychometric results about person sensitivity rather than design discriminability. A simulation study demonstrates that scales can appear highly reliable psychometrically while being effectively unusable for ranking designs. Secondary analyses of eight commonly used UX scales across large design samples reveal unsystematic distortions in reliability estimates, item performance, and dimensionality when instruments are evaluated under the psychometric fallacy. We assess the impact of the psychometric fallacy for present users and designers of future rating scales and discuss more advanced methods in designometric modelling.

title: Governance as Code: How AI is Enforcing Information Policies Directly in the Tech Stack
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Governance as Code: How AI is Enforcing Information Policies Directly in the Tech Stack
detail.abstract: Traditional governance models, reliant on static documents and manual reviews, are fundamentally incompatible with the velocity and complexity of modern AI and software development. This paper examines the paradigm of "Governance as Code" (GaC), a transformative approach that embeds information policies, ethical guidelines, and compliance controls directly into the technology stack. By translating human-readable rules into machine-executable code, GaC enables proactive, automated enforcement within DevOps and AIOps pipelines. We explore practical implementations such as AI guardrails that filter sensitive prompts and automated risk-tiering systems that streamline project oversight.

detail.title: Co-Pilot, Not Autopilot: Navigating the Future of Qualitative Research
detail.abstract: Recently, a group of 3 published an open letter signed by over 400 qualitative researchers. Their message was clear: "Keep AI away from our work." They argue that using AI to find themes in data kills the "reflexive" process, the deeply human act of interpreting nuance, emotion, and meaning. I have spent my career championing the human touch in the EdTech works and research. I understand their fear. However, I believe this total rejection is a mistake. We should not be banning Gen AI; we should be teaching researchers how to master it.

title: The Human Stack: Why Soft Skills Are the Ultimate Competitive Advantage In Tech
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Human Stack: Why Soft Skills Are the Ultimate Competitive Advantage In Tech
detail.abstract: In an era defined by rapid technological advancement, the most durable competitive advantage may be fundamentally human. This article introduces the concept of the "Human Stack" the layered suite of soft skills like communication, empathy, and adaptability that employees bring to an organization. While technical skills are essential for entry, it is these uniquely human capabilities that drive true differentiation and success. As automation encroaches on routine tasks, soft skills become critical differentiators that machines cannot replicate.

detail.title: Agentic Algorithmic Amplification and the Choices We Face
detail.abstract: Whether we like it or not, know it or not, we have been living in the agentic age of algorithms long before the recent rush to building agentic systems. None of these systems were explicitly programmed to promote conspiracy theories. But they were programmed to maximize engagement, and they discovered—through the same machine learning techniques that help them recognize faces or translate languages—that false, emotionally charged content was engagement gold.

detail.abstract: In this chapter, I explore the property law treatment of cryptoassets-and, presumably, other digital artefacts that are not clearly rights to anything or against anyone. I argue that such artefacts are well described as "ideational objects", and draw together insights from private law theory and social ontology to explore how we should think about complex objects with a social and a technical dimension. I then examine how the law of property can accommodate ideational objects as possible objects of rights (including the right of ownership) and dealing such as transfer, and what challenges and implications this poses for the traditional doctrines and concepts of property law. The chapter aims to contribute to the emerging literature on cryptoassets (and digital assets more broadly), as well as to the broader debate on the nature and boundaries of property in the digital age. In particular, it defends the Law Commission's suggested approach of recognising a "third category" of personal property from criticisms made by Professor Kelvin Low, and introduces a new conceptual framework from Professor Christian von Bar's seminal treatise on the "things as objects of property rights".

title: Problems With Archiving and Replaying Web Advertisements

detail.title: Problems With Archiving and Replaying Web Advertisements
detail.abstract: Advertisements are an integral part of our cultural heritage, and this extends to online web advertisements. Unlike print ads, web ads are dynamic and interactive, which makes them difficult to archive and replay (i.e., load archived web resources in a web browser) successfully . To explore these challenges, we created a dataset of 279 archived web ads. During this study, we identified five major problems with archiving and replaying web ads, which we discuss in detail in our article "Problems With Archiving and Replaying Current Web Advertisements".

title: Towards a Regenerative Economic Architecture: Scaling Non-Extractive Capital Beyond Debt, Equity, and Philanthropy

detail.title: Towards a Regenerative Economic Architecture: Scaling Non-Extractive Capital Beyond Debt, Equity, and Philanthropy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial or personal conflicts of interest that could have influenced the research contained in this paper. The development of the theoretical framework and analysis was conducted independently, without external influence from funders, institutions, or related organisations.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants, clinical data, or field experiments. No ethics approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific external funding. All work was supported by the author’s independent research through the Institute for Regenerative Systems & Architecture (IRSA).

detail.abstract:
Modern economies rely on three capital forms—debt, equity, and grants—whose logics of extraction, dilution, and depletion make them structurally incompatible with long-horizon, fragility-dominated domains such as climate adaptation, scientific capability, public health infrastructure, and mission-driven enterprise. Recent advances in Perpetual Social Capital (PSC), Regenerative Capital Theory (RCT), and Alignment Capital identify a missing quadrant in the capital taxonomy: non-liability, non-extractive, multi-cycle regenerative capital.

This paper develops the macroeconomic architecture required for regenerative capital to operate at institutional and global scale. We formalise the capital phase-space in which regenerative systems remain stable; derive long-horizon regeneration dynamics under variable recycling and capability accrual; and explain why regenerative pools expand 20–100× relative to philanthropic inflows through temporal compounding rather than interest, leverage, or risk-transfer.

We show how regenerative capital outperforms debt in resilience-based sectors, stabilises institutions across political and financial volatility, and enables multi-decade capability formation through soft-obligation governance. We further outline the design of sovereign, sectoral, and global regenerative capital markets capable of absorbing far more capital than philanthropy. By linking micro-level capital design with macro-level architecture, this paper establishes the theoretical foundations for a post-extractive, multi-cycle economic system.

title: The AI-Powered Third-Party Risk Manager: Continuously Monitoring Vendor Security Posture
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The AI-Powered Third-Party Risk Manager: Continuously Monitoring Vendor Security Posture
detail.abstract: Modern enterprises are increasingly vulnerable to cyberattacks through their third-party vendors, with over half of all data breaches now originating in the supply chain. Traditional third-party risk management (TPRM), reliant on manual, point-in-time assessments like annual questionnaires, is ill-equipped to address the dynamic nature of cyber threats. This paper proposes an AI-powered TPRM framework as a transformative solution. By enabling continuous, real-time monitoring of vendor security posture - AI streamlines risk assessments using intelligent questionnaires and provides dynamic, multi-factor risk scoring to prioritize critical vendors. The integration of AI into TPRM represents a paradigm shift from a static, reactive process to a dynamic, intelligent, and continuous safeguard, essential for security in an interconnected digital ecosystem.

title: Sabrina's Law: A Control-Theoretic Principle of Human Suffering

detail.title: Sabrina's Law: A Control-Theoretic Principle of Human Suffering
detail.abstract: Sabrina's Law states: Any attempt to change another autonomous agent in order to regulate one's own emotional state guarantees suffering. This paper reframes emotion regulation research through a control-theoretic lens, demonstrating how variance amplification, instability, and falsecontrollability illusions create predictable emotional volatility. The principle is applied across interpersonal dynamics, organizational behavior, and internal psychological architecture, offering a structural explanation for patterns historically attributed to personality, pathology, or interpersonal conflict.

title: Proactive Privacy: Using AI to Automate PII Discovery and Data Subject Access Requests (DSARs)

detail.title: Proactive Privacy: Using AI to Automate PII Discovery and Data Subject Access Requests (DSARs)
detail.abstract: The regulatory landscape of GDPR, CCPA, and other privacy laws has made fulfilling Data Subject Access Requests (DSARs) a critical yet operationally complex challenge. Manual processes for locating an individual's data across fragmented systems are slow, error-prone, and struggle to meet mandated deadlines. This article explores how AI-driven privacy tools are transforming compliance from a reactive burden into a proactive strategy.

detail.abstract: Traditional legal scholarship and Law & Economics posit that all contractual interests are, and should be, protected by contract law. This article challenges this notion by examining whether public perceptions align with legal doctrine. In an experiment, respondents report their perceived social appropriateness of breach and the appropriate level of damages considering different types of losses suffered by the promisee. Contrary to the traditional legal and economic perspectives, the findings suggest that the public perceives loss of benefit as the most socially inappropriate, followed by loss of reliance, loss of expectancy, and no loss, in the ascending order of need for legal redress. Moreover, respondents award higher damages for loss of benefit compared to loss of reliance, and for loss of reliance compared to loss of expectancy. While contract law traditionally emphasizes the protection of the expectation interest, the public's moral intuitions suggest a nuanced approach. The study underscores the importance of considering public morality in shaping contract law, prompting a reassessment of the hierarchy of contractual interests and of the determination of damages for breach.

title: Implementation of Public-Private Partnership (PPP) Scheme and DBFOM Model as Efforts to Realize Sustainable Public Transportation at PT Transjakarta

detail.title: Implementation of Public-Private Partnership (PPP) Scheme and DBFOM Model as Efforts to Realize Sustainable Public Transportation at PT Transjakarta
detail.abstract: This study aims to analyze the implementation of the Public-Private Partnership (PPP) scheme and the Design-Build-Finance-Operate-Maintain (DBFOM) model at PT Transjakarta as an effort to realize sustainable public transportation in Jakarta. This method uses a qualitative descriptive approach through literature studies and document analysis sourced from academic journals, government policies, and official reports from PT Transjakarta. The results of the study show that the implementation of PPP and DBFOM plays an important role in increasing financing efficiency, encouraging technological innovation, and strengthening collaboration between local governments and the private sector. Through this collaboration, Transjakarta has successfully implemented bus fleet electrification, reduced carbon emissions, and strengthened domestic industrial independence. However, challenges remain in terms of long-term financing, supporting infrastructure readiness, and institutional capacity. Overall, the implementation of PPP and DBFOM in Transjakarta is a concrete example of the synergy between public policy and private innovation in supporting the transformation of urban transportation towards a green and sustainable mobility system.

title: Legacy Trade Models, Evolving Contours of Regulations, And Growing Digital Trade: Concerns and Challenges for Policy Makers

detail.abstract:
The various data gaps, both structural and intentional, have entered the global trading landscape. Providing a detailed overview of the imbalance in international trade data and information collection, and its potential to improve trade governance, predictability, and trust among trading partners. The imbalance in proper registration of tariff data, especially regarding missing Ad Valorem Equivalent (AVE) calculations as agreed under the WTO’s Doha Development Agenda for many developed countries’ agricultural products, leads to an underestimation of average tariffs (for example, a 3.4% average tariff can rise to 36.4% when AVEs are applied). This affects the market access potential of many developing countries that are members of the WTO. A similar imbalance exists in how SPS and TBT measures (technical NTMs) are notified. Often, these measures are notified without specifying trade coverage (HSN codes), making them unusable for market access assessments. Many other such imbalances were discussed, like the lack of proper evaluation of the bilateral overall balance of trade between two partners, due to the absence of bilateral service sector flow data. This results in the inability to register cross-border trade flows through digital modes, especially for products that have shifted from physical to digital modes and others that may increasingly use additive manufacturing via 3D printing. I also discussed the growing data gap caused by the increasing control of the private sector, which leads to higher costs and a shift from the Census to Surveys to address immediate operational issues and concerns. Furthermore, various other aspects, such as the rising use of regulatory controls instead of conventional trade policy tools like tariffs, are contributing to a shift from GVCs to GSCs.

Another aspect discussed was the imbalance caused by focusing only on imports and neglecting exports in partial equilibrium models, which led to an overemphasis on consumer welfare at the expense of producer welfare. This also highlights the redundancy of legacy trade and economic models, such as Partial Equilibrium (PEs), General Equilibrium (GE), and Dynamic models, as they all rely on SAM or Input-Output Tables, which are often outdated for specific members. Furthermore, a warning is issued that if these issues are not adequately addressed and considered, the Artificial Intelligence (AI)-generated trade and investment predictions may lead to misleading global economic outcomes.

detail.abstract: E-commerce has become a transformative force in Telangana’s economy. Over the last five years, the state has experienced rapid online business expansion, supported by technology adoption, improved logistics, and a proactive government. This research analyzes e-commerce’s economic influence on GDP, MSME participation, and employment generation. Using descriptive and analytical methods, it interprets data collected from credible secondary sources covering 2023–2025. The findings suggest that while e-commerce enhances market access and efficiency, disparities exist between urban and rural regions. Strengthening digital infrastructure and ensuring equitable access are crucial for maintaining economic balance.

detail.abstract: Judicial expertise is the ability of a court to understand the evidence produced by the parties. While the expert can distinguish between informative and uninformative signals, the generalist cannot, and hence it can be more easily swayed by the party with cheaper access to evidence. The different incentives for evidence production before expert and generalist courts generate a trade-off between more information and better information. We show that contracting parties prefer enforcement before an expert when the stakes are high and their costs of evidence production differ. The availability of experts enhances the scope of contingent contracts. Our analysis has implications for the use of arbitration and forum-selection clauses in commercial contracts, corporations' jurisdictional choices — such as incorporating in Delaware — and the domain of specialized courts — such as bankruptcy, tax or family courts.

title: Business as Usual on the Highway to Hell? Limits to Growth and Future World Orders
affiliations: and Universidad de Valladolid

detail.title: Business as Usual on the Highway to Hell? Limits to Growth and Future World Orders

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal Futures, Forthcoming

detail.abstract: Combining fundamental premises from international relations, political economy and ecological economics, we show that (1) the reproduction of the current world order structurally depends on the violation of the precautionary principle in favor of 'business as usual' (BAU), understood as continued economic growth and environmental degradation; and (2) BAU rather than successful sustainability transitions constitutes the most probable short-term future, due to the difficulties of consistently implementing global 'green growth' and 'degrowth' proposals. Based on this analysis, we construct four global socio-ecological futures emerging after a period of unsustainable BAU. These scenarios feature different structural changes away from the status quo by exacerbating or transcending the capitalist, state-based world order: Hyperimperialist Exploitation describes an increasing polarization between the world's centers and peripheries whereas Interimperialist Competition includes great power rivalries similar to those leading to the first world war. In Global Emergency Governance, social forces achieve the establishment of a supranational organization capable of managing environmental disaster, economic development and migratory flows. Last, Fragmented Diversity describes a radically de-globalized world with small societies integrated in local ecosystems. The scenarios highlight the structural lock-in of the global society into a risky, potentially catastrophic development pathway but also point to the importance of societal power struggles in shaping socio-ecological futures.

title: Exploring Alternative Data in Systematic Investing for Retail Investors

detail.title: Exploring Alternative Data in Systematic Investing for Retail Investors
detail.abstract: There are three main types of company analysis: fundamental, technical, and behavioral: each involving a different way of looking at and analyzing companies. The fourth type of analysis that has emerged in recent years involves alternative data. It relates to any kind of unofficially obtained data that is nonetheless publicly available and can give additional insight into companies’ performance and operations. It can include sentiment analysis, web traffic, oil imports, satellite imagery, etc. and it has gained popularity tremendously among institutional investors in recent years. However, retail investors have largely been excluded from access to alternative data, due to the cost of obtaining and difficulty processing it, which is why this study explores various ways that they can leverage it. This is a largely unexplored research gap, as there are few papers that study how this type of data can be implemented and instead focus on the rate of adoption, they are rarely quantitative in nature and if they are – they don’t explore data beyond sentiment analysis. That is why this paper will divide the research into the sector-wide shaping trends and company-specific factors sections and quantitatively explore different types of alternative data that can help predict stock prices, revenue levels, and cost of goods sold using multivariable linear regression and correlation analysis. For the sector-wide analysis, the study will focus on the iShares Global Clean Energy ETF (ICLN) and for the company-specific section on Tesla, Inc. The paper will showcase which specific types of data can help in predicting the above-mentioned factors, introduce various conceptual and academic evidence, and then explore these quantitively for the specific securities inspected. The thesis relies on secondary data sources and uses data from platforms like: Nasdaq Data Link, Yahoo Finance, Google Trends, Altindex, etc. Further, the study explains how these alternative data types can be included in the systematic investment process, especially if it involves the top-down approach and is longer-term oriented. The paper finds that including alternative data after identifying relevant data points increases the accuracy of the multivariable linear regression by increasing the adjusted R2 and reducing the RMSE, compared with the benchmark models without these non-standard inputs. However, the study also finds that multivariable linear regression fails to capture nonlinear patterns, which are sometimes inherent to alternative data, even if the academic sources and correlation analysis suggest they should be relevant. Finally, the paper presents the most significant hindrances for retail investors to accessing alternative data, how they can overcome some of them, and include it in their investment analysis process. Despite the study being oriented to retail investors, the results may be used by investors of all sizes wishing to enrich their data- driven investment approach with alternative data.

detail.abstract: Personalized nutrition leveraging continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) data holds significant promise for optimizing postprandial glycemic responses, yet accessible predictive models remain limited by proprietary datasets. We applied an interpretable machine learning framework using XGBoost regression to predict postprandial glucose response parameters from meal composition and individual characteristics. Using the Hall dataset comprising 112 meals from 19 non-diabetic adults, we parameterized glucose curves using normalized Gaussian functions, extracting amplitude, time-to-peak, and curve width features. The XGBoost model achieved limited predictive performance with R² values of 0.46,-0.76, and 0.10 for amplitude, time-to-peak, and curve width parameters, respectively. Results indicate significant challenges in predicting postprandial glucose dynamics from basic meal composition and individual characteristics, highlighting the complexity of glucose metabolism and the need for more comprehensive feature sets in personalized nutrition applications.

detail.abstract:
Environmental protections and the processes of the administrative state are under attack. In recent years, the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) has drawn outsized criticism from across the political and legal spectrum as a major impediment to climate friendly infrastructure and the clean energy transition. NEPA enables private groups to challenge development through litigation. Critics are moving to strip public oversight over federal permitting based on claims that these private groups bring largely frivolous environmental claims to court, driving up costs for developers and delaying progress responding to climate change. But is this really true? 

Drawing on an original dataset of over 2,000 cases involving challenges to federal environmental reviews from 2009–2023, this Article presents the largest study of federal permitting litigation and reveals novel descriptive and empirical dimensions to the scholarly literature on private enforcement of NEPA. This study adds new, important empirical details about clean energy litigation that is highly relevant to the NEPA reform debate. I find that critics’ claims distort the reality of NEPA litigation. 

Although the threat of NEPA litigation may chill some development, the litigation itself is broadly useful in ensuring well-informed decision-making across the government. Contrary to popular narratives, litigation is dominant in projects involving extraction such as forestry and fossil fuels, but plays only a minimal, at best, role in clean energy development. This data suggests that calls for reforms that excise or minimize public participation are not likely to accelerate the clean energy transition but, paradoxically, will almost certainly accelerate greenhouse gas emissions that drive climate change, increase environmental harm, and deepen economic and health disparities. This Article concludes by proposing a new path for permitting reform that would enhance rather than hobble democratic functioning and truly serve the public interest.

detail.abstract: Money has recently regained a history.  Long set aside as a commodity, convention, or empty instrumentality, money figures increasingly in recent scholarship as a consequential subject of debate and design in early America.  That development invites attention to the strange historiography of money and its recent turn.  Money’s modern historiography dates to the Enlightenment, when the narrative took hold that money was essentially a transparent technology, one that transmitted determinations about value made independently by individuals as agents.  After tracing that narrative and its impact organizing contemporary assumptions and disciplines, the essay considers emerging approaches to money as represented by the papers presented at the WMQ-EMSI Workshop.  While those approaches vary, they tend to read money as a practice that organizes value rather than simply expressing it.  Money appears as a complexly crafted system with formative influence rather than mere marker or straightforward mode of measure.  Analyzing the historical drama in the Workshop papers, the essay argues that societies create money as a respiratory system for capital, one that sources value in viable form, circulates it, and channels its use distinctively around the society that engineers it.   Recognizing money as that expansive phenomenon opens a wide new avenue for insight on early America and its capitalist aftermath.

detail.abstract: The aim of this study is to examine the linkages between ownership of households' agricultural landholding and child nutritional status in rural India. Agricultural landholding is a critical indicator of socioeconomic well-being in rural areas. More than 56 per cent of the working population in rural India is involved in agriculture as its main or marginal economic activity. Ownership of agricultural land and engagement in related activities not only makes access to food materials easy but also provides the crucial socioeconomic security that is essential to improving the nutritional status of the rural population in India. Our empirical analyses support theoretical arguments: bivariate analyses revealed that about 11 per cent more underweight children reside in households with no land or with marginal agricultural landholdings as compared to households with the larger size of agricultural landholdings. Similar differences are also observed in the case of child stunting and food security by the size of household agricultural landholding. Regression analyses also suggest that the size of a household's agricultural landholding is a critical determinant of a child's nutritional status in rural India after controlling for other important socioeconomic factors that are known to affect the child's nutritional status. Pathways that influence the relationship between ownership of households' agricultural landholding and child nutritional status include direct access to sufficient and diverse food and indirectly through improved livelihoods and social status.

title: Testing a Contrarian Hypothesis: The Predictive Power of Overnight News Sentiment on S&P 500 Intraday Returns

detail.title: Testing a Contrarian Hypothesis: The Predictive Power of Overnight News Sentiment on S&P 500 Intraday Returns
detail.abstract:
This study tests a common contrarian hypothesis: that aggregated overnight financial news sentiment moves opposite to the subsequent day's market performance. We developed a novel "Market Sentiment Score" (MSS), a 10-point bearishness scale, to quantify news from 6:00 PM to 8:00 AM EST, and analyzed 20 trading days leading to November 5, 2025.

We find the data refutes the contrarian hypothesis. We document a strong inverse statistical correlation of -0.88 between our adjusted sentiment score and the full-day (9:30 AM-4:00 PM) S&P 500 E-mini futures return. A linear regression model (Return % = -0.19 * Sentiment + 1.03) quantifies this relationship. This strong negative correlation shows a congruent practical outcome: as overnight sentiment becomes more bearish (score increases), the subsequent market return becomes more negative (return decreases).

detail.abstract: This memorandum provides an analysis of an investment strategy based on a hypothetical but highly probable scenario for the development of events in the United States. The core of the scenario is the emergence of a "fiscal trap": a combination of irreversible corporate tax cuts and a shock loss of budget revenues due to the judicial cancellation of large-scale protectionist duties. The pressure on public finances is compounded by the potential need for compensation payments to businesses. The Memorandum details two key macroeconomic outcomes (high and low inflation) and offers a unique combined strategy that is neutral to the inflationary scenario. The strategy is aimed at extracting benefits from: • The inevitable change of the Fed's monetary regime through the "steeper" position on the yield curve. • A fundamental deterioration in the creditworthiness of the United States through the purchase of credit default swaps (CDS). The purpose of the document is to justify a diversified approach that hedges the risks of uncertainty and allows you to profit from structural imbalances rather than speculative guessing of short-term trends.

title: Assessment of Heavy Metals Levels in Vegetables on Artisanal Mining Areas (Geita and Msalala) in Tanzania

detail.abstract: Heavy metals pose significant health risks, including acute and chronic toxicities that may lead to serious diseases such as cancer. Elevated levels of heavy metals are often found near mining areas. This study investigated heavy metal levels in vegetables grown in artisanal mining regions of Tanzania’s Lake Zone.To evaluate mercury and other heavy metal concentrations in leaf and root vegetables collected from Msalala and Geita in TanzaniaDietary habits were assessed via oral interviews. Vegetable samples were air-dried, powdered, and digested with a nitric acid and hydrogen peroxide mixture (1:1, v/v). Mercury concentrations were measured using Atomic Absorption Spectrophotometry (AAS), while other metals were analyzed by Inductively Coupled Plasma Optical Emission Spectroscopy (ICP-OES).Most respondents reported consuming spring water (97%) and lake fish (96%). Over half frequently consumed cereals, legumes, and leafy vegetables. Heavy metal levels in vegetables were generally below WHO maximum permissible limits, with no significant differences between mining and non-mining areas (p > 0.05). However, 17% of the 245 vegetable samples exceeded WHO recommendations for mercury levels.Vegetable samples exhibited elevated mercury levels, indicating potential health risks. Further research is warranted to investigate the variability in heavy metal concentrations, which may contribute to exposure.

detail.abstract: The increase in national energy needs amid government fiscal constraints demands innovation in financing through public-private partnerships. The Public-Private Partnership (PPP) scheme and the Design-Build-Finance-Operate-Maintain (DBFOM) model become important strategies in supporting efficient, accountable, and sustainable energy resilience. This research aims to analyze the implementation of PPP and DBFOM by PT Migas Utama Jabar (MUJ) as an energy Regional-Owned Enterprise (BUMD) owned by the West Java Provincial Government in strengthening regional energy resilience. The research method uses a qualitative descriptive approach based on literature studies with secondary data analysis from scientific journals, books, government policies, and official reports from the 2021-2025 period. The research results show that the application of PPP and DBFOM by MUJ has created effective synergy between the government and the private sector in financing and managing regional energy infrastructure. MUJ has successfully optimized its 10% Participating Interest in the ONWJ Block, expanded its renewable energy portfolio, and implemented Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) principles through green financing. Based on the latest theories from Delmon (2021), Lessambo (2022), Netshiswinzhe et al. (2024), and Bappenas (2023), the integration of PPP and DBFOM not only increases investment efficiency but also strengthens performance-based governance. However, there are still challenges in the form of regulatory limitations, institutional coordination, and access to green financing. Therefore, strengthening the capacity of energy BUMD, harmonization of central-regional policies, and expansion of ESG-based financing schemes are needed. This research provides theoretical and practical contributions to the development of adaptive and competitive regional energy partnership models, as well as strengthening the direction of sustainable energy development in Indonesia.

title: Evolution of Compliance Testing in Compliance Risk Management

detail.title: Evolution of Compliance Testing in Compliance Risk Management
detail.abstract:
This paper examines the evolution of compliance testing within the framework of compliance risk management in Canada’s federally regulated financial institutions (FRFIs). Once regarded as a reactive, checklist-driven control, compliance testing has transformed into a proactive governance tool that supports strategic risk management and regulatory compliance. Anchored in the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions’ (OSFI) Guideline E-13: Regulatory Compliance Management, the study traces the development of compliance testing from its origins in policy adherence to its emerging role as an integral component of enterprise risk governance.

Drawing on comparative frameworks from the UK Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), the U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), and Canadian securities regulators such as the Ontario Securities Commission (OSC) and Canadian Investment Regulatory Organization (CIRO), the paper analyzes how international best practices have informed OSFI’s expectations for independence, risk-based planning, and board-level accountability. It argues that compliance testing must evolve beyond periodic reviews toward data-enabled, continuous, and integrated assurance models that reinforce organizational accountability and strengthen institutional resilience.

Through a review of regulatory guidance, risk governance models, and institutional practices, the paper proposes a series of reform recommendations—including the adoption of data analytics, automation, assurance mapping, and capability maturity frameworks—to advance compliance testing as a strategic function. The analysis concludes that modernized, independent, and risk-informed compliance testing is essential not only for regulatory adherence but for enhancing governance, promoting a culture of integrity, and sustaining public trust in Canada’s financial system.

title: A Quantitative Framework for Sharing Monetary Expansion with Taxpayers: Citizen Seigniorage Shares (CSS)

detail.title: A Quantitative Framework for Sharing Monetary Expansion with Taxpayers: Citizen Seigniorage Shares (CSS)
detail.abstract: Citizen Seigniorage Shares (CSS) introduce a rules-based mechanism that allocates a fraction of monetary-expansion-driven wealth directly to taxpayers, without altering fiscal spending, monetary policy, or the money supply. Modern U.S. monetary operations—including reserve creation, credit expansion, and portfolio rebalancing— generate significant private-sector wealth via liquidity channels. Yet taxpayers, who ultimately underwrite the credibility of Treasury securities, deposit insurance, and central-bank operations, capture none of this upside. CSS addresses this structural asymmetry by allocating non-transferable, vesting asset units whenever system liquidity expands. We formalize the Citizen Seigniorage Allocation Rule (CSAR), which mints CSS units according to a linear function of reserve creation and broad-money growth. CSS units accumulate in individual accounts and are backed by a sovereign investment portfolio, ensuring that CSS operates as an asset, not a currency. Using empirical estimates of the reserve–asset and credit–wealth elasticities, we show that CSS could have generated meaningful household asset accumulation from 2003–2024 while remaining strictly non-inflationary. Simulations across multiple monetary regimes demonstrate that CSS scales proportionally with liquidity conditions and naturally pauses during tightening cycles. The mechanism is compatible with the Federal Reserve’s independence and Treasury operations. CSS therefore represents a structural modification to the distributional consequences of monetary expansion, not a modification of macroeconomic policy itself.

title: Beyond Efficiency: Market Cognition and Information Filtering under Range-Clearing

detail.title: Beyond Efficiency: Market Cognition and Information Filtering under Range-Clearing
detail.abstract: This paper challenges the efficient-market hypothesis (EMH) at its epistemological root by replacing its "point equilibrium" microfoundation with a more realistic framework termed "range-clearing." We argue that subjective value is not a precise point but a range of acceptability, and that market transactions clear not at a singular price but within a zone of overlapping value ranges. From this single premise, a fundamental re-evaluation of market efficiency emerges. We demonstrate, first, that the market’s apparent "stickiness" or hesitation to react to minor informational stimuli is not a sign of inefficiency, but is instead the hallmark of a higher-order cognitive efficiency, whereby rational actors conserve scarce mental resources by strategically ignoring noise that falls within their acceptance range. Second, we show that this mechanism structurally ensures that the market functions as a low-pass information filter, systematically and rationally culling high-frequency "noise" at each transactional node. This finding renders the strong and semi-strong forms of EMH ontologically impossible, as the market price cannot, even in theory, reflect "all" available information. By reconceptualizing the market not as a flawless information-processing machine but as a profoundly human institution of cognitive economizing and selective judgment, this paper provides a robust, rational explanation for real-world phenomena such as price momentum and financial crashes. We conclude that EMH is not so much incorrect as it is a special, and unrealistic, case of our more general theory, and call for a paradigm shift in financial economics—away from the sterile mechanics of informational efficiency and toward a more fruitful science of human judgment in an uncertain world.

detail.abstract: Results in the Heterogeneous Agent Model (HAM) literature determine the proportion of fundamentalists and trend followers in the financial market. This proportion varies according to the periods analyzed. In this paper, we use a large language model (LLM) to construct a generative agent (GA) that determines the probability of adopting one of the two strategies based on current information. The probabilities of strategy adoption are compared with those in the HAM literature for the S&P 500 index between 1990 and 2020. Our findings suggest that the resulting artificial intelligence (AI) expectations align with those reported in the HAM literature. At the same time, extending the analysis to artificial market data helps us to filter the decision-making process of the AI agent. In the artificial market, results confirm the heterogeneity in expectations but reveal systematic asymmetry toward the fundamentalist behavior.

title: Resource Control Agitation and Political Instability in Nigeria: A Case study of Akwa Ibom State

detail.title: Resource Control Agitation and Political Instability in Nigeria: A Case study of Akwa Ibom State
detail.abstract: Akwa Ibom State ranks among Nigeria’s major oil-producing regions, contributing substantially to the nation’s petroleum output. Despite its resource wealth, the state has witnessed persistent unrest and political instability driven by disputes surrounding resource ownership and revenue distribution. This study explores the nexus between resource control agitation and political instability in Nigeria, focusing on Akwa Ibom State, with particular attention to issues of economic marginalization and environmental degradation. Data were collected through a questionnaire survey administered to 399 respondents drawn from a population of 220,600 in Eket Local Government Area, a region significantly impacted by resource-based conflicts. The data were analyzed using Pearson’s product-moment correlation to test the formulated hypotheses. Findings reveal that economic marginalization does not exhibit a statistically significant relationship with political instability, while environmental degradation demonstrates a strong positive correlation. The results suggest that environmental deterioration linked to resource extraction serves as a major catalyst for political unrest, surpassing economic inequality in its influence. The study underscores the importance of sustainable resource governance and environmental protection as vital tools for promoting peace and stability in Nigeria. It contributes to a broader understanding of how resource exploitation and environmental neglect intertwine with political dynamics, providing useful insights for policymakers and stakeholders.

title: Credit Availability, Intergenerational Interactions and Family Fertility Decisions
affiliations: Jinan University and Jinan University

detail.title: Credit Availability, Intergenerational Interactions and Family Fertility Decisions
detail.abstract: This study examines the impact of household credit accessibility on fertility decisions within the context of low fertility rates, delayed retirement policies, and complex intergenerational interactions. Using three waves (2018–2022) of panel data from the China Family Panel Studies, we employ a fixed-effects Poisson regression model and an instrumental variable approach to identify the nonlinear relationship between household credit and fertility rates. Furthermore, we develop an overlapping generations model with endogenous credit supply, and classify intergenerational interactions into four distinct patterns based on transfer direction to examine the underlying transmission mechanisms. Key findings reveal that: (1) Credit expansion exhibits an ​​inverted U-shaped effect​​ on fertility, with its marginal impact being highly heterogeneous and dependent on household structure and intergenerational support patterns; (2) A ​​significant substitution effect​​ exists between elderly care and childrearing due to competition for scarce time resources; (3) Intergenerational economic transfers influence fertility divergently: bequests enhance fertility intentions by alleviating liquidity constraints, whereas educational investments suppress fertility by intensifying the child ‘quantity-quality’ trade-off; (4) Under delayed retirement policies, households relying on time transfers experience a ​​significantly larger decline in fertility than those dependent on economic transfers, highlighting the critical role of care resource competition. To counter fertility's intergenerational resource competition, policies should establish a cost-sharing system that blends short-term credit access for young families with longer-term pension and tax incentives.

detail.abstract:
The Republic Act 11203, known as the Rice Tariffication Law, marked a significant transition in the Philippine rice policy, substituting import quotas with tariffs to bolster food security. A Difference-in-Difference approach was employed, utilizing data from the Family Income and Expenditure Survey spanning 2009 to 2021, to assess the law's immediate impact on poor rural households.

The findings revealed that rural poor households within the treatment group experienced a proportional increase in their real income and overall household expenditures. Such outcomes can be attributed to the reduction in rice retail prices, which improved purchasing power despite the declining farmgate prices, as most rural-poor households are net rice consumers. Nonetheless, the decrease in farmgate prices adversely affected small-scale rice producers, raising concerns regarding the implications of the law for rural livelihoods and agricultural resilience.

In conclusion, the study asserts that the government must sustain the policy's advantages for consumers while simultaneously alleviating the adverse effects on rice producers. Addressing these issues is vital in navigating the challenges encountered in agricultural trade policy during economic transition. Furthermore, this study provides empirical evidence on the immediate effects of trade liberalization on food security and the rural economy in Asia.

detail.abstract: This study investigates the lack of structured economics and financial literacy education in the CBSE secondary curriculum and its impact on student preparedness for senior school economics. Existing literature and curriculum reviews suggest that economics is introduced late and treated primarily as a theoretical subject, in contrast to disciplines such as science that receive extensive experiential support. To examine how this disparity affects students, the study employs a mixed methods approach that includes a survey of more than sixty students across Grades 10 to 12, along with semi structured interviews with students and an expert educator. Survey findings reveal limited early exposure to workshops, internships, and applied learning in economics, with participation rates significantly lower than those in science based subjects. Grade wise analysis shows only marginal increases in exposure over time, while correlation results indicate that opportunities are not systematically connected to seniority. Interview insights further highlight a lack of guidance, minimal real world engagement, and a steep learning curve upon entering Grade 11. The study concludes that the CBSE framework provides inadequate preparation for students pursuing economics, resulting in uneven academic readiness and restricted understanding of economic concepts. It calls for earlier introduction of economic reasoning, strengthened financial literacy modules, and greater institutional support for practical learning within the secondary school system.

title: Employment Impact Analysis: US Tariff Hike and EU Employment

detail.title: Employment Impact Analysis: US Tariff Hike and EU Employment
detail.abstract: This section reports an empirical demonstration (using synthetic-constructed employment variable) analyzing whether the US tariff hikes from 2018 affected employment in EU reporting countries. The dataset is synthetic for demonstration; replace with real merged data for final policy conclusions. This paper examines the impact of U.S. tariff hikes on employment patterns across European Union (EU) member states. Using a constructed dataset combining trade flows, tariff schedules, and macroeconomic indicators, the analysis applies a simple linear regression framework to evaluate how sectors and countries exposed to higher U.S. tariffs experienced changes in employment. Results indicate that U.S. tariffs generated significant disruptions in certain manufacturing sectors within the EU, particularly those oriented toward U.S. markets such as steel, aluminum, and automotive industries. However, the magnitude of employment effects varied widely across member states depending on export specialization and domestic labor policies. Graphical evidence shows both short-term employment contractions and longer-term adjustments. While EU-wide employment remained relatively stable, the findings highlight regional vulnerabilities and underscore the need for coordinated EU responses to trade shocks.

title: Experiencing Carbon Pricing
affiliations: Georgia State University, University of Wyoming, University of Miami, University of Alabama and Georgia State University

detail.title: Experiencing Carbon Pricing
detail.abstract:
Many socially desirable policies are not implemented because of their ex-ante unpopularity, but this unpopularity may be overcome through experience with the policy. In this paper, we examine how opposition to carbon pricing in the state of Washington turned into support after voters experienced a cap-and-trade policy with revenues earmarked for environmental purposes – "cap-and-invest." Analyzing voting behavior at the census block group level, we observe that support varies by political affiliation as expected, but experience consistently increases support across the board. Using a proprietary survey, we further show that the increase in support among voters in Washington state is specific to the cap-and invest policy they experienced; support for carbon pricing or climate policies more generally remained unchanged.

title: Well-Conditioned Covariance Estimation via Bayesian Eigenvalue Regularization
affiliations: Ghent University, , Vrije Universiteit Brussel (VUB) and

detail.title: Well-Conditioned Covariance Estimation via Bayesian Eigenvalue Regularization

declarations.funderStatement: We gratefully acknowledge financial support from the Flemish Science Foundation (S006721N).

detail.abstract: Covariance matrices and their inverses are central to many statistical applications. Traditional estimators are often ill-conditioned or nearly singular due to overly dispersed eigenvalues. We propose an explicit eigenvalue regularization approach for a broad class of covariance estimators. Our method builds on Bayes' theorem and uses a flexible prior that guarantees positive semi-definiteness. A data-driven procedure selects the optimal degree of regularization, under which insights can be drawn regarding its behavior. The resulting estimators are well-conditioned, available in closed-form and outperform well-known (non-)linear shrinkage benchmarks in terms of accurateness. We validate its practical relevance in an empirical application to minimum-variance portfolios. Our approach significantly reduces out-of-sample variances and portfolio turnover levels.

title: In-situ Upgrading or Population Relocation? Direct Impacts and Spatial Spillovers of Slum Renewal Policies
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley - Haas School of Business, UC Berkeley, New York University (NYU) and Wake Forest University

detail.title: In-situ Upgrading or Population Relocation? Direct Impacts and Spatial Spillovers of Slum Renewal Policies
detail.abstract:
Slums are widely viewed as disadvantaged areas characterized by substandard housing and negative neighborhood spillovers that constrain local economic development. Governments typically respond with one of two place-based interventions: (a) in-situ upgrading that improves infrastructure and housing conditions within existing settlements, or (b) relocation of slum households to formal housing elsewhere in the city, freeing valuable urban land for alternative uses. We compare the direct effects and local spatial spillovers of these two approaches in Chile. We construct a 20-year national panel of slum polygons that integrates satellite imagery, census microdata, construction permits, administrative records, crime reports, and property-tax data. Using this dataset, we estimate how each policy affects the physical characteristics of slums and adjacent areas, and whether either intervention shifts the socioeconomic composition of residents. Our empirical strategy relies on Synthetic Difference-in-Differences for causal identification. We find that both policies reduce the share of land devoted to housing within the original slum perimeter — in-situ upgrading by reallocating land toward neighborhood infrastructure, and population relocation by reducing the number of slum households and housing structures. However, only in-situ upgrading generates durable improvements in housing quality and the socioeconomic status of residents. In addition, upgrading produces substantial positive spillovers in nearby neighborhoods, increasing formal housing investment and reducing crime. Moreover, administrative cost data show that in-situ upgrading is roughly one-third less expensive per household than population relocation, underscoring its greater cost-effectiveness.

title: Monthly Earnings Volatility and Household Pooling

detail.title: Monthly Earnings Volatility and Household Pooling
detail.abstract:
This paper examines monthly earnings volatility and its transmission to household earnings volatility using Norwegian data on the universe of monthly pay histories. We document substantial month-to-month earnings changes: within a job, while over one-quarter of months have no earnings changes, another quarter have at least a 23% change. Accounting for multiple jobs and non-employment increases volatility, while aggregating to households reduces volatility by 12-35%. Event studies around job loss and couple formation, along with decomposition and bounding exercises, show that most of this decline reflects pooling effects rather than sorting or responses to shocks.

This study sequentially evaluates a soft-skills course implemented in Ugandan and Kenyan primary schools that replaced academic review time with lessons on goal-setting and related skills as students prepared for high-stakes primary school-leaving exams. An exploratory evaluation in Uganda provided evidence of positive impacts on girls’ test scores. A confirmatory evaluation in Kenya found that the course led to improvements in self-reported soft skills, especially among girls, although no gains in test scores. The study illustrates the utility of sequential evaluation, with exploratory analysis to identify promising hypotheses, followed by out-of-sample testing, as a tool to uncover heterogeneous effects.

title: The Future of Wealth Management in the Era of Generational Wealth Transfer: The Guided Autonomy Framework
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Future of Wealth Management in the Era of Generational Wealth Transfer: The Guided Autonomy Framework
detail.abstract: The wealth management industry faces unprecedented transformation driven by artificial intelligence adoption, an unprecedented amount of intergenerational wealth transfer to younger generations, sustainable investing imperatives, and margin compression from passive investment vehicles. Despite ever-rising global financial wealth, traditional advisory models confront mounting pressures from technological innovation, demographic shifts, and evolving investment paradigms. This paper develops an integrated conceptual framework, the "guided autonomy paradigm", that synthesizes extensions of Modern Portfolio Theory with behavioral finance insights, causal inference methodologies, and dynamic risk management approaches. Through systematic literature review and analysis of industry reports, we demonstrate how this framework transcends the dichotomy between robo-advisors and traditional advisors by positioning sophisticated clients as active portfolio architects supported by advanced analytics and expert guidance. Our analysis reveals strategic heterogeneity rather than convergence: democratization serving mass affluent clients via hybrid models, , and guided autonomy for sophisticated professionals and high-net-worth families. Success requires integration of seven capabilities: quantitative expertise, domain knowledge capture, technology infrastructure, regulatory compliance, user experience design, change management, and human capital development. We identify implications for portfolio theory (tax-adjusted optimization integration), behavioral finance (constructive mental accounting), and technology acceptance (requiring transparent causality beyond ease of use). Critical to our framework is addressing the AI transparency challenge through both explainable AI methods for operational transparency and causal inference approaches for strategic decision-making, ensuring both interpretability and scientific rigor in AI-driven financial systems. While direct empirical validation remains limited, our framework provides actionable guidance for strategic positioning, technology investment priorities including causal inference engines for tactical asset allocation processes, and client experience design in an era of profound industry transformation.

title: Round Bidding in Auctions
affiliations: University of Groningen, Dartmouth College and University of Groningen

detail.title: Round Bidding in Auctions
detail.abstract:
Our analysis of novel data from hundreds of thousands of online auctions on a large platform operating in the Netherlands uncovers a tendency to bid round numbers. Round winning bids are higher than average for a given item and are eschewed by bidders as they gain experience. These findings lead us to hypothesize that, rather than delivering a strategic benefit (say, adding salience to a jump bid), round bidding is a symptom of a behavioral bias. We construct a structural model of behavioral bidding in auctions, estimated for each of a subsample of the most frequently auctioned items. Our median estimate is that 21% of bidders are prone to round-number bias, reducing their expected surplus by nearly 10%.

title: Distribution Agreements as Monopolisation: Insights from the United States versus Google Case

detail.title: Distribution Agreements as Monopolisation: Insights from the United States versus Google Case
detail.abstract:
The paper discusses the groundbreaking opinion delivered last summer by Judge Amit P. Mehta of the United States District Court for the District of Columbia in the United States et al. v. Google LLC case («Google Search»). This decision found Google liable for monopolisation in the relevant product markets of general search services and general search text advertising in the Us in breach of Section 2 of the Sherman Act and the legal framework established in the renowned case against Microsoft in the early 2000s.

The ruling raises several interesting questions about fair competition and duty to deal, the role of data as a consolidating market strategy and as a barrier to entry for rivals, and the right balance between innovation, competition, and consumer choices. The opinion is particularly significant because Judge Mehta found that exclusive distribution agreements, usually scrutinised from the perspective of cartel collusion, can be a

means to maintaining monopoly power and, despite declaring Google liable, declined to impose sanctions. The case recently returned to the spotlight due to the ongoing remedies trial, where the Us Department of Justice is arguing in favour of sweeping measures, including a possible breakup of Google. The final decision is expected this summer.

title: The Role of Constitutional Courts in Protecting Democratic Rights: A Comparative Analysis of the US, Germany and France
affiliations: , University of Management and Technology, Sialkot and University of the Punjab (PU) - Punjab University Law College

detail.title: The Role of Constitutional Courts in Protecting Democratic Rights: A Comparative Analysis of the US, Germany and France
detail.abstract: The main role of constitutional courts therefore is to defend democracy as well as the rights of citizens. This paper gives a brief comparative analysis of the constitutional courts of a selected trilateral nation, namely United States of America, Germany and France. Both courts feature in their approaches in line with their respective country's legal frameworks as well as political systems. The United States Supreme Court, also known as SCOTUS, applies judicial precedents and exercises judical review over Constitution interpretations and has impacting decisions regarding civil rights, women's rights, and campaign finance. Germany's Federal Constitutional Court concentrates on constitutional issues such as the rights of the German citizens and conforming of the nation's laws to European Union requirements. Some of its cases involve question related to free speech, sovereignty, and privacy, particularly in the context of the Internets impact. Unlike France's Constitutional Council, it has a more restricted power-that of checking legislation before it is implemented, to see if it conforms to the Constitution. It makes decisions concerning important issues of secularism and environmentalism as well as issues of social justice. The article also provides a contrast between these courts revealing their guarding role of democracy as well as their flexibility in facing such threats as political interference, globalisation and the contemporary issues including climate change and privacy. The findings actually show how constitutional courts are very crucial especially in continuing to translate the rule of law and the democratization of the society in various legal arenas.

title: Electoral Margins and Political Competition
affiliations: University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) and UCLA Anderson School of Management

detail.title: Electoral Margins and Political Competition
detail.abstract:
In this paper, we argue that recent trends in party seat margins and election vote margins result from structural changes in the nature of US political competition. We assemble a comprehensive database of electoral results for the House, Senate and presidential contests, from the 19th century until today. Seat margins declined in the recent period, so the margins of control of the House, Senate, and Electoral College by either party have become smaller. However, this was not accompanied by a decline in the margins of victory at the constituency level. We propose a model of electoral competition with multiple districts that can rationalize these trends. We show theoretically that an increase in politicians’ information about voter preferences, together with the growing nationalization of politics, can account for the decrease in seat margins and the concurrent stability in vote margins. As implied by the model, we document that campaign contributions received by House and Senate candidates are increasingly concentrated in a dwindling set of swing constituencies.

title: Examining the Effect of Cannabis Legalization on Youth Cannabis Use: Evidence on the Importance of Enforcing Retailer Compliance
affiliations: William Paterson University, George Mason University and University of Southern California - Schaeffer Center for Health Policy  and Economics

detail.title: Examining the Effect of Cannabis Legalization on Youth Cannabis Use: Evidence on the Importance of Enforcing Retailer Compliance
detail.abstract:
Studies show that U.S. state cannabis legalization has increased adult cannabis use, but the effects on youth use are mixed. This study considers whether omission of enforcement of the minimum legal sales age (MLSA) might help explain prior mixed findings. We combine biennial survey data for 6th, 8th, 10th, and 12th grade students from the 2010-2023 Washington Healthy Youth Survey with administrative data on premise and compliance checks from the Washington State Liquor and Cannabis Board (WSLCB). Premise checks educate retailers on any potential violations but do not involve penalties or fines. Compliance checks, on the other hand, involve increasing penalties imposed on retailers if they are found to be noncompliant with sales to minors. We use difference-in-differences (DID) methods that are robust to a staggered policy rollout with dynamic and heterogeneous treatment effects and assess impacts of both types of inspections on past month cannabis use. We conduct a series of sensitivity and robustness checks of the impact of both types of inspections based on student’s grade, length of time since inspection, inclusion of alcohol/tobacco retail compliance checks, and alternative measures of cannabis use. Our research suggests that the implementation of regular random compliance checks with stiff penalties on retailers for noncompliance may help reduce the influence of legal markets on youth use. Unobserved heterogeneity within and across states in the enforcement of MLSAs may contribute to mixed findings of the impact of legalization on youth cannabis use.
