title: The Role of Insurers in Health Care Spending and Production: Evidence from Utah
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley, University of Ottawa, University of California, Berkeley - Haas School of Business and Ohio State University

detail.title: The Role of Insurers in Health Care Spending and Production: Evidence from Utah
detail.abstract:
Private health insurers play a central role in determining the cost and quantity of health care in the United States. Despite this centrality, there has been limited empirical work studying how insurers differentially affect spending and consumption, especially for expensive and pervasive chronic conditions. We use hundreds of natural experiments involving employers switching their primary health insurer, together with a movers design, to estimate these causal effects. We find meaningful differences in total cost and prices for medical and pharmaceutical spending. Within-person changes in spending caused by forced reassignment across pairs of insurers, holding fixed plan generosity, are as large as 30% of total medical spending and 37% of drug spending. We also find substantial dispersion in insurer causal effects on health care spending and quantities for patients with diabetes, hypertension, and other chronic conditions. We find strong evidence for drug offsets as insurers who causally increase drug utilization also reduce medical costs and quantities overall and by condition. Finally, we find that employers do not select plans that reduce costs for their employees based on the match between employee conditions and estimated plan treatment effects, leaving significant cost savings on the table.

title: Lenin's Shadow on the Istanbul Convention: The Legacy of Communism and Attitudes Toward Violence Against Women in Europe
affiliations: Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge - Department of Economics and Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge

detail.title: Lenin's Shadow on the Istanbul Convention: The Legacy of Communism and Attitudes Toward Violence Against Women in Europe
detail.abstract:
The Istanbul Convention is an international treaty aimed at protecting women against violence. We employ survey datasets and investigate its effect on attitudes toward violence against women in Europe. Using difference-in-differences models we compare individuals in countries that signed and ratified the Convention with those in countries that signed but either never ratified or did so after the surveys were fielded. Entry into the Convention significantly reduced the likelihood that lower-educated individuals view violence against women as acceptable, but only in countries outside the former Eastern Bloc. In former Eastern Bloc countries, the Convention affected attitudes only among younger less-educated individuals who had limited exposure to communism—those who were no older than teenagers when the Soviet Union collapsed in 1990. We show that younger cohorts in these countries tend to hold more individualistic and less pro-government attitudes and express greater trust in the courts and the justice system than older individuals. Finally, we find no effect of the Convention on attitudes toward other forms of norm-violating behavior, such as tax evasion, bribery, fare evasion, or drug use. These results indicate that the Convention had a targeted impact, and that its influence on shaping preferences depends on the broader cultural context which is itself shaped by institutions.

title: The State Pension Age and Inequality in Old-age Social Security Wealth in the Netherlands
affiliations: Utrecht University and University of Southern California - Center for Economic and Social Research (CESR)

detail.title: The State Pension Age and Inequality in Old-age Social Security Wealth in the Netherlands
detail.abstract:
Since the early 2010s, the state pension age (SPA) is one of the main public policy instruments in the Netherlands for inducing people to postpone retirement. The SPA has gradually increased from 65 years in 2012 to 66 years and 4 months in 2021. In the context of the Dutch old-age social security system, an increase in the SPA is hypothesized to decrease the retirement probability and to increase inequality in pension benefits entitlements. Empirical support for the two hypotheses is found with data on individuals aged 55–69 over the period 2011-2021. Inequality in old-age social security wealth has increased after 2015 for non-retirees. However, the findings do not support that this increase is because of the SPA increase.

title: Antitrust Enforcement in Labor Markets
affiliations: University of Rochester

detail.title: Antitrust Enforcement in Labor Markets
detail.abstract:
Until recently, antitrust laws were rarely enforced in labor markets. Although the existence of labor market power has long been recognized, evidence only recently emerged that such market power regularly arises from sources that are actionable under antitrust law. Since 2010, antitrust agencies have substantially increased labor market enforcement actions. However, many questions relevant to enforcement remain unanswered, such as how to conduct market definition for labor markets, and how best to incorporate concentration into models of the labor market. This article reviews how antitrust is beginning to be used in labor markets, the evidence for and against its use, and the remaining evidence gaps standing in the way of more effective use.

title: Skill-Based Migration Cost Disparities, Aggregate Productivity, and Regional Income Inequality

detail.title: Skill-Based Migration Cost Disparities, Aggregate Productivity, and Regional Income Inequality

declarations.funderStatement: Financial support from CUHK Research Postgraduate Student Grants for Overseas Academic Activities is gratefully acknowledged.

detail.abstract: This paper evaluates the efficiency of relatively cost-effective and implementable policies aiming at reducing migration costs for low-skilled workers. Motivating facts from China reveal higher average migration costs for low-skilled workers compared to their high-skilled counterparts. Using a model that incorporates skill-based migration cost disparities and worker sorting, I estimate potential gains from migration cost reduction. While eliminating all migration barriers yields substantial benefits in total output, reducing low-skilled workers' migration costs to high-skilled levels alone also generates remarkable gains, with total productivity increasing by 12.9%. These aggregate productivity gains mask significant heterogeneity, and counterfactual analyses reveal that reduced migration costs marginally exacerbate regional income inequality, which might suggest the persistent role of educational and amenity disparities.

title: Economics of Climate Attitudes in Oil-rich Regions
affiliations: Bank of Finland

detail.title: Economics of Climate Attitudes in Oil-rich Regions

publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Finland Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: The study aims to identify economic measures that enhance support for climate change mitigation, particularly in oil-rich communities. Using US county-level data, the research shows that the presence of oil reserves is negatively associated with the attribution of human influence to climate change and policies regulating CO2 emissions. Interestingly, a high current dependence on mineral extraction is associated with greater support for climate policies, while a decline in the mining-income share in oil-rich regions does not correlate with increased support for climate action, underpinning our hypothesis of persistence of climate attitudes. This suggests that a region’s current economic dependence on mining is not necessarily an obstacle to greater action to mitigate human impacts on climate. While evidence on the impact of extreme weather events on climate attitudes is mixed, we also present evidence that regional economic losses from natural disasters and rising home insurance costs may help convince people of the need for climate policy measures.

title: Technopolitics and Sociomaterial Power in International Organisations' Futuring Practices for Digital Transformation of Education

detail.title: Technopolitics and Sociomaterial Power in International Organisations' Futuring Practices for Digital Transformation of Education

detail.abstract: This paper inquires into how international organisations (IOs) have operated global events, which kinds of policy networks and development aid have influenced policy initiatives of IOs’ divisions, and how, in their post-COVID digital transformation of education initiatives. This examination aims at illuminating the historical and technopolitical relations underlying the IOs’ global futuring practices. The IOs’ contemporary policy practices resonate with the history of international development, where the post-war powerful countries and institutions utilised their social and material power to realise the neoliberal globalisation project. What has been shifting in this global power dynamics is the ascendancy of techno-entrepreneurs who take positions in government to drive the digital transformation of education and the economy, leveraging their networks with IOs and the involvement of big tech, including Microsoft and the Gates Foundation. Meanwhile, the presence of Chinese technology companies has also been salient in UNESCO and the World Bank's partnerships and events. The US government has continued to exercise its power as the top donor with voting power at the OECD and the World Bank, whereas China has expanded its global influence through its funding to UNESCO and the World Bank, and through expanded networks in African countries enabled by the partnership activities of these two organisations. What seems to be repeated in IOs’ digital transformation initiatives is the dependence of these countries on international forces in the development of their national education systems in the context of digitalisation. Thus, this paper explores how these disproportionate international and business forces have influenced the sociomaterial futuring practices of international organisations (IOs) through money, networks, and events within the digital transformation of education movement.

title: Joint Child Custody and Interstate Migration
affiliations: Northwestern University, , University of Copenhagen, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago and Stanford University

detail.title: Joint Child Custody and Interstate Migration
detail.abstract:
Joint custody following divorce is widespread, but implementation is costly when individuals live in different states and so affects interstate mobility. Migration of separated fathers has fallen significantly more than that of married fathers. We show the causal effect of joint custody using two strategies. First, we survey separated parents to elicit beliefs about the likelihood of interstate moves. Second, we use the staggered adoption of joint custody laws across US states, and show a reduction in actual migration of 11 percentage points for fathers. For mothers, there is no impact on mobility but suggestive evidence of beneficial labor market outcomes.

title: On Productivity and Distortions across Countries

detail.title: On Productivity and Distortions across Countries
detail.abstract:
I examine the empirical properties of firm-level productivity and distortions across countries using the newly released World Bank Enterprise Surveys (WBES). Using a standard framework of production heterogeneity, I show that the gap in productivity and distortions between high and low productivity firms is larger in developing countries, generating large aggregate productivity losses from misallocation. A key empirical property of distortions in developing countries is that they systematically weaken the relationship between firm size and firm productivity. I exploit a unique feature of the WBES data to document which specific aspects of the economic environment faced by firms, such as financial constraints, regulation, corruption, and weak infrastructure, are consistent with the empirical pattern of distortions across countries.

We found that SSW declined for all groups after the social security reforms, which aimed to reduce generosity; however, the size of the negative impact was larger for richer individuals. These results indicate that a series of recent social security reforms have reduced inequality in SSW.

title: The Algorithmic Antitrust Paradox: Challenging Algorithmic Tacit Collusion Under Section 1
affiliations: Yale University

detail.title: The Algorithmic Antitrust Paradox: Challenging Algorithmic Tacit Collusion Under Section 1
detail.abstract:
When algorithms collude instead of CEOs, does antitrust law have an answer? Scholars have in unison lamented the so-called liability gap, dismissing algorithmic tacit collusion as lacking an agreement between competitors and thereby evading the watchful eye of Section 1 of the Sherman Act.

This Article advances a novel legal interpretation under which algorithmic tacit collusion necessarily falls within the Sherman Act’s reach. Algorithmic pricing disrupts the very assumptions on which the doctrine of tacit collusion rests. Algorithms—by making observable and intelligible the strategic logic underlying firms’ pricing decisions—solve the problems of proof and remedy that justify treating tacit collusion as beyond Section 1’s reach. If the purpose of the Sherman Act is, as courts have long affirmed, to safeguard the competitive process, then its doctrines must be construed with sufficient flexibility to address any anticompetitive coordination which is both demonstrable and remediable.

The presumption that algorithmic tacit collusion fails to constitute concerted action implies an internally inconsistent view of concerted action as it ought to be understood for the unique purposes of the Sherman Act. This Article terms that contradiction the algorithmic antitrust paradox, refutes it, and offers practical recommendations for resolving it.

title: When Absence Speaks: Modeling Hidden Technological Complexity Through Bayesian Epistemic Reconstruction
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: When Absence Speaks: Modeling Hidden Technological Complexity Through Bayesian Epistemic Reconstruction
detail.abstract: The Deep Signal Reconstruction (DSR) experiment investigates the epistemic limits of technological inference under severe data-loss conditions. Rather than reconstructing absolute prehistory, it models the boundary of recoverability — where genuine innovation could exist yet remain undetectable. Using harmonized archaeological, environmental, and genetic proxies, the model implements a taphonomic survival function ps(m,e,Δt) to estimate evidence persistence across materials and environments. This decay surface constrains a Bayesian inference of the latent innovation rate R(t), producing posterior distributions that quantify how innovation intensity can be inferred despite fragmentary records. Phase I establishes survival likelihoods and global coverage; Phase II recovers R(t) trajectories across 500-year bins; Phase III maps a detectability atlas linking regional preservation dynamics to systemic innovation probability. Results reveal a structured frontier between observable and lost complexity—an epistemic horizon quantifying not what happened, but what can still be known.

title: Recovery Housing Works: Outcomes from a Level II MAT-Compatible Recovery Housing Model Serving Justice-Involved Individuals

detail.title: Recovery Housing Works: Outcomes from a Level II MAT-Compatible Recovery Housing Model Serving Justice-Involved Individuals

keywords.keywords: 1.Recovery housing2.Criminal Justice3.Medication for opioid use disorder (MOUD)4.MAT Housing5.Recovery capital (REC-CAP)6.Drug Court and Department of Corrections7.Substance Use Disorder

detail.abstract: The recovery housing program operates and owns seven accredited MAT homes serving justice-involved adults referred by the Drug Court and the Department of Corrections (DOC). The program emphasizes trauma-informed care, no rapid-exit policies, and prohibits resident “vote-outs.” Because all participants were justice-involved at entry, the realistic alternative to remaining in housing was the possibility of losing drug court benefits or returning to jail or prison for relapse or non-compliance. Within this high-risk context, the longer lengths of stay observed in this cohort represent extended periods in the community in lieu of incarceration, underscoring the preventive impact of a non-punitive, stabilization-first recovery housing model. The study evaluated early exits, length of stay (LOS), completion/active status, employment change, and age patterns using assessments at ~0, 45, and 90 days (REC-CAP).10, 12. Mean LOS was ~141 days (median ~97), and among residents engaged beyond 30 days the mean LOS was 181 days. Using LOS ≥60 days as a priori “engagement success,” retention was strongest among older adults, while residents <25 showed the weakest ≥60-day retention.5, 6 REC-CAP Social Capital & Meaningful Activities scores skewed high (94% scoring 4–5 on a 5-point scale across 394 responses), indicating substantial perceived connection and purposeful activity during residence. Uniquely, this large single-system cohort spans seven houses run by one foundation under consistent policies, with data collected by two trained staff—reducing site-level variability common in multi-operator studies. In this cohort, Drug Court participants achieved retention patterns similar to DOC participants, supporting the role of non-punitive, MAT-compatible housing in maintaining community placement across justice-system categories

title: Taxing Mobile Money: Theory and Evidence
affiliations: , International Monetary Fund (IMF) - Fiscal Affairs Department, Université d'Auvergne - Clermont 1, Centre d'Etudes et de Recherches sur le Developpement International (CERDI), Students and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Taxing Mobile Money: Theory and Evidence
detail.abstract: Mobile money has become a central digital alternative to traditional banking in developing countries, yet several African governments have introduced taxes on mobile money transactions. We develop a model that characterizes how such taxes affect payment choices and generate excess burden. The model predicts that taxation reduces mobile money use, with elasticities shaped by access to substitutes and transaction costs: banked users substitute into formal alternatives, while unbanked users face higher effective costs, making the tax regressive. Taxation also induces substitution into cash, raising informality. We empirically test these predictions using cross-country survey data and novel transaction-level data from Cameroon, the Central African Republic, and Mali. Results show sharp declines in mobile money usage, with stronger responses among the banked. Unbanked and rural users bear a disproportionate burden. We use the empirical estimates to gauge the excess burden of the tax, which we quantify at 35% of revenue - highlighting its significant efficiency cost alongside its regressive impact.

title: The Performance of Randomly Constructed Equal-Weighted Portfolios: A Backtesting Study Against the S&P 500 with Survivorship Bias

detail.title: The Performance of Randomly Constructed Equal-Weighted Portfolios: A Backtesting Study Against the S&P 500 with Survivorship Bias
detail.abstract: This study backtested the performance of randomly constructed equal-weighted portfolios against a market benchmark-S&P 500 ETF (SPY). Based on 20 years of historical data, a total of 8000 portfolios were simulated. The stocks were randomly selected from the current S&P 500 constituent list. The portfolios performance-return, risk, and Sharpe ratio-was calculated and compared with the benchmark. The initial results found that the randomly generated portfolios outperformed the benchmark. To justify this finding, two key factors were identified and analyzed. The primary factor is survivorship bias, which was caused by the exclusion of underperforming stocks-stocks delisted from the S&P 500 index but still traded ("removed stocks") and stocks delisted completely from the market and no longer traded ("defunct stocks"). By only including the long-term survivors in the simulation, the portfolio performance was artificially inflated. Further analysis was conducted considering both the removed and the defunct stocks, and the results showed that this bias had a significant impact on the portfolio performance. The other factor is the equal-weighted strategy employed in the simulation, which is different from the capitalization-weighted strategy used by the benchmark. An equal-weighted strategy increases portfolio's exposure to smaller-capitalization stocks, which have historically delivered higher average returns. These findings showed that the observed "outperformance" of these random portfolios does not contradict market efficiency, but instead a direct result of survivorship bias, weighting strategy, and other potential methodological limitations employed in the study.

This working paper presents a two-year field study of a two-family property in Brooklyn, New York, managed by RLB Realty Group between 2023 and 2025. What began as a modest post-estate management assignment evolved into a deeper exploration of procedural illiteracy, administrative paralysis, and the structural fragility of small-building ownership within New York City’s housing ecosystem.

It documents how fragmented communication, incomplete recordkeeping, and reactive regulatory oversight collectively erode housing stability and accountability.

Drawing upon case documentation, vendor systems, and agency correspondence, the study proposes a model for compliance modernization and owner-support infrastructure grounded in digital governance, administrative fluency, and equitable policy design.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a conceptual framework that unifies the multiple roles of central banks in providing liquidity to financial markets. It distinguishes three operational modescomplementary, substitutional, and exit-each defined by the degree of market dysfunction, systemic risk, and erosion of peer discipline. Building on both classical doctrines (Bagehot, Thornton) and modern institutional practice (BIS, ECB, BoE), the framework offers a structured continuum between market-based and central bank liquidity. It aims to replace discretionary crisis management with rule-based principles anchored in observable indicators such as interbank spreads, repo-market volumes, and collateral haircuts. Comparative analysis of the Federal Reserve, European Central Bank, Bank of England, and Banco Central de Chile demonstrates the framework's applicability across advanced and emerging markets. The paper concludes that structured, conditional liquidity provision enhances credibility, preserves market discipline, and strengthens the resilience of monetary frameworks.

title: Will the Global Minimum Tax Hurt Developing Countries?
affiliations: University of Munich - Seminar for Economic Policy, Okayama University and Erasmus School of Economics

detail.title: Will the Global Minimum Tax Hurt Developing Countries?
detail.abstract: We study the effects that the introduction of the Global Minimum Tax (GMT) has from the perspective of developing countries. Our model features two asymmetric host countries for FDI that compete with each other for the location of multinational firms, and simultaneously fight profit shifting to a tax haven. The developing country has the weaker enforcement technology to fight profit shifting; it therefore loses more revenue from profit shifting, but also becomes a more attractive location for multinationals. The GMT reduces both profit shifting and the tax-avoidance advantage of the developing country. If tax competition for real investment is sufficiently severe, the introduction of the GMT reduces tax rates and tax revenues in the developing country while tax revenues in the developed country rise. Our results help explaining the opposition of developing countries to the GMT.

title: The End of Consumer Surplus: Reconstructing Welfare Economics under the Range-Clearing Theory

detail.title: The End of Consumer Surplus: Reconstructing Welfare Economics under the Range-Clearing Theory
detail.abstract: The concept of consumer surplus serves as a foundational pillar of modern neoclassical welfare economics, providing the quantitative basis for a vast range of interventionist policies. This paper challenges this entire edifice at its epistemological root. We argue that the traditional calculation of consumer surplus is predicated on the unrealistic assumption of "point equilibrium," where both subjective valuation and market prices are treated as precise, single-valued points. We introduce a more realistic microfoundation, termed "range-clearing," which posits that subjective value is a range, not a point, and that market transactions clear within a zone of overlapping value ranges. Under this new framework, we demonstrate that consumer surplus, as traditionally conceived, is revealed to be a theoretical chimera—fundamentally unmeasurable, interpersonally incomparable, and thus scientifically incoherent. This finding triggers a cascading collapse of the policies that depend on its calculation, such as Pigouvian taxation and antitrust regulation, exposing them not as scientific applications of welfare maximization, but as arbitrary acts of political value imposition. We conclude by calling for a paradigm shift in economics: a move away from the "fatal conceit" of the economist as a social engineer calculating illusory welfare aggregates, and a return to the more humble, yet more vital, mission of analyzing the institutional rules that make a free and prosperous social order possible.

title: Big Hassle on the Decarbonization Frontier
affiliations: University of Lausanne - Faculty of Business and Economics (HEC Lausanne), Carleton University - Department of Economics, University of Ottawa - Graduate School of Public and International Affairs and Hitotsubashi University

detail.title: Big Hassle on the Decarbonization Frontier
detail.abstract: We introduce the concept of marginal hassle cost (MHC)–the opportunity cost of time required to complete burdensome administrative tasks–as a measure of non-pecuniary transaction costs. We then propose an experimental procedure to elicit the MHC and validate the approach through a large-scale field experiment on heat pump adoption in Canada. On average, the MHC is equal to respondents’ wage rate, but it exhibits substantial individual heterogeneity and is only weakly correlated with wages. MHCs are systematically higher for human-assisted than for computer-assisted tasks. Our findings highlight that total hassle costs are economically significant and deter participation in government programs aimed at decarbonization.

title: Digital News Consumption: Evidence from Smartphone Content in the 2024 US Elections
affiliations: Northwestern University - Kellogg School of Management, Tel Aviv University, Bocconi University, Tel Aviv University and University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign

detail.title: Digital News Consumption: Evidence from Smartphone Content in the 2024 US Elections
detail.abstract: Using novel smartphone content data, we document that exposure to election-related content for the median American is arguably small. Moreover, exposure rarely comes from news apps and instead mostly occurs through non-traditional sources, such as social media and video apps. While the median was low, we find substantial heterogeneity: individuals in the 90th percentile consume over 50 times the content of those in the 10th percentile. A variance decomposition shows that apps play a role in driving exposure gaps (e.g., X versus Facebook), but individual characteristics (e.g., living in a swing state) are the dominant drivers of election-related exposure.

title: An Evolutionary Game-Theoretic Reformulation of the Lux--Marchesi Model of Financial Markets
affiliations: Heriot-Watt University and Rajamangala University of Technology Suvarnabhumi

detail.title: An Evolutionary Game-Theoretic Reformulation of the Lux--Marchesi Model of Financial Markets
detail.abstract: This paper reformulates the Lux-Marchesi (LM) asset-pricing model within an evolutionarygame framework to examine how payoff-driven strategy selection shapes market dynamics. We consider three trading types-fundamentalists, optimistic chartists, and pessimistic chartists-whose population shares evolve endogenously through a discrete-time logit-replicator dynamic with mutation. As in LM, prices adjust in response to aggregate excess demand, constructed as a composition-weighted sum of strategy demands, while strategy payoffs are computed from realized trading profits averaged over a finite evaluation window. The resulting coupled price-selection system captures a competition between stabilizing mean-reverting forces (fundamental trading) and destabilizing directional forces (chartist trading), generating distinct market regimes. To provide analytical insight, we study a reduced two-strategy specification and characterize the stability of boundary regimes, as well as the conditions for tipping when the chartist share crosses an interior threshold. Numerical experiments across baseline, stable, bistable, and switching parameterizations demonstrate that endogenous reallocation of trader shares can produce bubbles and crashes, heavy-tailed return distributions, and volatility clustering. Importantly, these stylized facts arise from persistence and switching in the composition dynamics, rather than from imposing non-Gaussian exogenous shocks.

title: The Role of Trade Compliance in Strengthening U.S.–Africa Economic Relations

detail.title: The Role of Trade Compliance in Strengthening U.S.–Africa Economic Relations
detail.abstract: This paper examines the strategic role of trade compliance in strengthening U.S.-Africa economic relations. While the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) has expanded duty-free access to the U.S. market, evolving trade policies and regulatory complexities pose challenges for sustainable engagement. Compliance professionals, particularly those with cross-jurisdictional expertise in African, U.S., and maritime law, are essential to mitigating risks, ensuring lawful and ethical commerce, and fostering transparency. Their work enables U.S. companies to participate in procurement, attract investment, and uphold fair trade practices. By advancing a rules-based trading system, trade compliance contributes to economic diplomacy, competitiveness, and long-term partnership between the United States and Africa. This analysis highlights how compliance frameworks are not merely technical requirements but strategic instruments for building trust, stability, and sustainable growth in international trade.

title: The Quiet Payoff: Mafia Electoral Support and Policy Inaction
affiliations: University of Bologna, University of Bologna, Department of Economics and University of Bologna

detail.title: The Quiet Payoff: Mafia Electoral Support and Policy Inaction
detail.abstract: Organised crime groups often deliver electoral support to politicians, yet how they are rewarded remains unclear. Using data from Sicilian municipalities (1992–2022), we show that narrowly won races by Forza Italia, Silvio Berlusconi’s party, coincide with sharp declines in the reallocation of confiscated mafia assets—but only in mafia-controlled areas. Exploiting historical variation in the mafia’s vote-buying capacity, we find that municipalities with stronger historical ties experience larger post-election declines, exclusively under Berlusconi’s governments. Instrumenting modern support with this proxy further reinforces the plausibly causal evidence that national authorities reward organised crime through policy inaction.

title: Investigating the Asymmetric Impact of Energy on India's Development: Insights from the NARDL Model

detail.title: Investigating the Asymmetric Impact of Energy on India's Development: Insights from the NARDL Model

detail.abstract: Purpose-Energy is a pivotal factor for achieving sustainable development goals for India. This study examines the critical supply-side factors of Energy Generation (EG) in India, with a particular focus on the role of Fiscal Deficit (FD), Transmission Deficit (TD), and per capita GDP (PGDP). Design/Methodology-The study utilizes yearly data from 1970 to 2023 and applies the Nonlinear Autoregressive Distributed Lag (NARDL) model with a structural lag to capture potential asymmetries. A Toda-Yamamoto Granger causality has been applied to observe the causal effect among the regressors and regressand. Findings-It shows asymmetric effects, wherein economic downturns disproportionately lower energy production, underscoring the energy supply's susceptibility to downturns. While FD, TD, and PGDP significantly reduce energy generation by 0.419%, 1.075%, and 0.084%, respectively. Whereas policy shift tends to bring in more fiscal discipline across the centre and state governments. The Toda and Yamamoto Causality found a positive unidirectional relationship from PGDP to EG. The study also discovers a unidirectional relationship from EG to FD, suggesting a mounting fiscal burden on the government due to persisting structural problems in the energy sector. Originality-This is the first study to apply the NARDL framework with a structural break to India's electricity sector from the generation side. It captures asymmetric causal associations and provides novel insights into the interplay of demand-delivery constraints and macroeconomic indicators in determining the energy security of the country. This study offers evidence-based implications for energy reforms in emerging economies. Social Implications-Reliable and sustained electricity supply has far-reaching impacts on poverty alleviation and improved quality of life. Policies aimed at stabilising energy generation and income growth can therefore directly contribute to exclusive and equitable socioeconomic development.

title: Quantifying Conflict Risk in School Zones using Bayesian Extreme Value Theory: A Pre and Post Intervention Study
affiliations: ,  and

detail.title: Quantifying Conflict Risk in School Zones using Bayesian Extreme Value Theory: A Pre and Post Intervention Study
detail.abstract: School zones are the critical safety hotspots where children are frequently exposed to high-risk traffic environments, often without adult supervision. In low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), inadequate pedestrian infrastructure, weak enforcement, and mixed traffic conditions amplify this vulnerability. Although many jurisdictions have introduced low-cost interventions, such as traffic control devices (TCDs), advanced signage, and improved crossing designs to enhance child pedestrian safety, the long-term effectiveness of these measures remains uncertain due to the scarcity and under-reporting of crash data. Traditional crash-based before-after evaluations are limited by low sample sizes, regression-to-the-mean bias, and long observation periods required for statistical significance. This study presents a conflict-based, multi-period evaluation of school-zone interventions using a Bayesian Extreme Value Theory (EVT) framework. High-resolution video data were collected at two urban school sites in India across three distinct periods: Before, Immediately After (After-1), and One Year After (After-2) intervention. Post-Encroachment Time (PET) was employed as the surrogate safety measure to quantify pedestrian-vehicle conflict severity. PET exceedances were modelled using the Peaks-Over-Threshold (POT) method with a Generalized Pareto Distribution (GPD). Bayesian inference via Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) was used to estimate distribution parameters and quantify uncertainty. Crash probability was evaluated across multiple PET thresholds (1.0-0.5 s, in 0.1 s intervals) to capture the gradations in risk severity. Four derived indicators- Odds Ratio, Treatment Effect, Relative Risk Reduction, and Return Level Ratio were estimated to quantify the short- and long-term intervention effectiveness. Results revealed modest but consistent reductions in high-risk conflicts immediately after implementation, particularly at stricter PET thresholds, followed by partial rebound after one year, indicating possible behavioural adaptation or enforcement fatigue. Findings underscore the importance of multi-period, surrogate-based evaluations for evidence-driven school-zone safety management and highlight the need for sustained monitoring and behavioural reinforcement to maintain long-term safety gains.

title: Battery-Electric Buses in Belize City: Performance, Economics and Equity
affiliations: The University of Trinidad and Tobago

detail.title: Battery-Electric Buses in Belize City: Performance, Economics and Equity
detail.abstract: Battery-electric buses are central to urban transport decarbonisation, yet most empirical evidence comes from temperate, high-income cities rather than hot, low-speed Small Island Developing States (SIDS). This paper quantifies the technical, environmental, economic and equity performance of two BYD B87 battery-electric buses on a core corridor in Belize City. Over more than a year of operation and ~87,000 km, we combine 1 Hz telematics, automated passenger counting, charger metering, weather data and financial records in a physics-informed analysis. Energy use clusters around 1.5–1.7 kWh/km, implying a practical range of 120–150 km, roughly 40–60% of the manufacturer rating. Auxiliary (HVAC and hotel) loads account for 50–70% of traction-battery discharge and often exceed propulsion energy. The buses carried ~220,000 passengers, about 70% women, with electricity cost per kilometre ~41% below diesel and a negative operating-phase abatement cost, demonstrating the viability of gender-responsive electric bus deployment in tropical SIDS.

title: Improvement of Regulatory and Legal Provision of Innovative Activity Accounting
affiliations: Scientific and Research Institute of Providing Legal Framework for the Innovative Development of National Academy of Law Sciences of Ukraine

detail.title: Improvement of Regulatory and Legal Provision of Innovative Activity Accounting
detail.abstract:
The scientific paper is dedicated to the problems associated with normative and legal acts of Ukraine that define the framework for establishing an accounting system for innovation activities. The aim of the article is to analyze the national regulatory and legal support for the accounting of innovation activities for its compliance with international standards, as well as to develop practical recommendations for its improvement.

The study compares the provisions of the Law of Ukraine "On Innovation Activity," the Law of Ukraine "On Investment Activity," and the international standard—the Oslo Manual—regarding the definitions and classifications of innovations and innovation activities. This comparison revealed a significant difference in the types of innovations, the degree of novelty of goods and services, and the criteria for recognizing products as innovative. An analysis of the Methodological Provisions for State Statistical Observation on the innovation activity of enterprises showed contradictions in their classifications with national legislation and certain inconsistencies with the Oslo Manual.

It is argued that the identified shortcomings in the basic concepts and classifications within the regulatory framework for innovation activity, which form the basis for establishing the system of financial and statistical accounting, distort accounting data and render them unsuitable for objective evaluation, particularly making them incompatible for comparing countries' innovation development. Amendments are proposed to the definitions of innovations, innovation activities, classifications of innovative processes, products, financing, costs, and other accounting objects by harmonizing them with the methodological guidelines of the Oslo Manual. The expediency of assigning the function of developing methodological recommendations for the accounting of innovation activities to the Ministry of Economy of Ukraine is substantiated.

title: Sampling of Alternatives in MEV Models: Evidence From Migration Aspiration Models with Large Choice Sets
affiliations: École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), , University of Luxemburg and École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL)

detail.title: Sampling of Alternatives in MEV Models: Evidence From Migration Aspiration Models with Large Choice Sets
detail.abstract: Certain case studies require the estimation of discrete choice models with a very large number of alternatives and attributes, which in turn increases the computational cost. This challenge becomes even more pronounced in the family of Multivariate Extreme Value (MEV) models such as the cross-nested logit (CNL) model due to the additional complexity in the model specification. In this study, we investigate the use of sampling of alternatives to make the estimation of MEV models more tractable. Using migration aspiration data, we assess how different sampling protocols and sample sizes approximate the parameters of the full choice set model. Our results show that importance sampling strategies informed by observed choice frequencies outperform random sampling, providing more stable estimates even with small subsets of alternatives. These findings highlight that carefully designed sampling can substantially reduce estimation time without compromising accuracy, thereby making MEV models a practical tool for studying migration destination choice.

title: Understanding the Effects of Government Spending Shocks: It's in the Size as Well
affiliations: Mississippi State University,  and University of Mississippi - Department of Economics

detail.title: Understanding the Effects of Government Spending Shocks: It's in the Size as Well
detail.abstract: This paper investigates whether the macroeconomic effects of government spending depend on the size of the fiscal shock. Using U.S. quarterly data from 1947Q1 to 2015Q4, we estimate state-dependent effects of "large" versus "small" spending shocks via local projections. We find strong evidence of size-dependent fiscal multipliers. Large shocks generate an output multiplier near one by crowding in private consumption, whereas small shocks yield a significantly smaller multiplier. These results suggest an intervention's magnitude is critical to its effectiveness, providing empirical support for a "go big or go home" approach to fiscal stimulus.

title: Pipeline Capacity Turnback: Problems and Options
affiliations: Dr. Momtaz Begum University of Science and Technology and Unaffiliated Author

detail.title: Pipeline Capacity Turnback: Problems and Options
detail.abstract: Over the last decade, the interaction of market forces, Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) policy actions and changes in state public utility commission (PUC) regulation has resulted in an increasingly competitive industry. As the industry becomes more competitive, there is an increasing focus on cost minimization, and efficient use of resources. Local distribution companies (LDCs) and other players in the market face increasing pressure to minimize costs and to use their resources, such as their transportation arrangements, efficiently. As a result, LDCs may reduce their entitlements of long-term firm capacity on interstate pipelines, once their current transportation contracts expire. This may cause an excess capacity problem for pipelines, and under recovery of their capital investments in pipeline construction. The resulting problem, known as the “capacity turnback problem” or “decontracting problem,” may confront pipelines, LDCs and other stakeholders in the gas industry with a significant challenge. The study examines the causes, the magnitude and scope, and the implications of the capacity turnback problem. The study discusses the three large turnback cases that have been brought before the FERC so far, and examines the policy implications of FERC decisions on these cases. The capacity turnback problem can be traced back to FERC actions (the straight fixed-variable rate design, rules for capacity release, and electronic bidding requirements), state PUC policies (performance-based regulation, unbundling), and market-driven changes in the industry (growth of market hubs and centers, and proliferation of ancillary services). The study finds that there are significant regional differences in excess capacity and the potential for capacity turnback, and that the problem is likely to be most significant in the West and the Midwest. The study finds that most of the turned back capacity will be resubscribed, but on shorter term contracts (typically with five year terms compared to ten to twenty year terms in the past), and at discounted rates. Therefore, pipelines may be faced with significant revenue erosion. Studies published by trade organizations of LDCs and pipelines indicate that both LDCs and pipelines anticipate a significant capacity turnback and related revenue erosion problem. This study examines a number of options for addressing the capacity turnback problem that include departures from the straight fixed-variable (SFV) rate design for allocating fixed costs, alternative rate designs (such as seasonal rates and a price floor for interruptible capacity), revision of capacity release rules, revision of bidding requirements of secondary capacity, unilateral exit fees on decontracting customers, reallocation of decontracting costs on remaining customers, negotiated cost-sharing settlements, rate discounts based on duration of contracts, market-based pricing of pipeline services with flexible terms and conditions, and more stringent certification requirements for new pipelines. Among these options, the study finds the following choices to be preferable because they are market-oriented and economically efficient.

title: Rules for Law Writing (That Doesn't Suck): A Manifesto for Public-Facing Legal Communication

detail.title: Rules for Law Writing (That Doesn't Suck): A Manifesto for Public-Facing Legal Communication
detail.abstract:
Legal systems shape every aspect of modern life. The way we write about those systems often obscures more than it illuminates. This document outlines 25 rules for writing about the law in a way that is more clear, precise, and publicly accountable. 

I intend to offer this list as something more imperative than a style guide, but less binding than established rules of grammar. These rules should not be ignored. But every rule that follows is open to challenge—where a challenge is a decision arrived at after consideration.

This genesis of this document is equal parts notes I have received and notes I have given. I explicitly disclaim any expertise.

title: Bioinspired Glycolipids as Dust Mitigation Agents for Mining Environments
affiliations: , , University of Arizona, ,  and University of Arizona

detail.title: Bioinspired Glycolipids as Dust Mitigation Agents for Mining Environments
detail.abstract: Airborne particulate matter (PM) from natural and anthropogenic sources continues to pose serious human and environmental health risks. While many dust suppression materials exist, innovations in sustainable and biodegradable alternatives remain a priority.  Here, we present a systematic evaluation of sixteen bioinspired glycolipids as PM suppressants for mine tailings, a fine-grained mineral waste generated during ore processing. The glycolipids were designed with controlled variations in sugar headgroup type (e.g., xylose vs. rhamnose) and number (e.g., mono- vs. disaccharide), as well as lipid tail length (C10-C18) and multiplicity (single vs. double tail), facilitating targeted comparisons of molecular features and dust reduction capabilities. Structure-property-performance analyses indicate that aliphatic tail characteristics and molecular amphiphilicity considerably affect dust suppression efficacy. Single head, single tail glycolipids exhibited enhanced performance with increasing tail length, while double tail variants consistently outperformed their single tail analogues. Molecular amphiphilicity, quantified via calculated logP values, displayed an optimal range in which suppression was maximized. In simulated wind erosion tests, fifteen glycolipids outperformed water, the most widely used suppressant, and eight achieved >90% PM reduction. Altogether, this work demonstrates that bioinspired glycolipids are a prospective effective and environmentally responsible technology for managing airborne dust emissions from mining, with tunable molecular designs that may be adapted for other dust-generating environments.

detail.abstract: In this publication, we set ourselves the objectively complex task of analyzing the possibilities for making strategic decisions during a crisis, trying to partially analyse the ongoing crises caused by various circumstances. Crisis circumstances require societies to quickly rethink and develop adequate strategies and, accordingly, to formulate strategic goals and plan processes. In many cases, preliminary analysis and assessment are practically impossible, especially when it comes to natural disasters or other types of crises, such as military conflicts. All this puts entire systems and societies to the test, and those who are empowered to manage the process - under strong pressure from unforeseen circumstances and not always objective assessments. The oncoming social transformations are unpredictable, and people find themselves unprepared to deal with new and different challenges. Researching and analyzing these processes is a particular challenge, that cannot always be accomplished with traditional approaches and research methods. This paper presents the expert analysis of the authors, as well as their views and assessment of the ongoing processes.

title: Russia and ASEAN Monetary Policy in the Face of Global Uncertainty: Convergence Points and Challenges for Cooperation in the Asia-Pacific Region
affiliations: Moscow State Institute of International Relations (MGIMO)

detail.title: Russia and ASEAN Monetary Policy in the Face of Global Uncertainty: Convergence Points and Challenges for Cooperation in the Asia-Pacific Region
detail.abstract: This paper analyzes the monetary policy frameworks of Russia and the ASEAN member states within the context of heightened global uncertainty, marked by financial volatility, shifting trade flows, and geopolitical tensions. It identifies key areas of convergence in their policy objectives and challenges, focusing on inflation control, exchange rate stability, and financial sovereignty. The research explores the potential for enhanced monetary and financial cooperation in the Asia-Pacific Region (APR), considering existing mechanisms and new platforms. The study concludes by outlining strategic recommendations for fostering dialogue and coordinated approaches to mitigate shared risks and promote regional economic resilience.

title: Spatial-Network Treatment Effects: A Continuous Functional Approach
affiliations: University of Tokyo

detail.title: Spatial-Network Treatment Effects: A Continuous Functional Approach
detail.abstract: This paper develops a continuous functional framework for treatment effects that propagate through geographic space and economic networks. We derive a master equation governing propagation from three economic foundations---heterogeneous agent aggregation, market equilibrium, and cost minimization---establishing that the framework rests on fundamental principles rather than ad hoc specifications. A key result shows that the spatial-network interaction coefficient equals the mutual information between geographic and market coordinates. The Feynman-Kac representation decomposes effects into inherited and accumulated components along stochastic paths representing economic linkages. The framework nests the no-spillover case as a testable restriction. Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate that conventional estimators---two-way fixed effects, difference-in-differences, and generalized propensity score---exhibit 25--38% bias and severe undercoverage when spillovers exist, while our estimator maintains correct inference regardless of whether spillovers are present. Applying the framework to U.S. minimum wage policy, we reject the no-spillover null and find total effects at state borders four times larger than direct effects---conventional methods capture only one-quarter of policy impact. Structural estimates reveal spatial diffusion consistent with commuting-distance labor mobility, network diffusion consistent with quarterly supply chain adjustment, and significant spatial-network interaction reflecting geographic clustering of industries.

title: Pricing Flood Risk and Resilience Features in the Italian Housing Market
affiliations: Polytechnic University of Milan and Samuel Talk Lee Professor of Urban and Real Estate Sustainability, Faculty Director of MIT Center for Real Estate

detail.title: Pricing Flood Risk and Resilience Features in the Italian Housing Market

publicationDetails.detailsText: MIT Center for Real Estate Research Paper No. 25/11
publicationDetails.journalName: MIT Center for Real Estate Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This study examines how flood risk and resilience features are capitalized into housing prices in the Italian real estate market, focusing on the Lombardy Region. Leveraging a high-resolution dataset of over one million residential listings, we integrate simulated flood hazard maps, geocoded property characteristics, public flood mitigation investment data, and records of recent flood events. Using a spatial hedonic pricing model, we find that flood risk-proxied by hazard in official national hazard maps-is associated with a small but significant price discount. This discount is heterogeneous: it is largest for properties on lower floors and diminishes with elevation, indicating a vertical resilience gradient. Well-maintained properties are also perceived as more resilient and experience smaller discounts. Furthermore, we show that public investments in flood mitigation reduce the negative price effect, suggesting that infrastructure investments bolster perceived safety and market confidence. These findings contribute novel evidence from a European context and underscore the role of both structural and perceived resilience in shaping housing market responses to climate risk.

title: PSC as a Unified Architecture for Catalytic Capital: A Mathematical and Functional Synthesis of Blended Finance Models

detail.title: PSC as a Unified Architecture for Catalytic Capital: A Mathematical and Functional Synthesis of Blended Finance Models

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants, animal subjects, or personal data. Ethical approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
Blended finance has emerged as a core mechanism for mobilising private capital into climate, community, and social impact projects. Yet despite widespread use by governments, development finance institutions, philanthropic foundations, and private investors, the field lacks a unifying architecture explaining why blended finance works, how catalytic capital de-risks systems over time, and how these structures can be replicated at scale. 


This paper introduces Perpetual Social Capital (PSC) as the first general capital architecture that unifies the seven dominant global models of catalytic finance — including concessional debt, junior equity, guarantees, price support mechanisms, reserve accounts, community capital, and temporal leasing innovations. We develop three new mathematical constructs: (1) the Catalytic Leverage Ratio (L₍cat₎) capturing capital mobilisation effects; (2) the Temporal Smoothing Coefficient (τ₍smooth₎) modelling the reduction in risk through time-structured capital layers; and (3) the Replicability Efficiency Metric (R₍eff₎) quantifying the scalability and cost-effectiveness of capital stack templating. 


We further introduce the Capital Stack Tensor (Cᵢⱼₜ) and a Function–Instrument Matrix (Mᵢⱼ) to distinguish structural roles from financial instruments, providing the first formal framework for designing catalytic capital stacks independent of context-specific tooling. 


Applying this architecture across seven cases (CEFC, SEFA, Trawalla Group, Grok Ventures, Asian Development Bank, IFC/BHP Forests Bond, and Macquarie/GCF), we show that PSC captures the shared functional logic underlying blended finance — risk absorption, temporal uncertainty smoothing, crowd-in effects, and system value amplification — and offers a replicable, mathematically grounded model for scaling catalytic capital. 


PSC reframes blended finance from a set of bespoke transactions to a repeatable system architecture, enabling the development of digital infrastructure for automated structuring, measurement, and replication. This work provides a conceptual foundation for policymakers, philanthropic capital providers, and institutional investors seeking to accelerate capital mobilisation for climate and community transitions.

title: Entropy and Complexity in Major League Baseball Game Durations
affiliations: American Institute for Economic Research

detail.title: Entropy and Complexity in Major League Baseball Game Durations

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract: Major League Baseball's introduction of the pitch clock in 2023 provides a rare natural experiment for the study of complex systems. Using game-level data from 2018 to 2025 (20,000 games), this paper investigates whether the pitch clock altered the statistical properties of game durations beyond simple averages. Descriptive statistics establish that average game length fell by roughly 25-30 minutes, with a marked compression of variance and the disappearance of marathon games. Formal variance tests confirm the significance of this reduction. Entropy-based measures indicate that Shannon and sample entropy declined, signaling reduced unpredictability, while Hurst exponent analysis shows a weakening of long-memory dynamics in favor of mean reversion. Counterfactual modeling, trained on pre-2023 data, predicts a distribution centered near 188 minutes; observed outcomes deviate by nearly half an hour on average, with Wasserstein and Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests demonstrating sharp divergence from historical norms. These results suggest that MLB effectively engineered a reduction in system entropy, transforming game durations from a semi-chaotic process with fat-tailed variability into a tightly bounded regime. More broadly, the case illustrates how deliberate institutional design can regulate the temporal dynamics of complex social systems.

title: The Three Paradigms of Physics-Informed Learning: Neural Networks (PINNs), Neural Operators (PINOs), and Reinforcement Learning (PIRL)
affiliations: Artificial Intelligence in Finance Institute

detail.title: The Three Paradigms of Physics-Informed Learning: Neural Networks (PINNs), Neural Operators (PINOs), and Reinforcement Learning (PIRL)
detail.abstract: We develop a unified functional-analytic framework for three physics-informed learning paradigms: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), which approximate individual PDE solutions; Physics-Informed Neural Operators (PINOs), which learn solution maps between function spaces; and Physics-Informed Reinforcement Learning (PIRL), which learns optimal policies under physics-constrained dynamics. Our central contribution is a stability-driven error calculus that decomposes total error into approximation, optimization, statistical, and discretization components, with explicit constants determined by problem-specific coercivity estimates. For elliptic and parabolic problems satisfying strong monotonicity in weak form, we derive quantitative bounds linking physics residual control in dual Sobolev norms to solution error in primal norms. We extend the framework beyond strong monotonicity using pseudo-monotone operator theory for Navier-Stokes and reaction-diffusion systems, providing existence guarantees without quantitative stability. For neural operators, we establish approximation rates governed by Kolmogorov n-widths and derive explicit amortization thresholds determining when operator learning outperforms repeated PINN solves. For reinforcement learning, we prove sample complexity reductions proportional to the effective dimension of physics-constrained state-action manifolds under explicit rank conditions. We provide complete proofs, finite-width neural network error bounds beyond the NTK regime, systematic numerical validation of theoretical convergence rates, and comparison to classical finite element error estimates. We clarify where informal claims in the literature require explicit assumptions and identify fundamental limitations through informationtheoretic lower bounds.

title: Financial Contagion in Production Network and Business Cycle Fluctuation
affiliations: Shanghai University of Finance and Economics - School of Economics, Shanghai Univeristy of Finance and Economics and Zhongnan University of Economics and Law - School of Economics

detail.title: Financial Contagion in Production Network and Business Cycle Fluctuation
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the presence of highly correlated sectoral financial distortion, providing an alternative synchronization upon production linkage. To explore the sources of financial co-movement, a dynamic multi-sector model incorporating input-output linkage and borrowing constraint on firm is constructed to characterize the determinants of sectoral financial distortion. Theoretical analysis reveals how sectoral financial distortion endogenously propagate across sectors, leading to financial contagion in a production network. The determinant of sectoral exposure to common financial distortion is empirically validated. We construct an EM algorithm for estimation of DSGE models with large dimension shock, to quantify the contribution of financial contagion and business cycle volatility in US data. Our results show the financial contagion contributes 30% of the observed correlations in sectoral credit spread and it resonates with the amplification effect of the production network, leading to a nearly doubled fluctuation in GDP during the financial crisis.
