keywords: Periodic Technical Inspection Cost-Benefit Analysis Road Safety Economics Welfare Loss per Savings Transport Regulation External Costs of Transport Vehicle Inspection Policy Accident Externalities Regulatory Impact Assessment Flanders

detail.abstract:
This paper evaluates the welfare effects of proposed reforms to the system of Periodic Technical Inspections (PTI) in Flanders. The analysis assesses whether reductions in inspection coverage—including lower inspection frequency, exemptions for new or second-hand vehicles, and the abolition of specific inspection requirements—can be justified on economic grounds.

Using a comprehensive cost–benefit framework, the study quantifies private savings from reduced inspection fees and time costs and contrasts them with additional societal costs arising from increased accident risks, congestion, and emissions. Accident costs are monetized using nationally calibrated values for fatalities and injuries, while congestion and emission impacts are assessed in line with European transport appraisal standards.

The results show that all reform scenarios generate positive Welfare Loss per Savings (WLPS) values, indicating that private savings are consistently outweighed by societal costs. Even scenarios with WLPS values below unity imply welfare losses once the non-compensable nature of traffic fatalities and serious injuries is taken into account. From a regulatory economics perspective, the findings demonstrate that efficiency gains from deregulation cannot justify increased safety risks.

The paper concludes that maintaining a comprehensive PTI regime remains economically justified and that the examined reform options would lead to a deterioration of overall societal welfare. The results provide policy-relevant evidence for the ongoing European debate on the EU Roadworthiness Package.

title: Profit-Shifting Through Transfer Pricing in Nigeria: An Empirical Study of Multinational Corporations
affiliations: and Kaduna State Board of Internal Revenue

detail.title: Profit-Shifting Through Transfer Pricing in Nigeria: An Empirical Study of Multinational Corporations
detail.abstract: An effective tax system is a critical mechanism for sustainable development, as it enhances domestic revenue mobilization and enables countries to reduce dependence on foreign aid and single-resource revenues. In Nigeria, despite the presence of a large and diverse market with multinational corporate activities, revenue generation relies more heavily on foreign grants and borrowing than on taxation. The Nigerian tax system is characterized by low and unstable revenue performance within a macroeconomic environment marked by persistent fiscal deficits and rising debt servicing obligations. The recent global collapse in crude oil prices further exposed Nigeria's revenue vulnerability and reinforced the need to strengthen taxation as an alternative and more reliable source of public revenue. Although taxation offers greater revenue certainty, increased trade liberalization and capital mobility have created new challenges for tax policy, particularly through aggressive tax planning by multinational corporations (MNCs). Global tax debates increasingly focus on the manipulation of transfer pricing arrangements by MNCs to shift profits across jurisdictions and minimize tax liabilities. Transfer pricing involves allocating profits among related entities as if they were independent firms transacting at arm's length, a practice that has intensified pressure on international tax regimes due to widespread profit shifting. This study examined the relationship between profit shifting and transfer pricing among multinational corporations operating in Nigeria and assessed the extent of profit shifting from the Nigerian economy. An experimental/correlational research design was adopted using a sample of 15 multinational corporations over a five-year period (2012-2016). Regression analysis revealed a strong and statistically significant positive relationship between transfer pricing practices and profit shifting by MNCs in Nigeria. The findings also indicate that the extent of profit shifting is considerably high. The study concludes that Nigeria's tax system is misaligned with the evolving global tax framework, thereby facilitating profit shifting through transfer pricing. It recommends a comprehensive reform of Nigeria's tax system in line with the OECD Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS) initiative and the European Union's Common Consolidated Corporate Tax Base (CCCTB).

title: #EconTwitter and Elon Musk: Anatomy of a Failed Exodus
affiliations: Wake Forest University - Department of Economics and Virginia Tech

detail.title: #EconTwitter and Elon Musk: Anatomy of a Failed Exodus
detail.abstract: We study the attempted migration of the #EconTwitter community from Twitter/X to Mastodon following Elon Musk’s acquisition of the platform. Leveraging a dataset of 4.3 million tweets from over 2,000 economists---including detailed records of their weekly activity and network-mediated exposure to peers' Mastodon-related retweets---we examine how peer discussions relate to platform engagement. In a difference-in-differences framework, we estimate that greater exposure to Mastodon-related discussions is followed by a short-run decline in activity on Twitter/X. However, this relationship attenuates substantially when we control for economist fixed effects or examine longer-run behavior. Two years later, economists with higher Mastodon exposure are somewhat more likely to multi-home across platforms but only marginally less active on Twitter/X. These findings highlight the strength of network effects and the difficulty of disrupting incumbent platforms, even during periods of widespread discontent.

title: Motivating Green Investment
affiliations: University of Vienna

detail.title: Motivating Green Investment
detail.abstract: Authorities often design programs to channel private capital toward projects with high social returns, such as green technologies. Entrepreneurs’ incentive to exaggerate their projects social returns to extract rents from the authority can distort investment. However, since an entrepreneur cannot commit to reducing the agency rent he extracts from outside investors, as long as the project’s private return reflects its social return, the entrepreneur produces less pledgeable income to outside investors than if his claim on his technology were true. A planner can design her scheme around two principles: projects with higher social returns should generate higher private returns, and projects that can receive more outside investors should receive greater government support. The optimal scheme matches several commonly observed features of real-world programs.

title: Extraterritorial Sanctions and Judicial Accountability: The Complete Cycle of the Alexandre de Moraes Case - From Unprecedented Designation to Unprecedented Delisting (July-December 2025)
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Extraterritorial Sanctions and Judicial Accountability: The Complete Cycle of the Alexandre de Moraes Case - From Unprecedented Designation to Unprecedented Delisting (July-December 2025)
detail.abstract:
This study analyzes the unprecedented complete lifecycle of American extraterritorial sanctions applied against Brazilian Supreme Federal Court (STF) Justice Alexandre de Moraes under the Global Magnitsky Human Rights Accountability Act. Building upon the author's initial real-time analysis of the designation on July 30, 2025, this working paper examines the equally unprecedented silent delisting after exactly 135 days, without official explanation or press release from the U.S. Treasury Department.

The original designation, confirmed by OFAC Press Release SB0211, was based on allegations of "arbitrary pre-trial detentions and suppression of freedom of expression," marking the first application of Global Magnitsky sanctions against a Latin American supreme court justice and the first against a sitting magistrate of a consolidated democracy. On December 12, 2025, all designations were removed from the Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) list in an administrative update, with no accompanying justification.

Through rigorous comparative analysis of Global Magnitsky delisting precedents since 2012, this research reveals that the 135-day sanctions duration represents the fastest complete reversal in program history for human rights violations allegations. The study examines three competing hypotheses: (1) diplomatic negotiation under commercial pressure, (2) technical-legal unsustainability of allegations, and (3) geopolitical recalibration by the Trump administration.

The research confirms systemic vulnerabilities in the Global Magnitsky sanctions architecture, demonstrating political selectivity, susceptibility to bilateral pressure, and erosion of institutional credibility through inconsistent application. The case establishes precedent for future delisting strategies and exposes double standards in enforcement between strategic adversaries and commercial partners.

This work contributes to international law scholarship on extraterritorial jurisdiction limits, judicial independence boundaries in democratic systems, and emerging accountability mechanisms' effectiveness. It provides the first comprehensive academic analysis of both the designation and delisting phases of this landmark case.

This paper builds upon and substantially expands the author’s prior working paper published on SSRN (No. 5373930), which analyzed the initial designation phase of the case

title: Artificial Intelligence and Skills: Evidence from Contrastive Learning in Online Job Vacancies
affiliations: Independent, Zhejiang University and Zhejiang University

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence and Skills: Evidence from Contrastive Learning in Online Job Vacancies
detail.abstract: We examine the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) adoption on skill requirements, leveraging over 200 million online job vacancies from China (2015-2023). Using a novel Extreme Multi-Label Classification (XMLC) algorithm, trained with contrastive learning and augmented by a large language model-driven synthetic data protocol, we map sentence-level skill requirements to the ESCO framework. Focusing on Chinese listed firms, we establish a robust, causal link between AI adoption and increased diversity in occupational skill portfolios. Our findings reveal that AI reduces information asymmetry in labor markets, enabling firms to specify essential skills more precisely (12% increase in coverage) and boosting demand for optional skills (18% increase) as firms expand into new business domains. Conversely, AI substitutes standard skills, reducing their demand by 10-15%, consistent with prior automation literature. This study underscores AI's transformative role in reshaping labor market skill structures, offering insights for workforce reskilling and policy interventions in emerging economies.

title: New Tech, New Threat? Occupational Exposure to Artificial Intelligence Increases Support for AI Regulation
affiliations: Nuffield College, University of Oxford, Nuffield College, University of Oxford and Nuffield College, University of Oxford

detail.title: New Tech, New Threat? Occupational Exposure to Artificial Intelligence Increases Support for AI Regulation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author(s) declared no potential conflicts of interest with respect to the research, authorship, and/or publication of this article.
declarations.ethicsApproval: We sought research ethics approval from the University of Oxford’s Department of Politics and International Relations Ethics Committee (DPIR DREC) prior to commencing our research, in accordance with the procedures laid down by the University for ethical approval of all research involving human participants, and this was granted on 15th January 2024 (Ref No: SSH/DPIR_C1A_24_001). Our research involved surveying a representative sample of British adults who had opted into YouGov’s online sample pool. We therefore operated on the basis of informed consent, with the respondents able to terminate the interview process at any time.
declarations.funderStatement: Funding for this project was generously provided by the Joseph Rowntree Foundation (a charity registered in England, Wales, and Scotland under numbers 1184957 and SCO49712, of The Homestead, 40 Water End, YORK, YO30 6WP) as part of the larger ongoing research project, ‘Economic Insecurity: Finding Answers and Solutions’ (2023–2025).

detail.abstract: Are workers in occupations that are more exposed to artificial intelligence [AI] also more likely to support government regulation of these emerging technologies? We address this question by matching fine-grained, occupation-level data on AI's task capabilities with original survey data on political preferences and perceptions of job threat. This approach allows us to examine the regulatory preferences of workers who are objectively more or less exposed to AI, as well as those who are subjectively more optimistic or pessimistic about its personal impact. Across model specifications, we find robust evidence that greater occupational exposure to AI, and subjective AI-risk, strongly predicts support for regulation in Britain. A supplementary study also links concern about AI to regulatory support in the United States, but only among self-identified liberals. We conclude by discussing both the relevance and potential limitations of occupational self-interest for understanding the political contestation of technology in the AI era.

title: Does Government-Assisted Relocation Help Households

detail.title: Does Government-Assisted Relocation Help Households
detail.abstract: Climate change is intensifying floods and storms, leading governments to consider relocating households away from high-risk areas. Yet there is little evidence on whether such programs reduce risk or improve household well-being. I evaluate the U.S. Federal Emergency Management Agency's property acquisition ("buyout") program using nationwide longitudinal records that track households before and after approval. By comparing participants with similar neighbors in the same flood zones, I identify the program's e!ects on relocation, flood exposure, and financial outcomes. Households that participate move sooner, relocate to safer areas, and experience modest short-term reductions in debt and improvements in neighborhood socioeconomic conditions. However, these benefits are concentrated among participants from wealthier and predominantly white neighborhoods, who relocate more quickly and achieve larger reductions in risk. A benefit-cost analysis indicates that buyouts are roughly cost-neutral to taxpayers, with potential for net savings under faster implementation and higher participation. These results show that governmentassisted relocation can be an e!ective adaptation tool, but its social and economic benefits remain unevenly distributed.

title: Empty Nest Syndrome: Parents' Labor Supply and Well-Being

detail.title: Empty Nest Syndrome: Parents' Labor Supply and Well-Being

declarations.funderStatement: This study is part of the Gender and Health Inequalities (GENDHI) project, ERC-2019-SyG. This project has received funding from the European Research Council (ERC) under the European Union’s Horizon 2020 research and innovation programme (grant agreement No. [856478])

detail.abstract: When children leave the parental home, parents may gain additional time to allocate to either leisure or employment. This paper examines how the transition to an empty nest-defined as the point when all children have moved out of the parental household, affects parents' labour supply and well-being. Focusing on mothers and fathers separately, I employ an event-study approach using data from the Survey of Health, Ageing, and Retirement in Europe (SHARE). The results show that mothers who are already working tend to increase their weekly hours following the empty-nest transition, while there is little change in fathers' labour supply. However, there is no evidence of mothers re-entering the labour market, nor are there significant effects on depressive outcomes for either parent.

title: Style Investing, Style Timing, and IPO Return Predictability
affiliations: University of Alabama at Birmingham and University of Texas at Arlington

detail.title: Style Investing, Style Timing, and IPO Return Predictability
detail.abstract: Style investing is often viewed as a phenomenon confined to seasoned stocks, yet its influence emerges during the IPO process. Using a sample of U.S. IPOs from 1975 to 2022, we find that higher pre-IPO style returns are significantly associated with greater IPO underpricing. We further find evidence of style timing: firms are more likely to go public when their associated style is performing well, and such IPOs proceed to market more quickly. However, IPO stocks linked to hot styles subsequently underperform within a year, suggesting a reversal in stock performance after going public. Our findings reveal that style investing influences IPO pricing, timing, and aftermarket performance, extending behavioral theories of style momentum to the primary market.

title: Mechanizing Saffron: An Economic Feasibility Study

detail.title: Mechanizing Saffron: An Economic Feasibility Study
detail.abstract: This paper examines the feasibility of mechanizing saffron (Crocus sativus L.) cultivation, a highly labor-intensive specialty crop, by integrating economic and biological perspectives. Traditional economic theory frames labor and capital as substitutes, suggesting that labor scarcity should drive mechanization. However, evidence from viticulture, floriculture, and saffron production indicates that mechanization is influenced by a combination of institutional, economic, and biological constraints. Using a comparative analysis of the United States (capital-rich, poor climate) and Spain (moderate wealth, ideal climate), this study evaluates whether environmental, labor, and capital factors alone can overcome the inherent delicacy and corm-based propagation of saffron. Results indicate that while greenhouse-based interventions can extend flowering periods and facilitate harvest, biological limitations and resource-intensive requirements make widespread mechanization unfeasible under typical field conditions. These findings support traditional economic theory that less wealthy countries are less likely to mechanize specialty crops, while also aligning with Madhok (2025) in demonstrating that this outcome is driven not by labor-capital substitution, but by structural and institutional constraints. The research identifies gaps where economic and biological studies intersect and highlights avenues for future work on sustainable automation in specialty agriculture.

title: Data Regulation, Platform Encroachment, and the Matthew Effect
affiliations: Monash University - Department of Economics , , The University of Osaka - Osaka School of International Public Policy (OSIPP) and Tilburg University - Tilburg University School of Economics and Management

detail.title: Data Regulation, Platform Encroachment, and the Matthew Effect
detail.abstract: Marketplace platforms are central players in online retail and are in an advantageous position to leverage data generated by third-party sellers. This paper analyzes how a platform's encroachment decision--whether to enter its marketplace as a direct competitor--is shaped by regulations that restrict its use of seller data. We show that the platform's encroachment decision follows a non-monotonic pattern: it enters against sellers with either relatively low or sufficiently high brand value, but remains a pure intermediary for intermediate brand values. The data ban regulation alters this strategy by making the platform more likely to exclude low brand-value sellers and more likely to accommodate high brand-value sellers. This creates a Matthew Effect in platform ecosystems:  the regulation favors high-value sellers and harms low-value sellers. These results underscore the need for more nuanced regulatory approaches that promote data sharing in emerging markets and targeted bans in mature, established markets to better balance welfare and competition.

title: Impact of Pesticide Reduction Policies on the Economy and Environment in Quebec: A CGE Model Analysis
affiliations: University of Quebec at Montreal (UQAM) and UQAM

detail.title: Impact of Pesticide Reduction Policies on the Economy and Environment in Quebec: A CGE Model Analysis
detail.abstract: This article analyzes the economic and environmental impacts of pesticide reduction policies in Quebec through a scenario of pesticide taxation, aimed at aligning the agricultural sector with the objectives of the Sustainable Agriculture Plan. The study is based on a computable general equilibrium model that disaggregates the agricultural sector into two sub-sectors: conventional agriculture and organic agriculture. The results show that pesticide taxation reduces agricultural production, farmers' profits, and consumption due to rising prices of agricultural goods and increased imports in the conventional sector. Conversely, this taxation promotes the adoption of organic farming and stimulates consumption, imports, and exports in this sector. The reduction in pesticide use by Quebec farmers leads to a decline in their productivity, benefiting other regions. However, an adjusted tax applies to the importation of pesticide-intensive agricultural goods could increase production and profitability of crops in Quebec. Finally, the study highlights that economic benefits, particularly in terms of profitability for both conventional and organic farming, are observed when tax revenues are redistributed to households, while greater environmental benefits are achieved when these revenues are allocated to organic farmers.

title: Why ESG Fails as a Priced Factor? Investor Heterogeneity, Carbon Risk, and Regulatory Transitions
affiliations: University of Finance and Administration

detail.title: Why ESG Fails as a Priced Factor? Investor Heterogeneity, Carbon Risk, and Regulatory Transitions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known personal or financial relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted as part of the author’s academic research activities.

detail.abstract: This paper examines why ESG-related risk premia appear weak and unstable in standard asset pricing tests. Using European data, dynamic ESG, carbon, and controversy exposures are estimated via a state-space framework and priced using Bayesian and panel-based methods. The author show that aggregate ESG premia vanish under homogeneous-investor assumptions, not because ESG risks are irrelevant, but because pricing is conditional on investor heterogeneity, regulatory regimes, and information quality. Carbon risk is priced primarily during regulatory transition periods, while controversy risk is priced selectively by investor clienteles with strong non-pecuniary preferences. Allowing for dynamic exposures and heterogeneous pricing reconciles conflicting findings in the ESG asset-pricing literature and highlights the limits of static, representative-agent models in sustainability contexts.

title: Analysis & Policy  Implications of Azerbaijan's Energy Strategy: Gas Laundromat, Sanctions Exposure, & Transition Pathways
affiliations: Economic Research Center (ERC)

detail.title: Analysis & Policy  Implications of Azerbaijan's Energy Strategy: Gas Laundromat, Sanctions Exposure, & Transition Pathways
detail.abstract:
Despite hosting COP29 in November 2024 and assuming a leadership role in global climate governance, Azerbaijan is not only increasing its investments in the national oil and gas industry, but also—through its state energy company, the State  Oil Company of the Azerbaijan Republic (SOCAR)—expanding investments  abroad, and—through its state shipping company, the Azerbaijan Caspian  Shipping Closed Joint-Stock Company (ASCO)—participating in the transport of  sanctioned Russian oil. These activities undermine the COP’s stated goals of  moving away from fossil fuels and contradict 
Azerbaijan’s commitments in international climate negotiations.  
Accordingly, this paper analyzes how, during a period when it would be expected to lead global calls for decarbonization, the Azerbaijani government presents itself as an expanding petrostate. The paper examines Azerbaijan’s intensifying partnerships with major transnational oil companies such as BP, TotalEnergies, Eni, ExxonMobil, Chevron, and Lukoil; the country’s oil and gas sector investments abroad; and cases of selling Russian oil and gas under its own brand—both retrospectively and in terms of Azerbaijan’s current energy transition prospects.

The study evaluates Azerbaijan’s use of COP29 as an opportunity to increase fossil fuel investment, along with its renewed post-COP29 strategies of engaging with energy companies from the United Kingdom, the United States, European Union, Türkiye, UAE and Russia. It argues that Azerbaijan’s prioritization of hydrocarbons not only contradicts the spirit of its COP29 presidency but also reflects the broader global failure to reconcile geopolitical energy interests with climate commitments.

title: Estimating the Effects of Austerity on the Labour Market: Evidence from Great Britain
affiliations: University of Greenwich - Business School, University of the West of England (UWE),  and University of Greenwich - University of Greenwich

detail.title: Estimating the Effects of Austerity on the Labour Market: Evidence from Great Britain

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We have no conflict of interest to declare.
declarations.funderStatement: This paper received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Between 2010 and 2019, in response to concern about the public finances, the UK government imposed substantial cuts to public spending. This austerity programme was justified in public using theories of 'expansionary fiscal contractions', which posited both aggregate demand and labour supply effects. While the former have been explored in depth, the supply-side effects of austerity have received less attention. In this paper, we estimate the effects of austerity on the labour market using evidence from Great Britain. Using continuous treatment difference-in-differences models estimated on district-level data, we find that austerity reduced labour costs and increased employment rates. Our results also suggest that austerity reduced local output, implying that austerity was partly responsible for the UK's low productivity growth after 2010.

title: “From ‘Closing Down the Deep-Bore Wells’ to the Wandering Earth: A Re-Examination of Environmental Governance Legitimacy in China”
affiliations: Colorado State University

detail.title: “From ‘Closing Down the Deep-Bore Wells’ to the Wandering Earth: A Re-Examination of Environmental Governance Legitimacy in China”

declarations.funderStatement: This article received support from the Chiang Chin-Kuo Foundation American Region Scholar Grant (CCKFGS045-A-20).

detail.abstract: The article critically examines the role of environmental law in Chi-na’s state-capitalist system from a structural Marxist perspective. The author argues that the Chinese environmental regulatory regime, often perceived as arbitrary and chaotic, is not a mere byproduct of a develop-ing legal system but a deliberate strategy to legitimize state authority and control. Through case studies on integrated water resources management and the prevention of husbandry waste pollution, the article illustrates how environmental laws serve as both Repressive State Apparatuses (RSA) and Ideological State Apparatuses (ISA), enforcing social control and shap-ing public consciousness. The state’s top-down enforcement methods, reliance on technocratic solutions, and manipulation of legal and moral ideologies are shown to maintain and obscure the relations of produc-tion, reinforcing the state-capitalist model of accumulation. The article also explores how China’s cultural products like the film, The Wander-ing Earth, normalize authoritarian state authority in global environmental governance. The analysis concludes that to fully understand China’s envi-ronmental governance, one must view it through the lens of state-capitalist accumulation, recognizing the role of environmental law in maintaining authoritarian state-society relations and shaping the broader political-eco-nomic landscape.

title: Versioned Meaning: How to Make Ontologies Audit-Stable

detail.title: Versioned Meaning: How to Make Ontologies Audit-Stable

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the research presented in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, patient data, or personal data. Ethics approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this research.

detail.abstract:
Ontology versioning is widely practiced across enterprise knowledge graphs, healthcare terminologies, and semantic standards. These practices effectively govern the publication and maintenance of meaning, but they do not ensure that automated or semi-automated decisions remain audit-reproducible over time. In regulated environments, this gap is consequential: a compliance determination is valid only with respect to the precise semantic meaning in force at the moment the decision was made.

This paper introduces audit-stable meaning, a compliance-oriented semantic discipline defined by four invariants: (1) governed decisions are cryptographically bound to immutable semantic snapshots; (2) semantic evolution is explicitly non-retroactive with respect to prior decisions; (3) decisions are reproducible by independent auditors; and (4) semantic drift is explicitly visible and reviewable. We show how existing approaches—including ontology versioning, provenance frameworks, temporal modeling, and smart-contract immutability—fail to prevent silent semantic drift, retroactive reinterpretation, and audit non-reproducibility.

We present a reference architecture for audit-stable ontologies, including semantic snapshotting, version-scoped enforcement, decision artifact schemas, and controlled semantic migration with re-certification triggers. A maturity model distinguishes conventional “versioned ontologies” from systems capable of producing regulator-acceptable, replayable compliance evidence. The result reframes semantic governance as a control-plane integrity problem rather than a documentation or data-management concern, with direct implications for AI-assisted decision systems in regulated domains.

title: Analyse the Legal and Procedural Framework Governing Procurement and Tendering in Public-Private Partnership (PPP) Arrangements in Nigeria. In Your Discussion, Evaluate How Transparency, Competition, and Legal Safeguards are Embedded in the ICRC Act, the National Policy on PPPs, and Relevant Sector-Specific Regulations. Assess the Effectiveness of these Safeguards in Preventing Corruption, Ensuring Value for Money, and Promoting Investor Confidence. Draw on Comparative Practice from Another Jurisdiction to Propose Reforms that can Strengthen Nigeria's PPP Procurement Regime
affiliations: Independent, Nile University of Nigeria Abuja, Nile University of Nigeria Abuja, Nile University of Nigeria Abuja and Nile University of Nigeria Abuja

detail.title: Analyse the Legal and Procedural Framework Governing Procurement and Tendering in Public-Private Partnership (PPP) Arrangements in Nigeria. In Your Discussion, Evaluate How Transparency, Competition, and Legal Safeguards are Embedded in the ICRC Act, the National Policy on PPPs, and Relevant Sector-Specific Regulations. Assess the Effectiveness of these Safeguards in Preventing Corruption, Ensuring Value for Money, and Promoting Investor Confidence. Draw on Comparative Practice from Another Jurisdiction to Propose Reforms that can Strengthen Nigeria's PPP Procurement Regime
detail.abstract: Strengthening the foundations of transparent and competitive infrastructure delivery in Nigeria requires a clear understanding of how procurement and tendering operate within its Public–Private Partnership (PPP) framework. This research examined the legal and procedural mechanisms embedded in the Infrastructure Concession Regulatory Commission (ICRC) Act of 2005, the National Policy on PPPs, the Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2007, and sector-specific regulations, assessing how they promote value-for- money, foster competition, and enhance investor confidence. Using a doctrinal and comparative approach, the study drew on primary legal sources, including statutes, regulatory instruments, judicial decisions, and international guidelines, as well as authoritative secondary literature. The findings indicate that Nigeria’s PPP framework provides a solid foundation for transparent procurement, supported by well-organized processes for project selection, bidding, evaluation, and contract monitoring. Evidence also shows increasing alignment with international PPP standards through better procedural standardization and clearer risk-sharing practices. Insights from the United Kingdom, Kenya, and South Africa highlighted opportunities to improve these efforts by strengthening e-procurement systems, refining risk management tools, improving dispute-resolution mechanisms, and adopting standardized value-for- money assessments. Building on these results, the study has recommended not only harmonizing and updating existing laws, such as revising outdated provisions in the ICRC Act, FR Act, and related sectoral legislation, but also strengthening institutional oversight and expanding capacity-building initiatives. It emphasized the need for a renewed sense of patriotism among policymakers, regulators, and project sponsors, along with the political will to take decisive actions when necessary to protect national interests. Increasing the adoption of global best practices, combined with a committed national ethos and timely legal reforms, will enhance transparency, efficiency, and investor confidence in PPP procurement. Ultimately, these measures are vital for fostering sustainable infrastructure development and increasing public value in Nigeria.

title: Reliability and Admissibility of AI-Generated Forensic Evidence in Criminal Trials
affiliations: and Guru Nanak Dev University

detail.title: Reliability and Admissibility of AI-Generated Forensic Evidence in Criminal Trials

publicationDetails.detailsText: Book in Proceedings of The National Seminar Criminal Law and Justice Reforms, Pp. 45-53

detail.abstract: This paper examines the admissibility of AI-generated forensic evidence in criminal trials. The growing adoption of AI presents promising results for investigative efficiency. Despite advancements, significant research gaps persist in practically understanding the legal limits of AI evidence in judicial processes. Existing literature lacks focused assessment of the evidentiary value of AI outputs. The objective of this study is to evaluate whether AI-generated evidence satisfies established legal standards of reliability. The methodology involves a comparative doctrinal legal analysis of evidentiary standards across common law jurisdictions. Preliminary results indicate that AI forensic tools can enhance scale of evidence analysis. However, challenges arise from reproducibility deficits. Courts exhibit variability in acceptance of AI evidence due to limited technical literacy and lack of standardized validation protocols. Liability implications reveal that developers and investigators may bear accountability for flawed outputs. This raises critical concerns related to wrongful conviction. The paper emphasizes the necessity of independent validation and, development of AI-specific admissibility criteria. Findings inform policy development for the responsible AI integration within criminal justice systems. The research advances the objectives of Sustainable Development Goal 16 by reinforcing equitable access to justice. Preliminary results contribute for a foundation for future empirical research in AI deployed criminal forensics.

title: Fake Bidders, Real Consequences: Shill Bidding and Price Manipulation in Judicial Housing Auctions
affiliations: National University of Singapore, Zicklin School of Business, Baruch College - The City University of New York and

detail.title: Fake Bidders, Real Consequences: Shill Bidding and Price Manipulation in Judicial Housing Auctions
detail.abstract: We study strategic bid manipulation in high-stakes online housing auctions using comprehensive data from China's judicial foreclosure market, the world's largest courtadministered auction platform. We identify suspected shill bidders-participants who inflate prices without intent to purchase-using granular bid timing, frequency, and response speed. Shill bidders appear in 8% of auctions and increase transaction price premiums by 14.3%, implying an annual wealth transfer of approximately USD 80 million from buyers to judgment debtors. We establish causality using a quasi-experimental regulatory shock introduced by the Jiangsu High People's Court in 2017, which sharply increased penalties for defaulting bidders. Difference-indifferences estimates show that price premiums decline by 8.2% in treated courts following the reform, alongside a 14-20% reduction in shill activity. Instrumental variable estimates using city-level dishonest judgment debtor cases further corroborate the causal effect. Mechanism analysis reveals that shill bidders intensify competition among genuine bidders: auctions with shills exhibit higher bid frequency, faster bidding speeds, lower concentration, and more aggressive outbidding. The impact of shill bidding is attenuated by higher deposits, stronger legal institutions, and closer court proximity, but amplified in high-trust and highfraud regions. Our results provide the first large-scale causal evidence on auction fraud in judicial housing markets and highlight how weak enforcement in digital market design can generate large and hidden welfare losses. The findings offer direct guidance for platform design and judicial enforcement in online asset markets.

title:
Grants to Loans as Event Geometry: 
Mapping the 1986 HEA Shift on the Fiscal Plane (Fiscal Geometry)

detail.title:
Grants to Loans as Event Geometry: 
Mapping the 1986 HEA Shift on the Fiscal Plane (Fiscal Geometry)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal, financial, or institutional conflicts of interest that could be perceived to have influenced this research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is based exclusively on publicly available legal texts, policy documents, and aggregate administrative reports. It does not involve human subjects, personal data, or participant interaction, and therefore did not require ethics approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: This paper applies Fiscal Geometry to re-read the 1986 reauthorization of the U.S. Higher Education Act (HEA) as a rule-triggered geometric pivot rather than a narrative policy episode. The shift from grant-centered support toward expanded loan-based financing is represented as a sequence of rule-capital events—eligibility triggers, allocation constraints, borrowing authorizations, and repayment obligations—positioned on a two-axis fiscal plane. The X-axis registers cross-jurisdictional fiscal shift, i.e., the movement and fiscal reclassification of public and private capital across rule-based interfaces. The Y-axis registers intergenerational post-tax capacity, i.e., the downward path through which household carrying capacity and obligation settlement extend over time. Modeling 1986 as a pivot event yields an observable trajectory rotation: public-support pathways contract while household balance-sheet pathways expand, with corridor formation, density shifts, and localized bottlenecks becoming legible without predictive claims, attribution, or normative evaluation. Building on this mapping, the paper specifies a minimal, implementable definition of an Institutional Tension Index (ITI) as a structured readout of geometric strain when rule-intent and registered capital trajectories diverge on the fiscal plane. The contribution is methodological. Under a fiscal-epistemic evidence discipline that prioritizes legally accountable public sources, the paper demonstrates how a major financing redesign can be rendered as replicable event geometry, supporting transferability across education finance, taxation, and other public-facing systems.

detail.abstract: This chapter considers the role of the "state" in pharmaceutical research, development, and commercialization, focusing on the U.S. experience and considering its implications for development of a global market. It argues that the unusual structure and theory of the U.S. political system, and the diverse and unusual culture of the country, complicate any roles that the "state" could play, as well as any potential for U.S. involvement in a global market.

title: Experience and Advice in a Deferred Acceptance Matching Experiment
affiliations: The University of Sydney, The University of Sydney, Department of Economics, University of Melbourne, The University of Sydney and The University of Sydney

detail.title: Experience and Advice in a Deferred Acceptance Matching Experiment

declarations.declarationOfInterest: All authors declare that they have no conflicts of interest to disclose.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study was approved by The University of Sydney Human Research Ethics Committee, under protocol number 2022/717 (CI Silva-Goncalves).
declarations.funderStatement: Guillen acknowledges support from the Australian Research Council (DP160103699).

detail.abstract: Recent research suggests that truth-telling in strategy-proof mechanisms may be an artefact of the experimental design, and is vulnerable to misleading advice yet impervious to accurate advice. In this paper, we examine the effect of experience by providing participants with opportunities for practice, in which they receive feedback on the effects of submitting different preference rankings upon their match under the Gale-Shapley deferred acceptance mechanism. We also study the interaction between experience and mixed advice. We find no effect of practice upon the truthfulness of reported preferences, either alone or in combination with advice. However, presenting participants with both misleading and accurate advice significantly reduces truth-telling. The latter effect has previously been documented for the top trading cycles mechanism, but not for deferred acceptance.

title: Did Eighteenth Century China Go Backwards or Forwards?
affiliations: Yeungnam University

detail.title: Did Eighteenth Century China Go Backwards or Forwards?
detail.abstract: This article estimates factor prices in pre-Opium War China. Provincial interest rates are inferred from seasonal fluctuations in grain prices, which is used to convert farmland value based on land contracts into land rents. Assuming a Cobb-Douglas production function with a land share of 0.5, twice the land rents equals grain yields. Estimated interest rates and land rents trended downwards in the eighteenth century, which, given the undisputed fact of growing population, predicts a decline in workers' earnings consistent with available wage evidence. Falling factor prices imply that eighteenth century China experienced income and total factor productivity decline, rather than achieving Smithian growth or traversing an involutionary path. Sectoral TFP duals indicate that the productivity failure was not sector-specific but generalized, suggesting that the Qing misperformance was policy-induced.

title: The Evolution of Economic Behavior

detail.title: The Evolution of Economic Behavior
detail.abstract: Mainstream economics is based on the rationality assumption: that people act to promote their interests. Behavioural economics holds that people act by behavioural rules of thumb. We suggest that these positions are perfectly consistent: people indeed act by rules, which usually work well, but may work poorly in exceptional or contrived scenarios. The reason is that like physical features, behavioural rules are the product of evolutionary processes; and evolution works on the usual, the common—not the exception, not the contrived scenario.

title: On the Linearization of Bilinear Mortality Models
affiliations: Ulm University - Institute of Insurance Science and Masaryk University

detail.title: On the Linearization of Bilinear Mortality Models
detail.abstract: We propose a general framework that reduces the bilinear structure of the Lee-Carter mortality model and a broad class of its extensions to a fully linear form. The key insight is that once the time-varying mortality indices are obtained through an external procedure-most naturally as the first principal components from principal component analysis-the bilinear interaction terms become fixed. In the single-population setting, this involves treating the common mortality index k_t as observed, while in multi-population settings both the common factor k_t and population-specific deviation factors k_cgt are extracted externally. Conditioning on these factors eliminates bilinearity and yields a standard linear regression structure. The PCA-derived mortality indices are mathematically equivalent, up to normalization, to the time indices obtained in the first step of the classical Lee-Carter and Li-Lee singular value decompositions, thereby establishing a direct theoretical connection between the two approaches. With bilinearity removed, parameters are estimated using generalized estimating equations, allowing for principled modeling of serial dependence while relying on standard linear tools. The resulting PCA-GEE framework applies broadly to single-and multi-population mortality models, including cohort-augmented specifications, and provides a transparent and computationally simple platform for mortality forecasting. Using data from the Human Mortality Database, we show that the proposed approach delivers consistently improved out-of-sample forecast accuracy relative to classical Lee-Carter and Li-Lee models.

title: Who are the Players?

detail.title: Who are the Players?
detail.abstract: In applications of game theory, a "player" may be a person; household (or family); sports team; country; political party; community; corporation; labor union; species or other population; and so on. Usually, this is understood as an idealization, a kind of "small worlds" principle. In games where, say, countries are modeled as players, the "real" players are the individual citizens, with their individual goals and individual decisions and individual free will. It's only because this "true" game is too big and unwieldy to analyze that, it is held, game theorists model players as they do. Here, we will explore the idea that this is not an idealization; that in large part, collectives are like individual people, and may be thought of as such. And, perhaps, not only in game theory.

title: The Geometry of Fairness
affiliations: Northumbria University

detail.title: The Geometry of Fairness
detail.abstract: We develop a geometric theory of distributive justice, proposing that fairness is not a scalar preference or penalty but a metric geometry on the space of welfare, where the curvature of moral distance governs how inequality is perceived, corrected, and stabilized. Our framework introduces a tractable fairness metric whose curvature parameter captures how sharply small welfare gaps expand into moral distance. Positive curvature produces endogenous equality, convex redistribution, and a moral force that compresses inequality without exogenous social weights. Embedding this structure into a planner's problem yields a set of analytical laws linking fairness curvature to inequality, efficiency, and policy: inequality declines elastically with curvature (the Curvature-Compression Law), convergence toward equality accelerates but becomes more oscillatory (the Curvature-Stability Trade-Off), and optimal taxation rises with curvature (the Curvature-Policy Elasticity). Structurally calibrating the model using crosscountry data on inequality, fiscal effort, and subjective well-being identifies fairness curvature as a slow-moving moral constant that varies systematically across societies. Economies with higher curvature exhibit lower inequality, stronger welfare states, and higher life satisfaction. These findings reveal that moral geometry is an independent determinant of distributive outcomes, bridging welfare theory, behavioral fairness, and macroeconomic inequality dynamics. Fairness, in this view, is the curvature of moral space, the hidden topology through which societies translate economic distance into justice.

title: Hidden reservoirs: The role of soils and forests during droughts
affiliations: World Bank and World Bank

detail.title: Hidden reservoirs: The role of soils and forests during droughts
detail.abstract: Droughts are widely recognized for their adverse effects on economies, especially on agriculture. With approximately 75% of global food production occurring under rainfed conditions understanding the role of soil moisture is critical.  Yet its influence on the economic impacts of drought remains poorly understood.  Using global gridded data spanning 25 years, we find that locations with higher pre-shock root-zone soil moisture are associated with smaller drought-year growth losses. We also study a plausible determinant of elevated soil moisture —upstream forest cover— and find that grid cells with greater upstream forest cover correlate with higher soil moisture storage and exhibit losses about half as large as in low-forest settings. Taken together, the evidence highlights the potential value of considering soil moisture and its forest-based drivers alongside conventional “blue” water management, and climate adaptation strategies.

title: A Note on the Hitting Probability of a Drifting Brownian Motion
affiliations: Hong Kong US invest

detail.title: A Note on the Hitting Probability of a Drifting Brownian Motion
detail.abstract: This note derives and demonstrates the closed-form hitting probability for a drifted Brownian motion, extending the classic reflection principle via Girsanov's theorem. We provide complete proofs for the joint distribution of the process and its running maximum, yielding explicit formulas for barrier crossing probabilities. Through numerical applications with typical financial parameters, we show that naive Monte Carlo estimation substantially underestimates true hitting probabilities, while the closed-form solution offers both computational efficiency and accuracy. These results have direct applications in financial engineering, particularly for pricing barrier options, estimating knockout probabilities in structured products, and assessing event risks in continuous-time models.

title: Impact of CBN Anchor Borrowers' Program on Agricultural Financing in Kebbi State
affiliations: , Kaduna State Board of Internal Revenue and Federal University Birnin Kebbi

detail.title: Impact of CBN Anchor Borrowers' Program on Agricultural Financing in Kebbi State
detail.abstract: This study examined the role of the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) Anchor Borrowers' Programme in agricultural financing in Kebbi State. A survey research design was employed, with a sample of 34 respondents, and data were collected via structured questionnaires. The Chi-square test and Kendall's Coefficient of Concordance (W) were used for data analysis. The findings revealed that the CBN Anchor Borrowers' Programme is faced with several challenges, including high interest rates, short repayment periods, and a lack of collateral security. The study also found that the credit amount provided under the programme is inadequate, as only 21% of the respondents agreed that the benefits received from the programme were sufficient. Furthermore, the findings indicated that 35% of the respondents identified farming as a business as the main prospect of the programme. The study concludes that the CBN Anchor Borrowers' Programme in Kebbi State has significantly improved agricultural financing. Consequently, the study recommends that the Federal Government and the CBN should review the programme by increasing the credit amount in line with the size of farmers' operations. In addition, the interest rate should be reduced to at least 5% or below to boost agricultural activities and facilitate the achievement of the programme's objectives.

title: Aggregate Demand Externalities and Capacity Utilization: a Response to Gahn (2023)
affiliations: Belmont University and Colorado State University, Fort Collins - Department of Economics

detail.title: Aggregate Demand Externalities and Capacity Utilization: a Response to Gahn (2023)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflict of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding has been received for writing this article.

detail.abstract: This note provides a response to criticisms advanced by Gahn (2023) regarding the aggregate demand externality framework. Gahn criticizes the framework's assumptions, questions the robustness of the results when independent investment functions are introduced, and expresses skepticism about the empirical results in Petach and Tavani (2019). We show that none of these critiques survive scrutiny.

title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Agricultural Employment
affiliations: , University of Florida - Food & Resource Economics Department, University of Florida and University of Florida - Food & Resource Economics Department

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Agricultural Employment
detail.abstract: We quantify how artificial intelligence (AI) innovations affect U.S. agricultural employment. Using 2003-2023 U.S. Patent and Trademark Office records, we construct a measure of agriculture's exposure to AI by classifying AI patents and mapping them to subsectors through Cooperative Patent Classification (CPC) and North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) concordances. A shift-share design with an instrumental variable approach interacts national AI innovation trends with county-level lagged employment shares. Estimates indicate that AI exposure raises employment in crop production (NAICS 111) by 10.6% and in animal production (NAICS 112) by 6.8%, relative to mean employment levels in each subsector. Decomposing AI based on its underlying function reveals heterogeneity in employment effects. Execution-oriented AI (hardware and automation) reduces overall agricultural employment (NAICS 11) by 6.9%, while cognition-oriented AI (decision-support) and perception-oriented AI (sensing) increase employment (4.3% and 6%, respectively). These domain-specific patterns are consistent across crop and animal subsectors, with stronger employment effects in crop agriculture (-12.8% for execution-, 9.1% for cognition-, and 10% for perception-oriented AI) than in animal agriculture (-4.5% for execution-, and 7.8% for perception-oriented AI, respectively). Results show that AI does not uniformly displace farm labor; instead, its effects depend on technological complementarities and task reallocation. By uncovering domain-specific dynamics, this study demonstrates how targeted AI innovations can augment agricultural employment, informing policies that support skill upgrading and diffusion of complementary technologies.

title: Ecological and Economic Impacts of Ocean Deoxygenation on Pacific Halibut Fisheries: A Multidisciplinary Assessment of Projected Losses
affiliations: , , University of British Columbia (UBC) - Fisheries Economics Research Unit, ,  and University of British Columbia (UBC) - Fisheries Economics Research Unit

detail.title: Ecological and Economic Impacts of Ocean Deoxygenation on Pacific Halibut Fisheries: A Multidisciplinary Assessment of Projected Losses
detail.abstract: The ocean has been losing oxygen content since at least the last century, and the rate of decline is accelerated by climate-induced changes like ocean warming, acidification, and anthropogenic driven nutrient load. Oxygen loss alters marine ecosystems and life, and consequently, human-wellbeing based on fisheries. Since marine fishes are known to be the most sensitive to deoxygenation, their mortality, growth, and abundance are affected by dissolved oxygen levels. Hence, fisheries relying on fish stocks are also impacted, with significant economic repercussions for society. The ability to estimate the economic impacts of deoxygenation on fisheries is hampered by the uncertain link between biogeochemical pathways and socio-economic impacts. Thus, we conducted a multidisciplinary modeling approach integrating ecological (metabolic rate index), biological (stock biomass dynamics), and economic (economic rent based on MSY) components to assess the economic ramifications of ocean deoxygenation (2020-2100) on the British Columbia Pacific halibut fishery.We find that under conditions of up to 40% reduction in dissolved oxygen and a 30% increase in temperature by 2100, Pacific halibut biomass could decrease by 66% ~ 89%. This significant decrease in catch could lead to an estimated cumulative economic loss of around $100 million by 2100. Ripple effects throughout the supply chain, including secondary (processing) and tertiary industries (distribution, marketing), could cause an additional economic impact loss of up to $197 million by 2100. Therefore, our study suggests it is crucial for the Pacific Halibut Commission and fisheries to incorporate adaptation and mitigation strategies to counteract ongoing deoxygenation and warming.

title: Green amenities and perceived air pollution exposure beyond the urban boundaries
affiliations: ,  and

detail.title: Green amenities and perceived air pollution exposure beyond the urban boundaries
detail.abstract: Individual perception of air pollution is a crucial determinant of behaviour responses and efficiency of public policy. Urban expansion and households’ preferences for natural amenities increase traffic emissions and bring population closer to air pollution from agricultural activities. By focusing mainly on urban areas, previous literature has overlooked the mediating effect of household’s residential location choice, when addressing the effects of green areas on individuals' perception of air pollution and the presence of perception bias. Building on the predictions of a theoretical model of urban sprawl, this study distinguishes the direct, cognitive, effect of natural amenities on pollution perception from the indirect effect of these variables through household’s residential preferences. By connecting individual data from the EU-SILC survey for France for 2018 with environmental and biophysical data from different sources, we show that a neighbourhood “halo effect” is at play for households located in peri-urban and rural municipalities. The probability of an individual perceiving air pollution seems to be lowered by the presence of forest, grassland and agricultural areas. In the case of green spaces, the “halo effect” is significant only for Paris. The results also show that young households tend to locate in peri-urban areas in order to benefit from green amenities. However, this choice is mainly attributable to an eviction effect of market mechanisms (high housing costs near urban parks). This underscores the often-unacknowledged trade-offs faced by individuals residing in peri-urban and rural areas. Based on these findings, public policy implications are discussed.

title: Corporate Footprints and the "Rest of the World": A Geographical Extension of FIGARO
affiliations: and WifOR Institute

detail.title: Corporate Footprints and the "Rest of the World": A Geographical Extension of FIGARO
detail.abstract: In recent years, increasing attention has been devoted to assessing the impact of companies on society and the environment. Various regulatory frameworks require information on the supply-chain impacts of corporate activities. However, the data needed to support such disclosures and to conduct materiality analyses are often lacking or costly to obtain. Multi-Regional Input-Output (MRIO) analysis, coupled with environmental and social satellite accounts, oers an inexpensive alternative for estimating such impacts by relying on industry averages. Yet, the scope and availability of existing I-O databases remain limited: sectoral and geographical aggregation often obscures important details in footprint assessments. To demonstrate the importance of geographical disaggregation, we construct an I-O table for 194 countries and 64 sectors by expanding the Eurostat FIGARO tables using a gravity model of trade and the KRAS matrix-balancing algorithm. We compare the environmental and social footprints of households in major economies using both the original and the expanded tables. While indicators concentrated in the major economies represented in the original FIGARO database yield highly consistent footprints, we observe considerable variation for indicators whose impacts are concentrated in the so-called Rest-of-the-World aggregate. This highlights the risk of misreportingparticularly for supply chains that extend into poorer countries.

title: Community-based Initiatives for Energy Access: A Qualitative Assessment of the Processes and Outcomes of Five Implementations in Mayotte
affiliations: Independent, Independent,  and

detail.title: Community-based Initiatives for Energy Access: A Qualitative Assessment of the Processes and Outcomes of Five Implementations in Mayotte
detail.abstract: Energy Communities (ECs) have become central to contemporary debates on the energy transition as a collective, democratic and bottom-up form of energy governance, yet limited empirical evidence exists on how they develop in low-resource contexts and island settings marked by energy poverty and structural constraints. This article addresses this gap by examining the conditions that enable their successful realization through an in-depth analysis of five EC initiatives implemented in Mayotte with a community-based approach. Drawing on ten semi-structured interviews with community members and stakeholders, the study concentrates on the processes and outcomes of EC implementation. Findings highlight the importance of inclusive participation, adaptive and transparent decision-making, and the influence of cultural and contextual factors in shaping implementation processes. With respect to outcomes, the findings reveal that the implemented ECs generated strong community engagement, empowerment through skills development, and improved access to energy and mobility services, while simultaneously confronted with regulatory complexity, limited technical capacity, and exposure to external shocks. Beyond tracing these conditions, the study provides insights into how participants collectively interpret and negotiate energy transitions in their everyday lives, offering valuable implications for policymakers seeking to design contextsensitive energy interventions. The article concludes by underscoring the need for more comparative research to assess the long-term success, resilience and scalability of communitybased energy initiatives in low-resource and vulnerable island settings.

title: Impure Public and Impure Private Goods - A Proposal for an Extended Economic Goods Framework

detail.title: Impure Public and Impure Private Goods - A Proposal for an Extended Economic Goods Framework
detail.abstract:
The traditional fourfold classification of economic goods, consisting of public goods, private goods, club goods, and common goods, faces two central limitations: its simplicity fails to capture the full complexity of real-world goods, in particular for the dimension of excludability, and it leaves conceptual ambiguity for impure types of goods that are neither purely public nor purely private.

This paper argues that this conceptual ambiguity has led to an inconsistent application of the terms impure public goods and impure private goods and, in consequence, has further resulted in an inconsistent choice of theoretical modelling approaches in the applied economic literature.

To address this conceptual gap, this paper proposes unambiguous definitions of impure public and impure private goods grounded in the legal protection of their underlying entitlements. Building on Calabresi and Melamed’s distinction between property rules and liability rules and on Demsetz’s theory of property rights, impure public goods are defined as goods protected predominantly by liability rules, while impure private goods are defined as goods protected predominantly by property rules. 

By further distinguishing between economic excludability as a theoretical construct and the factual possibility of exclusion, and accounting for dynamic aspects of rivalry and excludability, the Multi-Layered Framework of Economic Goods facilitates a more granular classification of resources into the economic goods typology, and further guides theoretical modelling approaches for different types of goods.

title: Regulating Automated Vehicle Markets
affiliations: and Hebrew University of Jerusalem

detail.title: Regulating Automated Vehicle Markets
detail.abstract: We examine how the organization of automated vehicle (AV) services influences commuter access, pricing and welfare in suburban areas. A game-theoretic model is developed in which commuters endogenously sort into three groups: non-travelers, users of AV feeder services to connect with public transport and direct AV riders. This threshold-based framework enables an analytical comparison of welfare outcomes across alternative market designs. Four service configurations are analyzed: a single monopolist, regional monopolists, a service-based duopoly and an oligopoly. The analysis shows that consumer surplus increases with competition, but overall welfare follows a non-monotonic pattern, peaking with limited competition. Both excessive concentration and fragmentation generate inefficiencies in commuter exclusion, pricing, frequencies and congestion. Perhaps surprisingly, we find that functional specialization in which feeder and direct AV services are served by different companies produces more equitable and efficient outcomes than geographic specialization, which is utilized in many countries around the globe. Optimal subsidy and pricing schemes differ substantially across settings, with targeted feeder subsidies preferred in concentrated markets and congestion charges necessary in fragmented markets. A calibrated case study from Hamilton, Ontario, demonstrates potential policy implications. The results highlight the importance of aligning regulatory instruments with industry structure to improve equity and efficiency in future AV-integrated transport systems.

title: The Industry Composition of Employment Centers in Large Urban Areas

detail.title: The Industry Composition of Employment Centers in Large Urban Areas
detail.abstract: The paper begins by examining the percentage distribution of employment by industry sector for employment centers within 55 large urban areas. The novel technique of Q-mode principal components analysis is used to classify centers into groups having similar industry compositions. Most common are the diversified commercial centers with office employment complemented by retail and accommodation and food service employment. The additional classes include centers with concentrations of employment in health care, education, public administration, goods production and distribution, and transportation and warehousing.

title: Alternative Pricing Strategies of Gasoline Stations: Insights from Actor-Based Simulations
affiliations: Heinrich Heine University Dusseldorf

detail.title: Alternative Pricing Strategies of Gasoline Stations: Insights from Actor-Based Simulations
detail.abstract: From an economic perspective, gasoline prices should be uniform and only respond to changes in crude prices. Empirically, this is not the case. How the price is set at the pump is primarily a strategic decision of gasoline stations. Existing research, using economic models, regression models, but also simulations, investigated the role of spatial locations of stations and the crude prices on the stations' profit. It is presumed that stations engage in Edgeworth pricing cycles, but recent empirical evidence indicates this to be not consistently the case. I inquire into how alternative pricing strategies affect the stations' profit and the customer surplus using a stylized agent-based simulation, with two competing stations, and customers differing in price sensitivity. While the behavioral assumptions are highly simplified and plausible, the simulation shows emergent and highly counter-intuitive phenomena. Overall, engaging in pricing based on random markups with high volatility is the most profitable strategy for the stations. This may account for both, the high volatility observable in retail gasoline markets and the deviations from the patterns implied by Edgeworth pricing.

title: Play-to-Earn Blockchain Video Games: A Glimpse into the Future of Work
affiliations: and University of Houston Clear Lake

detail.title: Play-to-Earn Blockchain Video Games: A Glimpse into the Future of Work
detail.abstract: An emerging trend in the video game industry is "Play-to-Earn", where consumers can monetarize their in-game achievement by trading a leveled-up game asset. This is made possible by the smart contract capability of blockchain. We use a two-period model in which a video game publisher sells both a video game and an asset. The publisher decides whether the asset is tradable. Consumers choose whether to purchase the video game and the asset, as well as how much effort to exert in leveling up the asset (grinding). Consumers can act as prosumers: both consuming the asset and producing a leveled-up version of it. If the asset is tradable, consumers can sell it. The play-to-earn scenario arises when consumers exert effort to level up their asset and then sell it to other consumers. First, although tradability introduces competition for the publisher in selling assets, we find that the publisher still benefits from allowing tradability when consumers face moderate leveling-up costs-even if the publisher earns no trading revenue and incurs administrative costs from allowing tradability. Second, consumers who choose to engage in play-to-earn may be worse off simply by having the option to participate in play-to-earn. Third, we find that higher "grinding" costs can benefit both publisher and consumers. Fourth, offering a more powerful basic asset may not only lead to lower price but also to reduced demand. Play-to-earn represents a potential "future-of-work", where consumers can monetarize their digital achievements. Trading occurs in a decentralized manner, allows the trading of a leveled-up asset that is co-created by the publisher and the consumers. Examining play-to-earn games provides valuable insights into how blockchain could be implemented in other industries.

title: Fiscal Geometry: Institutional Distortion in OECD Pillar Two Across an X-Y Fiscal Plane

detail.title: Fiscal Geometry: Institutional Distortion in OECD Pillar Two Across an X-Y Fiscal Plane

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests. This paper is a methodological study based on publicly available documents and does not involve any client-specific information.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, personal data, or confidential records. Ethics approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Contemporary analyses of the OECD Two-Pillar Solution primarily focus on legal design, policy coordination, or compliance mechanics within individual jurisdictions. While such approaches clarify rule content, they remain limited in explaining how repeated rule execution generates systemic institutional distortion across jurisdictions and over time.

This paper introduces a Fiscal Geometry framework to model OECD Pillar Two as a sequence of rule-capital events mapped onto a two-axis fiscal plane. The X-axis represents cross-jurisdictional fiscal positioning and treaty-based interfaces, while the Y-axis captures post-tax institutional capacity and intertemporal enforcement pressure. Within this representational grammar, Pillar Two enforcement produces dense trajectories, bottlenecks, and corridor-like distortions that are not readily observable through doctrinal or narrative analysis alone.

By situating Pillar One repositioning events, Pillar Two minimum tax enforcement, and treaty-based coordination mechanisms within a single structural space, the paper demonstrates how global minimum tax rules generate institutional tension independent of formal legal conflict. These patterns reflect constraints arising from limited enforceability, fragmented sovereignty, and asymmetric compliance obligations rather than from policy failure or normative deficiency.

The contribution of this study is methodological rather than prescriptive. Fiscal Geometry provides a neutral, reusable analytical interface for visualizing institutional distortion prior to index-based aggregation or normative evaluation. The framework is intended to support comparative analysis of global tax governance architectures and to inform future empirical and institutional research without advancing policy recommendations.

title: Halfway There? Labor-Market Equilibrium in a Sorting Model with Endogenous Discrimination
affiliations: Nova School of Business and Economics

detail.title: Halfway There? Labor-Market Equilibrium in a Sorting Model with Endogenous Discrimination
detail.abstract: I model a two-sector labor market where women pay a sector-specific "tax" on wages; and where the tax rate is the product of male over-representation and a latent discrimination factor. In this model, there always exists a stable efficient equilibrium with zero gender taxes. However, if latent discrimination is high enough and "meritocratic" enough, then there also exists a stable halfway-there equilibrium where females are under-represented in the top sector. Such equilibrium improves women's welfare relative to segregation; yet sometimes little, even if female representation is non-negligible. Moreover, and perhaps counter-intuitively, in halfway-there equilibria median female wages can be higher within both sectors.

title: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of International Law

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of International Law
detail.abstract:
Imagine a future of international law in which artificial intelligence reshapes human rights, trade, and arbitration. This work deals with the most burning issues of our times: how AI is no longer a tool but the force of transformation par excellence for global governance. Leading scholars and practitioners bring together an informed analysis of the challenges and opportunities artificial intelligence brings to the legal landscape. The text takes a comprehensive dimension - from ethical dilemmas to technical hurdles - by going in-depth concerning every chapter on what AI can do for international law.
Whether researcher, legal professional, or policymaker, there is much to learn from these insights and how they shape the view of the role AI could potentially play within the law and redefine what justice looks like on a global scale. Prepare to be challenged, enlightened, and inspired by a work that dares to ask the hard questions - and teases at the answers waiting just beyond the horizon.

title: The Effect of Online Sales Bans on E-Cigarette Use
affiliations: Revelio Labs, University of Kentucky, Bentley University - Department of Economics, National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) - NY Office, Georgia Institute of Technology, National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER), NY Office, San Diego State University, CUNY - The Graduate Center, Georgia  Institute  of  Technology, San Diego State University - Department of Economics and National Bureau of Economic Research

detail.title: The Effect of Online Sales Bans on E-Cigarette Use
detail.abstract: Policymakers at the state and federal levels have argued that restricting online sales of e-cigarettes is a crucial policy tool to curb youth vaping. This study is the first to explore the effectiveness of statewide restrictions on online sales of electronic nicotine delivery systems (ENDS) on teen and young adult ENDS use. Using data from four national datasets (Monitoring the Future, State and Combined Youth Risk Behavior Surveillance System surveys, Population Assessment of Tobacco and Health, and Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System survey) and a generalized difference-in-differences approach, we find no evidence that such laws are effective at curbing youth ENDS use. With 95 percent confidence, we can rule out that online sales restrictions reduced prior-month ENDS use by more than 3.6 percent of the pre-treatment mean vaping rate. An exploration of mechanisms suggests that (1) while restrictions on online sales may have a small negative effect on online purchases, youths are able to substitute to other sources for ENDS products to compensate for reduced online access, and (2) online sources are a very rare source of e-cigarettes for youths. Finally, we also find no evidence that online sales restrictions reduce adult ENDS use.

title: The Emerging Market for Intelligence: Pricing, Supply, and Demand for LLMs
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management, Boston University - Questrom School of Business, Microsoft Corp. and Microsoft Corporation

detail.title: The Emerging Market for Intelligence: Pricing, Supply, and Demand for LLMs
