detail.abstract: We document six facts about the structure and dynamics of the LLM market using API usage data from OpenRouter and Microsoft Azure. First, we show rapid growth in the number of models, creators, and inference providers, driven by open-source entrants. Second, we show price declines and persistent price heterogeneity across and within intelligence tiers, with open-source models being 90% cheaper than comparable closed-source models of the same intelligence. Third, we document market dynamism, with frequent turnover among leading models and creators. Fourth, we present evidence of horizontal and vertical differentiation, with no single model dominating across use cases, and demand for intelligence varying widely across applications. Fifth, we estimate preliminary short-run price elasticities just above one, suggesting limited scope for Jevons-Paradox effects. Finally, we show that although the share of firms that use multiple models increased over time, most firms concentrate their use on a single model, consistent with experimentation rather than persistent reliance on multiple models.

title: What Threshold Should be Applied to Tests of Factor Models?
affiliations: Duke University - Fuqua School of Business, University of London, Royal Holloway College - Department of Economics and University of Sussex

detail.title: What Threshold Should be Applied to Tests of Factor Models?
detail.abstract: Researchers broadly acknowledge that statistical tests must be adjusted when hundreds of factors and trading strategies have been examined. But how should these adjustments be made? Existing methods are often misunderstood or misapplied. We show that proper inference requires accounting for dependence across tests, correctly specifying the null distribution, and mitigating sample-selection bias. We develop a simple framework that avoids assumptions about the total number of tests run and yields a lower bound on valid significance thresholds - implying that researchers should employ a t-statistic cutoff of at least 3.0. In addition, we advocate using the local False Discovery Rate, which provides the probability that the null hypothesis is true for a given test-statistic realization - information that a conventional p-value cannot supply.

title: Fiscal Policy: Financing and Indebtedness
affiliations: , University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, Indiana University Bloomington - Department of Economics and Tsinghua University - PBC School of Finance

detail.title: Fiscal Policy: Financing and Indebtedness
detail.abstract: We conduct a large-scale information randomized controlled trial to study fiscal policy impacts. Surveying approximately 9,000 households across five eurozone countries with varying debt-to-GDP ratios enables a clean cross-country comparison. The key finding is that the fiscal multiplier depends jointly on the financing method and the country’s debt burden: multipliers are smaller in high-debt countries when debt-financed but remain similar across countries when tax-financed. Finally, we develop a New Keynesian model featuring fiscal discipline, which reproduces the empirical patterns observed in the survey and highlights their underlying economic mechanisms.

title: Short-Sighted Demands, Long-Term Consequences: When Political Competition Undermines Disaster Preparedness

detail.title: Short-Sighted Demands, Long-Term Consequences: When Political Competition Undermines Disaster Preparedness
detail.abstract: Natural disasters span political boundaries, yet their devastating impacts vary widely across political jurisdictions. I argue that this is because of the differences in political incentives to uphold regulations concerning disaster preparedness. Turkey's 2023 earthquake provides a rare empirical window to observe the cumulative effects of otherwise hidden political incentives. Leveraging the quasi-random shock of the earthquake, I employ a spatial regression discontinuity design along municipal boundaries in the earthquake region. I treat long-term party rule as the treatment and neighborhood-level destruction as the outcome. The analysis shows that neighborhoods governed by the same municipal party for more than 25 years experienced approximately 20% less destruction than their adjacent, politically contested counterparts. These findings translate into substantially lower exposure of hundreds of residents to known disaster risks. The results demonstrate that electoral competition without institutional brakes can deteriorate long-term policy outcomes. My paper underscores the importance of sharing accountability with technocratic oversight in policy areas requiring sustained infrastructural investment, such as disaster preparedness.

title: Generative AI and Its Effects on the Workforce: Understanding the Changing Nature of Work in the Age of AI

detail.title: Generative AI and Its Effects on the Workforce: Understanding the Changing Nature of Work in the Age of AI
detail.abstract: This research examines the effects of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) on the workforce. The primary focus includes how GenAI technologies are reshaping job roles, altering skill requirements, and societal integration between the workplace and industry. Drawing on case studies, industry reports, and scholarly research, the research highlights both the opportunities and complications that GenAI presents for employees and organizations. Additionally, this research presents a historical context of how GenAI came to its current state.

title: Optimal Binning in Logistic Regression From Naive Cuts to Constrained Optimisation in Regulated Settings
affiliations: Université Paris I Panthéon-Sorbonne

detail.title: Optimal Binning in Logistic Regression From Naive Cuts to Constrained Optimisation in Regulated Settings
detail.abstract:
Logistic regression remains a workhorse for credit risk and many other binary classification problems because it is fast, stable, and easy to interpret. Yet in practice, its strongest assumption—linear log-odds in each feature—often breaks on real-world drivers such as age, ratios, and lab values, which can be U-shaped, thresholded, or noisy in the tails. A common remedy is discretisation (“binning”), but naïve binning can be arbitrary, brittle, and hard to justify.

This talk introduces optimal binning as a principled optimisation problem: finding cut points that maximise a target-aware score (e.g., information value, log-likelihood, Gini) under practical constraints such as minimum bin size, minimum events per bin, a cap on the number of bins, and optional monotonicity. Using the optbinning library, we show how optimal binning produces stable, explainable transformations (often via Weight of Evidence) that improve robustness and calibration while preserving model interpretability. We compare raw logistic regression, tree-based binning, and optimal binning on a real credit-style dataset, highlighting when and why optimal binning can meaningfully improve performance without turning the model into a black box.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates how financial frictions shape the joint dynamics of firms' innovation and export behavior. Using firm-level survey data for Italian manufacturing companies, we document a mutually reinforcing relationship between innovation and exporting: innovation increases both the probability of exporting and the intensity of foreign sales, while export participation raises subsequent innovative effort. Credit rationing constrains both activities, limiting firms' ability to invest in R&D and to expand in foreign markets. Its effects, however, are asymmetric: financial constraints systematically depress innovation, but they hinder exporting only among non-innovative firms. Innovation thus partly insulates firms from the adverse impact of tight credit on internationalization. Overall, the results underscore the role of financial frictions in shaping firms' strategic choices and suggest that policies fostering innovation may indirectly promote export participation in credit-constrained environments.

title: Economic Baselines For Evaluating Disaster Resilience And Recovery
affiliations: Ohio State University (OSU), John Glenn College of Public Affairs, Kyoto University, Kyoto University, Kyoto University, University of Florida, Ohio State University (OSU) and University of Southern California - Sol Price School of Public Policy

detail.title: Economic Baselines For Evaluating Disaster Resilience And Recovery

declarations.declarationOfInterest: not applicable
declarations.ethicsApproval: not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: U.S. National Science Foundation and the Japanese Science and Technology Agency

detail.abstract: The vast majority of disaster literature does not adequately distinguish resilience from recovery. Quantifying resilience is often confounded by the challenge of identifying clear conceptual and empirical reference paths, or baselines, by which to trace system recovery in general or economic activity in particular. The baselines reflect recovery over time in the absence and presence of resilience actions, or tactics, individually or in groups. This paper addresses these challenges by providing working definitions, conceptual distinctions, and alternative baselines for differentiating and quantifying these two key concepts from an economic perspective. The paper first refines the conceptual distinction between static economic resilience and dynamic economic resilience. It then provides a justification for distinguishing resilience from recovery, and it provides a rationale for evaluating resilience as efficient recovery. To facilitate empirical research, the paper provides a framework for establishing both upper-bound and lower-bound recovery baselines. These baselines help identify important counterfactuals by which resilience can be distinguished from ordinary recovery, and through which resilience metrics at the microeconomic level can be quantified. Finally, the paper provides an empirical example using data from businesses impacted by the 2011 Great East Japan Earthquake. The example utilizes stochastic frontier analysis to quantify efficiency using the empirical baselines approach that the paper introduces. The conceptual and empirical concepts provided here have societal and public policy implications for improving public and private-sector decision making, resilience planning, business and other institutional continuity, insurance assessment, and recovery benchmarking.

title: Firms’ Legitimacy of Science Citations vs Business Citations and Duration of the SME’s Planned Acquisition Exit in the Biopharmaceutical Sector
affiliations: Northeastern University, ICOIS and Northeastern University

detail.title: Firms’ Legitimacy of Science Citations vs Business Citations and Duration of the SME’s Planned Acquisition Exit in the Biopharmaceutical Sector
detail.abstract: This article examines how academic and media citations affect the exit strategies of small and medium enterprises (SMEs) in the biotechnology sector. Using a strategic selling framework, we analyse the duration of acquisition exits (AEs) among SMEs. A shorter entry-exit duration signifies a more successful planned AE through the lenses of legitimacy theory and signalling view. Our study, which includes 744 acquisition exits (AEs), shows that SMEs with higher academic citations have shorter durations from the birth of the firm to the AE event.  Likewise, business media citations reduce this duration for high-tech biotechnology SMEs. Framing these citations as legitimacy mechanisms, we contribute to institutional theory by addressing uncertainty reduction between AE candidates and buyers. The implications of these results are discussed in terms of the strategic value of different types of citations for SMEs in the biotechnology sector.

title: Scarcity in an Age of AI Abundance
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Scarcity in an Age of AI Abundance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study does not involve human participants, patients, or case studies requiring ethics approval. All data used are publicly available.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was conducted independently, without external funding or institutional support.

detail.abstract: A growing narrative in technology commentary and macroeconomics claims that AI and robotics will usher in material abundance, near-zero marginal costs, and an erosion of prices and work. This paper argues that such post-scarcity visions are conceptually misleading: even when AI delivers AI technological abundance (ATA), understood as cost compression and capability expansion, it does not eliminate scarcity. It reorganizes scarcity by shifting which constraints bind and where rents are generated. I develop a five-layer framework in which scarcity and rent formation arise in (1) physical resources and space, (2) infrastructure such as energy, compute, fabs, data centers, and automation, (3) capabilities including high-trust organizational knowhow, (4) institutions that govern access, and (5) jurisdictions that supply enforcement capacity and security. Ownership and control cut across layers and shape distribution; in a minimal formulation, actor-level rent income is determined by the interaction of the layer rent vector and a cross-layer exposure matrix. A central distinction follows: ATA is not the same as AI economic abundance (AEA), defined as broad affordability of a basic living-standards bundle. AEA obtains only when household resources from labor income, rent claims, and net transfers keep pace with the bundle price, which depends on rent intensity in layers that load heavily on essentials such as housing, energy, infrastructure access, and jurisdictional safety. The framework maps plausible winners and losers across industries and households and draws implications for work, inequality, investment, and the political economy of transfers.

title: Wrong Fit, Missed Gains? Evidence from Skill Training Choices in Liberia

detail.abstract: Young job seekers commonly misperceive training returns; we test whether these beliefs misalign choices between two widely offered tracks—job-skills and business-skills training for young women in Liberia. We reassign 30\% of applicants from an oversubscribed job-skills program to business-skills and compare them to applicants who remain in their preferred track. In the short run, reassigned applicants outperform, with employment and earnings gains two to three times larger. By the medium run, most averages converge but mask sharp heterogeneity: some women gain substantially, others lose. Elicited expectations are consistent with misaligned track choices and suggest belief distortions.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes a non-medical, system-level account of institutional operation built on two irreducible mechanisms: circulation and respiration. The claim is deliberately minimal. Any institutional system that continues to function must (i) circulate resources-allocate, route, and recover fiscal capacity through rule-governed pathways-and (ii) "breathe" information-intake, filter, exchange, and expel legally accountable signals that make rule-based administration possible. These mechanisms are not presented as biological claims. They are used as operational primitives: necessary conditions for system continuity, renewal, and routine behavior.

The author examines how the modification of the fiscal system affects trade and investment flows, as well as Russia's position in international production chains. The methodology is based on the analysis of legislative initiatives, official statistics and comparative analysis. Stability, on the other hand, poses risks to the competitiveness of exporters and the inflow of investment, potentially accelerating the reorientation of economic cooperation towards Asian countries. The conclusion is made about the need for balanced compensatory measures.

title: When Green Dies in Greed: Environmental Externalities of Government Subsidies
affiliations: The University of Auckland Business School and The University of Auckland Business School

detail.title: When Green Dies in Greed: Environmental Externalities of Government Subsidies
detail.abstract: This study delves into the unintended consequences of government subsidies on corporate environmental responsibility. Our findings reveal a concerning positive association between subsidy amounts and firms' toxic emissions, suggesting that subsidized firms are more likely to prioritize production expansion over pollution mitigation. Furthermore, our analysis uncovers a pattern of regulatory leniency in enforcing pollution activities of subsidized firms, raising questions about the influence of political interests on oversight. The negative externalities of subsidies are particularly pronounced in firms facing lower reputational costs of pollution, greater financial constraints, and operating in less competitive product markets. These results call for a critical reassessment of government subsidy programs and the design of more effective regulatory mechanisms to ensure environmental sustainability.

title: The Departed: Italian Migration and American Mafia
affiliations: Bocconi University, Bocconi University - BAFFI Center on International Markets, Money, and Regulation and Bocconi University

detail.title: The Departed: Italian Migration and American Mafia

publicationDetails.journalName: BAFFI Centre on Economics, Finance & Regulation Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We study the short- and long-term effects of organized crime across neighborhoods in U.S. cities by exploiting the migration of Sicilian Mafia members in the 1920s who fled a large-scale repression campaign in Italy. Using newly linked administrative and historical data from the U.S. Census, Social Security records, and declassified files of the Federal Bureau of Narcotics, we show that neighborhoods hosting enclaves of migrants from Sicilian towns targeted by the repression later became centers of Italo-American Mafia activity. These neighborhoods experienced higher violence, incarceration, and financial exclusion in the short run, but higher educational attainment and employment in the long run. The results suggest that while the arrival of organized criminal networks initially intensified conflict and exclusion, their subsequent consolidation generated localized economic spillovers, helping to explain the long-term resilience and persistence of organized crime.

title: "Still Strong": The Effects of Hurricane Irene On The Preferences and Policy Views of Vermonters More Than One Decade Later"
affiliations: Middlebury College - Department of Economics, Middlebury College, Middlebury College - Department of Economics, Middlebury College and

detail.title: "Still Strong": The Effects of Hurricane Irene On The Preferences and Policy Views of Vermonters More Than One Decade Later"
detail.abstract: We examine the long-term effects of Hurricane Irene in 2011, Vermont's largest natural disaster, on economic preferences and climate policy support. Using survey data collected more than a decade later, we measure disaster exposure by individual experience, with the storm's uneven impact providing plausibly exogenous variation for a quasi-natural experimental design. We find that exposed individuals are more risk tolerant, more patient, and display significantly greater trust and community attachment, consistent with post-traumatic growth. These preference shifts align with stronger support for climate mitigation: those more affected by Irene are more likely to favor increased federal action on climate policy. To our knowledge, this is the first study to document preference changes persisting a decade after a natural disaster, highlighting the lasting behavioral legacy of large one-time shocks.

title: The Impact of Seattle's Sweetened Beverage Tax on Prices Persists after Two Years, but Does Not Vary by Neighborhood Characteristics
affiliations: University of Washington, University of Washington, University of Illinois at Chicago, University of Washington - School of Public Health, Seattle Children's Research Institute, University of Washington and University of Washington

detail.title: The Impact of Seattle's Sweetened Beverage Tax on Prices Persists after Two Years, but Does Not Vary by Neighborhood Characteristics
detail.abstract: Sugar sweetened beverages are a leading source of added sugar and believed to be a cause of health disparities in the U.S. Several U.S. cities implemented sweetened beverage taxes to reduce sugar consumption and improve health, yet little is known about the impact of these taxes by consumer characteristics. We estimate the impact of Seattle’s Sweetened Beverage Tax on prices by neighborhood income, race, and ethnicity 24 months after the tax was implemented. We find that retailers pass 84% or 1.47 cents of the 1.75 cents per ounce tax on to consumers in the form of higher prices. We do not find statistically significant differences in the amount of the tax passed through to consumers by the median income or racial and ethnic composition of the neighborhood where retailers are located.

title: The Labor Market and Health Impacts of Reducing Cesarean Section Deliveries
affiliations: University of Michigan at Ann Arbor, Stanford University, Stanford University and New York University (NYU) - New York University

detail.title: The Labor Market and Health Impacts of Reducing Cesarean Section Deliveries
detail.abstract:
One in three births in the United States is delivered by cesarean section (c-section). This paper studies the labor market and health effects of c-sections, using newly linked administrative data that combines the universe of California birth records with mothers’ quarterly earnings. We analyze the impact of an intervention that reduced c-section rates among low-risk first-time births, and find that mothers exposed to the intervention appear to have a higher likelihood of employment in the quarter following birth, as well as a higher likelihood of returning to their pre-birth employer. These impacts attenuate over time—suggesting that a c-section primarily delays return to the labor market following childbirth—but attachment to the pre-birth employer remains higher five quarters post-birth. We find no evidence of significant impacts on maternal or infant health, indicating that the intervention-induced decline in c-sections did not come at the cost of worse outcomes. Further, among mothers who have another child, we find that exposure to the intervention at the first birth leads to a lower likelihood of c-section and preterm delivery at the second one, implying that both the economic and health benefits of reduced c-sections may compound with birth order.

title: Explaining the Widening Divides in US Midlife Mortality: Is There a Smoking Gun?
affiliations: Federal Reserve Bank of Boston, Harvard School of Public Health, Dartmouth College - Department of Economics and University of Pennsylvania

detail.title: Explaining the Widening Divides in US Midlife Mortality: Is There a Smoking Gun?
detail.abstract:
The education-mortality gradient has increased sharply in the last three decades, with the life-expectancy gap between people with and without a college degree widening from 2.6 years in 1992 to 6.3 years in 2019 (Case and Deaton 2023). During the same period, mortality inequality across counties rose 30 percent, accompanied by an increasing rural health penalty. Using county- and state-level data from the 1992–2019 period, we demonstrate that these three trends arose due to a fundamental shift in the geographic patterns of mortality among college and non-college populations. First, we find a sharp decline in both mortality rates and geographic inequality for college graduates. Second, the reverse was true for people without a college degree; spatial inequality became amplified. Third, we find that rates of smoking play a key role in explaining all three empirical puzzles, with secondary roles attributed to income, other health behaviors, and state policies. Less well-understood is why “place effects” matter so much for smoking (and mortality) for those without a college degree.

title: Overlapping Policy Interventions: Evidence from Home Health
affiliations: Stanford University - Department of Economics, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Department of Economics, Georgetown University and Stanford University

detail.title: Overlapping Policy Interventions: Evidence from Home Health
detail.abstract:
Governments often concurrently deploy multiple policy instruments to tackle a common objective, yet researchers typically analyze each policy's impacts independently. We study interactions across policies and their implications within the context of efforts to reduce Medicare-financed home health services. We consider two geographically targeted policies: strike force prosecutions of suspected fraud and moratoria on the entry of new home health agencies. Depending on location and time, we observe either both, one, or neither policy in place. Individually, each policy reduced home health use substantially, and was well-targeted to places with higher treatment effects. Although we estimate only a modest interaction between the two policies, we find that optimally allocating them across the areas that received at least one policy could have increased their total impact by about 20% relative to the observed placement. Our exercise highlights the potential gains from coordination across different policy instruments pursuing similar objectives.

detail.abstract: This article examines the evolution of gender-based refugee protection in international law and the European Union. Initially, the Geneva Convention overlooked gender-based persecution, but persistent efforts by scholars and international bodies have led to significant advancements. Key international instruments, such as the UNHCR guidelines, the Istanbul Convention, and CEDAW, emphasize gender-sensitive asylum laws. Also, from the beginning, the common asylum system of the European Union incorporated a gender perspective in legislative instruments. The 2024 rulings by the Court of Justice of the European Union in this realm marked a pivotal moment, recognizing systemic oppression of women as grounds for asylum.

title: Financializing the Professions: The Rise of Private Equity in Accounting
affiliations: London Business School and Yale School of Management

detail.title: Financializing the Professions: The Rise of Private Equity in Accounting
detail.abstract:
Private equity (PE) has moved rapidly into professional services, yet its impact on accounting, where licensing regimes, reputational capital, and partnership governance traditionally limit external ownership, remains poorly understood. We examine how PE ownership alters the organization and market structure of accounting firms using data from 1999-2024 that link more than 3,600 PE transactions to detailed information on mergers and acquisitions (M&A), labor markets, and audit pricing. PE investment increases sharply after 2020 and extends to both CPA-licensed audit firms and non-CPA advisory practices, with most activity in large mid-tier PCAOB-registered firms. After PE entry, firms grow faster: non-audit revenues rise, employment expands, and cross-state M&A accelerates, consistent with platform-building and consolidation. These adjustments have market-level implications. PE investment raises labor-market concentration in key accounting occupations and drives up ERISA audit fees in a standardized setting, as confirmed by a synthetic difference-in-differences design. Our results reveal a key tension at the core of professions: preserving independence and competition in a market increasingly driven by financial capital.

title: Default and Interest Rate Shocks: Renegotiation Matters

detail.title: Default and Interest Rate Shocks: Renegotiation Matters
detail.abstract:
We develop a sovereign default model with debt renegotiation in which interest-rate shocks affect default incentives through two mechanisms. Under the standard mechanism, higher interest rates tighten the government’s budget constraint. Under the renegotiation mechanism, higher rates increase lenders’ opportunity cost of holding delinquent debt, which makes lenders accept larger haircuts and makes default more attractive for the government. We argue that our novel renegotiation mechanism reconciles standard sovereign default models with the narrative that the sharp increase in the real interest rate in the United States was a relevant factor in the defaults of the early 1980s.

detail.title: Pension Reforms and Inequalities in France
detail.abstract:
This study analyzes the distributional effects of French pension reforms from 1993 to 2014 across different socioeconomic groups. Using administrative data for individuals born between 1934 and 1950, we examine the impact on social security wealth (SSW) across lifetime earnings deciles and genders. Our methodology incorporates differential life expectancy and exploits the PENSIPP model for counterfactual scenarios. Results show that reforms generally decreased SSW across all income groups, with regressive tendencies. The 1993 reform had the most significant impact, reducing SSW by over 15% for men in the lowest earnings decile compared to 5% for the highest. Subsequent reforms had milder effects. These findings contribute to understanding the long-term consequences of pension reforms on inequality and inform future policy decisions in countries facing similar demographic challenges.

detail.title: Social Security Reforms and Inequality among Older Workers in Spain
detail.abstract:
This chapter studies social security reforms and trends in inequalities among older workers over the last decades in Spain. Its main goal is to analyze the redistributive impact of the various pension reforms on older income inequality. Compared to the rules in 1985, recent pension reforms have led to an average increase on Social Security Wealth of approximately 18,000€ for men and 15,000€ for women. This represents a ten and eight percent increase, respectively. This effect is mostly driven by the mechanical or direct effect (e.g. via benefit adjustments), while changes in retirement probability (secondary or behavioral effect) are close to zero. Furthermore, we find striking differences across income quartiles, for both men and women. In both cases, there is a clear income gradient, where the richest quartile has benefitted the most with an increase close to twenty percent, or over €50,000, for both men and women. Conversely, the change for the poorest income quartile for men and the two poorest income quartiles for women is close to zero or even slightly negative. This is likely due to the effect of minimum benefits (that mark the generosity of the system, see Boldrin et al, 1999) that automatically absorb any other effect for low-income individuals.

title: Social Security and Inequality in Belgium
affiliations: University of Liège, University of Liege and University of Strasbourg

detail.title: Social Security and Inequality in Belgium
detail.abstract:
Over the years, the Belgian social security system has undergone substantial reform with a prime focus on increasing older worker labor force participation. The paper explores the effect of past reforms on inequality in old age. We distinguish two separate effects: The mechanical effect considers the change in inequality and expected benefit levels due to the reforms for a fixed retirement age distribution. The behavioral effect accounts for the endogenous change caused by changes in the incentives to work. Our results show that mechanically, reforms have led to losses in expected benefits for all but the lowest income quintile. Behavioral changes had a positive but orders of magnitude smaller effect. Overall, inequality decreased as a result of reforms.

title: Anchoring Ecodesign in EU Primary Law: Proportionality and Environmental Principles
affiliations: Lisbon Public Law Research Centre; University of Lisbon - School of Law

detail.title: Anchoring Ecodesign in EU Primary Law: Proportionality and Environmental Principles

publicationDetails.detailsText: Lisbon Public Law Working Paper No. 2025-5
publicationDetails.journalName: Lisbon Public Law Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: The goal of this paper is to examine how the principle of proportionality, when applied alongside EU primary law environmental principles, can support ambitious environmental measures such as those introduced by the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation (ESPR). The first section sets out the transition to a circular economy and the need to embed sustainability into product design, while highlighting the significant restrictions this transition imposes on the fundamental rights to property and freedom to conduct a business. The second section analyses CJEU case law on proportionality in environmental matters, showing the wide discretion afforded to the EU legislature. The third section explores the integration of environmental principles – such as sustainable development, correction at source, precaution, and the polluter-pays principle – into proportionality assessments, demonstrating how they reinforce the legitimacy of far-reaching upstream regulation. The final section applies this analysis to the ESPR, arguing that ecodesign requirements represent a natural evolution of EU environmental policy rather than a rupture, particularly in light of the essentially preventative nature of the polluter-pays principle. We concluded that ecodesign requirements are grounded in EU primary law and that the proportionality test serves not only to limit excessive regulation but also to affirm the legitimacy of ambitious environmental action.

title: Meta-Analysis of Prospect Theory Parameters
affiliations: University of Osaka, Bocconi University,  and Ghent University

detail.title: Meta-Analysis of Prospect Theory Parameters
detail.abstract: We present a meta-analysis of prospect theory (PT ) parameters, summarizing data from 166 papers reporting 812 estimates. These parameters capture risk-taking propensities, thus holding interest beyond PT. We develop an inverse-variance weighted method that accounts for correlations in PT parameters and imputes missing information on standard errors. The mean patterns align with the stylized facts of diminishing sensitivity towards outcomes and probabilities discussed in PT. Beyond this, the analysis yields several new insights: 1) between-study variation in parameters is vast; 2) heterogeneity is difficult to explain with observable study characteristics; and 3) the strongest predictors are experimental and measurement indicators, revealing systematic violations of procedure invariance. These findings highlight the promise of cognitive accounts of behavior in organizing unexplained variation in risk-taking, which we discuss.

title: Asset Returns and CO2 Emissions: Evidence on Contemporaneous and Lagged Connectedness
affiliations: University of Sfax, Brunel University London - Department of Economics and Finance and University of Navarra - Department of Economics

detail.title: Asset Returns and CO2 Emissions: Evidence on Contemporaneous and Lagged Connectedness
detail.abstract: This study examines the contemporaneous and lagged connectedness between the daily returns of AI and robotics-related assets, a global stock market index, commodity prices (gold and Brent crude oil), cryptocurrencies, and a carbon index over the period from 3 January 2023 to 30 September 2025, against a backdrop of persistent geopolitical tensions, using the innovative R² connectedness method developed by Balli et al. (2023). The results reveal that contemporaneous effects predominate over lagged ones. Furthermore, AI and robotics-related assets behave primarily as net emitters of shocks, as does the MSCI World Index, which exerts positive contagion effects and plays a central role in risk transmission. By constrast, gold and Brent crude oil act as net receivers of shocks, which in the case of the former reflects its role as a safe-haven asset. Cryptocurrencies instead exhibit heterogeneous dynamics : Cardano (ADA) acts as a net transmitter of shocks, while Bitcoin (BTC) and Stellar (XLM) behave more as receivers, contributing to market stability. Finally, the CO₂ index displays net negative connectedness, which confirm its role as a receiver of shocks. These findings provide useful information to investors and portfolio managers for risk diversification purposes and to policy-makers for ensuring financial stabilily, especially during periods of market turbulence.

title: A Model of the Model: Unpacking CGE Results on Carbon Leakage
affiliations: , University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign - Department of Finance and University of California, Santa Barbara (UCSB)

detail.title: A Model of the Model: Unpacking CGE Results on Carbon Leakage
detail.abstract: Computational general equilibrium (CGE) models can evaluate detailed tax reforms, trade restrictions, or environmental policy. These models can capture many complexities, but these complexities can make results difficult to interpret. Analytical general equilibrium (AGE) models provide better intuition and interpretation but cannot capture relevant complexities. We propose a method that employs AGE models to understand CGE models – a “model of the model”. We apply this idea to climate policy and carbon leakage – the increase in emissions elsewhere. Our AGE models identify seven key economic determinants of leakage within any one outcome. We then unpack results from three existing CGE models.

title: Trade Negotiations Under Fire: Social Identity and the Rising Opposition to Free Trade
affiliations: and University of Passau

detail.title: Trade Negotiations Under Fire: Social Identity and the Rising Opposition to Free Trade
detail.abstract: Massive protests against - and spectacular failures of - international trade negotiations are an important element of the globalization backlash developed economies have experienced over the last two decades. We analyze a model of endogenous social identity where the government chooses between accepting or rejecting a trade agreement involving the recognition of a lower precautionary standard. We show that protests by an NGO against the trade agreement can alter the social identity equilibrium, feeding back into the political process and possibly resulting in a polarization of society. We focus on two possible outcomes: the trade agreement may either be maintained, but at lower welfare gains than initially expected (the "CETA-case"), or it may be abolished altogether (the "TTIP-case).

title: On Foot: The City Seen from the Pavement
affiliations: Fondazione Eni Enrico Mattei (FEEM) and Roma Tre University

detail.title: On Foot: The City Seen from the Pavement
detail.abstract:
Urban centres are the new epicentres of sustainable policies, where diverse paradigms of economy, social life and spatial organisation are developing. In this scenario, it is necessary to rethink the role and potential of pedestrians, no longer viewed as passive subjects to be protected but as central actors in the urban landscape. 

Following the inspiration of the 15-minute city policy, which proposes a polycentric reformulation of spaces in which all essential services can be reached by soft mobility methods in a maximum of 15 minutes, the brief presents an analysis of the walkability of the Municipality of Rome according to three guidelines: availability, proximity and accessibility.

In addition to examining essential services (including schools, supermarkets, parks and rapid public transport stops), this work presents an analysis of walkability taking into account the future tram lines financed by the City Council, comparing the results of the data with the current situation to assess the impact on walkability.

title: Patient Peer Effects: Evidence from Nursing Home Room Assignments
affiliations: and University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA)

detail.title: Patient Peer Effects: Evidence from Nursing Home Room Assignments
detail.abstract: We provide causal evidence that patient peer effects generate mortality impacts comparable to provider quality differences. Drawing on administrative records covering 2.6 million stays (2000–2010) across 7,200 U.S. nursing homes, we exploit plausibly exogenous roommate assignments identified through unique room identifiers. We estimate that assignment to a roommate diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease (AD) or Alzheimer’s disease related dementias (ADRD), relative to placement in a private room, increases 90-day mortality by 2.1 percentage points (14% of baseline)—equivalent to receiving care at a nursing home one full standard deviation worse in quality. Effects differ sharply by patient type: patients with AD/ADRD benefit substantially from cognitively healthy roommates but not from private rooms, suggesting important peer monitoring and support roles. In contrast, mortality of patients without AD/ADRD does not depend on roommate cognitive health but is reduced in private rooms. A simple assignment rule exploiting this heterogeneity could reduce overall mortality by 0.8 percentage points without additional resources.

title: Risk Limited Asset Allocation with a Budget Threshold Utility Function and Leptokurtotic Distributions of Returns
affiliations: Giller Investments

detail.title: Risk Limited Asset Allocation with a Budget Threshold Utility Function and Leptokurtotic Distributions of Returns
detail.abstract: An analytical solution to single-horizon asset allocation for an investor with a piecewise-linear utility function, called herein the "budget threshold utility," and exogenous position limits is presented. The resulting functional form has a surprisingly simple structure and can be readily interpreted as representing the addition of a simple "risk cost" to otherwise frictionless trading.

title: Reintegrating Older Long-Term Unemployed Workers: The Impact of Temporary Job Guarantees
affiliations: Johannes Kepler University Linz - Department of Economics, Vienna University of Economics and Business, Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU) - ifo Institute (Leibniz Institute for Economic Research at the University of Munich) and Johannes Kepler University Linz - Department of Economics

detail.title: Reintegrating Older Long-Term Unemployed Workers: The Impact of Temporary Job Guarantees
detail.abstract: Long-term unemployment among older workers is particularly difficult to overcome. We study the impacts of a large-scale job guarantee program that offered up to two years of fully subsidized employment to long-term unemployed individuals aged 50 and above. Using a sharp age-based discontinuity in eligibility, we find that participation increased regular, unsubsidized employment by 43 percentage points two years after the program ended. The gains are driven by transitions into new firms and industries, rather than continued subsidized employment, and we find no evidence of displacement effects for non-participants or spillovers to family members. The program had no measurable short-run health effects.

This study tests whether the escalation of US-led tariffs beginning in 2018 is associated with changes in South Asian merchandise exports to the United States. Using annual country-level export values for Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan, and Sri Lanka, we estimate a simple linear model where a post-2018 indicator proxies the tariff-war period. We present pooled and country-specific results with supporting figures. While the design is descriptive and not causal, it provides a compact baseline for future work that adds sectoral controls and alternative identification strategies. The United States' imposition of tariffs since 2018-primarily targeting China but extending to a wide range of global partners-has reshaped the global trade landscape. South Asia, although not the direct target of these measures, has been indirectly affected through disrupted supply chains, shifting trade flows, and heightened uncertainty in the global economy. This paper investigates the effects of the US-led tariff war on South Asian trade flows using a combination of descriptive analysis and econometric modeling. A simple linear regression is employed to measure whether South Asian exports to the United States declined after 2018, the onset of the trade war. The analysis combines country-level trade data with secondary information from global financial institutions. Results suggest a heterogeneous impact: India and Bangladesh show modest trade contractions, while smaller economies like Nepal and Bhutan exhibit minimal direct effects but are indirectly influenced through regional spillovers. The findings emphasize the vulnerability of South Asian economies to global tariff disputes and provide policy recommendations to strengthen resilience through diversification and regional integration.

title: Stochastic Choice and Noisy Beliefs in Games
affiliations: Paris School of Economics and

detail.title: Stochastic Choice and Noisy Beliefs in Games
detail.abstract: We elicit subjects’ beliefs over opponents’ behavior multiple times for a given game without feedback. A large majority of subjects have stochasticity in their belief reports, which we argue cannot be explained by learning or measurement error, suggesting significant noise in subjects’ unobserved “true” beliefs. Using a structural model applied to actions and beliefs data jointly, we find that such “noisy beliefs” are equally important for explaining our data as “noisy actions”—the sort of stochastic choice given fixed beliefs that is commonly assumed in empirical research. We argue that beliefs and belief-noise are driven by the payoff-salience of actions.

title: Monetary Policy Tech: A primer to novel techniques for monetary policy analysis and business processes
affiliations: European Central Bank (ECB) and

detail.title: Monetary Policy Tech: A primer to novel techniques for monetary policy analysis and business processes

keywords: Large Language Models. JEL codes: E52

detail.abstract: This paper reviews technical advances that are transforming monetary policy to help practitioners better understand their impact. We provide an organizing framework to make sense of these developments, covering a range of applications related to economic analysis and business processes supporting monetary policy. Most, but not all of these developments are related to artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning (ML). While AI and ML tools offer significant potential benefits, we emphasize the importance of human oversight and governance to ensure the reliability and accountability of these technologies. Ultimately, we highlight the need for a balanced approach that leverages the strengths of AI and ML while maintaining the critical role of human decisionmakers in the monetary policy process.

title: Spatial Inequality of Restaurant Availability in the Continental United States, 2000–2010
affiliations: HNU-DUP, Hunan University, Hunan University, Hunan University, Hunan University and Xiangtan Central Hospital

detail.title: Spatial Inequality of Restaurant Availability in the Continental United States, 2000–2010
detail.abstract: With the substantial increase in eating out in the United States, the restaurant environment has become a key factor influencing dietary health and the risk of chronic diseases. Thus, spatial inequality in restaurant distribution has attracted great attention. Addressing this issue, this study examined the long-term temporal changes in restaurant availability at the national scale. Using U.S. county-level data from 2000 to 2010, we analyzed spatiotemporal changes in the density of fast food and sit-down restaurants and their spatial inequality as measured by the Gini coefficient. Results show that counties with initially high restaurant density in 2000 experienced greater subsequent growth in density compared with counties having low restaurant density in 2000. The inequality in availability of restaurant density among census block groups within counties was high in 2000 and has widened with time, particularly for fast food restaurants and large urban areas. Increases in density and inequality are highly correlated spatially. These findings indicate that inequality in restaurant availability is worsening. To minimize gaps in health equity, policymakers should focus on counties having high fast food restaurant density in the baseline year.

title: Unethical Decisions and Coordination in Groups: The Role of Information and Communication
affiliations: EBS Universität für Wirtschaft und Recht - EBS Business School, Victoria University of Wellington - Te Herenga Waka, University of Hamburg, University of Hamburg - Department of Economics and Karlsruhe Institute of Technology

detail.title: Unethical Decisions and Coordination in Groups: The Role of Information and Communication
detail.abstract: Using a behavioral game-theoretical model and an experiment we study how information and communication influence coordination in groups when they can misreport the outcome of a binary lottery. Both group members receive a positive payoff only if their reports match. Consistent with our theory, nearly all groups coordinate when allowed to communicate prior to submitting their individual reports. The extent of coordination on either truth-telling or lying is correlated with the individual lying costs. Overall, both information and communication promote coordination on more dishonesty. These findings underscore how information and communication can increase coordination and dishonesty depending on intrinsic lying-aversion.

title: Defending the Ijtihadi-Empirical Theory of Secularization A Response to Dr. M. R. Taliban's Criticism

detail.title: Defending the Ijtihadi-Empirical Theory of Secularization A Response to Dr. M. R. Taliban's Criticism
detail.abstract: This article contains a scientific and critical discussion with Dr. Mohammad Reza Taliban regarding his criticism of my book entitled the theory of secularization with an empirical ijtihadi approach. In his article "Deriving Theory from Sociology and Improperly Adapting It to Religious Texts: A Criticism on the Theory of Secularization with an Empirical Ijtihadi Approach", he made two main criticisms on the theorizing effort of this book: firstly, mistaking and adapting intrareligious topics with sociological topics related to secularization, and secondly, confusing the explanatory model with the theory. In the following article, after referring to the main principles of the theory presented in this book, I have attempted to answer these two criticisms with a logical analysis method. For this purpose, it was shown with a sufficient explanation that none of the two aforementioned claims has case in my work.

title: Trade Sanctions
affiliations: , , , , University of Antwerp, Universitat Pompeu Fabra (UPF), Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management and London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE)

detail.title: Trade Sanctions
detail.abstract: How effective are trade sanctions? We study the unprecedented sanctions imposed on Russia following February 2022, when Western countries banned exports accounting for 36% of Russia's prewar import value. Combining novel, hand-collected records of these sanctions with Russian customs data, firm balance sheets, domestic railway shipments, and government procurement contracts, we provide the most comprehensive analysis to date of the economic impact of trade sanctions on a target country. Using a difference-in-differences approach, we find that imports of sanctioned country-product varieties into Russia saw a sharp 55% decline after the war's onset. Although we document substantial rerouting through third countries, it has not fully offset the direct import losses: total imports of sanctioned products fell by 27% through 2023. Russian firms that had relied on soon-to-be-sanctioned imports experienced a 14% decline in output during the same period, not offset by competing firms or entrants. Similar declines are present for manufacturing and technology firms, and firms along the military supply chain. Affected firms have also experienced reduced government procurement sales and incurred additional losses when their buyers or suppliers were exposed to sanctions. Overall, our findings suggest that, contrary to widespread claims of ineffectiveness, export sanctions on Russia have had far-reaching adverse effects.

title: Capabilities-Related Disclosures and Investors' Recognition of Organizational Resilience – An Automated Textual Analysis of 10-K Filings
affiliations: , Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg and Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg

detail.title: Capabilities-Related Disclosures and Investors' Recognition of Organizational Resilience – An Automated Textual Analysis of 10-K Filings
detail.abstract: We show that voluntarily provided accounting information relating to the capabilities of firms to create slack, support learning, and foster innovation are associated with investors' recognition of organizational resilience (i.e., specific share price patterns) during an adverse event (COVID-19). To quantify the extent of pre-crisis capabilities-related information, we apply an automated textual analysis to voluntary disclosures in the Item 1 and Item 7 of 10-K filings in a cross-sectional sample of firms listed in the S&P 1500 Index (2018-2022). We use the share prices of our sample firms to create three capital market indicators of organizational resilience, i.e., firms' absorption, adaptation, and transformation levels amid adversity. We find that disclosures about slack capabilities are negatively associated with an immediate decrease in the share price that occurs at the onset of adversity (absorption). For most sample firms, our results also suggest that disclosures about slack, learning, and innovation capabilities accelerate the share price recovery (adaptation), while disclosures about innovation capabilities appear to increase the share price in the longer term (transformation). Our results indicate that capabilities-related disclosures are differently associated with investor reactions as firms progress through sequential stages of adversity and add incremental value to existing measures of financial performance.

title: The Curious Case of Deterrence and Threats
affiliations: University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign

detail.title: The Curious Case of Deterrence and Threats
detail.abstract: This paper studies how strategic deterrence interacts with competitive urgency in dynamic oligopoly markets with entry and exit. Building on a Markov-perfect industry dynamics framework, the analysis decomposes firms' expansion incentives into contemporaneous forces and forward-looking deterrence motives that operate through rivals' future responses. The central theoretical result shows that deterrence incentives vanish at a quadratic rate as firms' effective planning horizons shorten, implying that deterrence requires sufficiently persistent strategic value. When entry threats compress that horizon, aggressive incumbent behavior may persist even as the strategic logic of deterrence collapses. The framework reconciles models of entry deterrence with empirical evidence on threat-driven behavior and clarifies when aggressive responses reflect long-run strategy versus short-run urgency.

title: A Fiscal Epistemology of Information: Mapping Evidence Through the X-Y Coordinate of Cross-Border Capital and Intergenerational Capacity

detail.title: A Fiscal Epistemology of Information: Mapping Evidence Through the X-Y Coordinate of Cross-Border Capital and Intergenerational Capacity

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is a theoretical and methodological analysis based solely on publicly available laws, policy documents, and aggregate administrative statistics. It does not involve human participants or identifiable personal data, and therefore formal ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency, commercial or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: In an era saturated with disinformation, media analysis, and competing truth claims, this paper asks a prior question: what kinds of information should count as reliable evidence for studying institutional inequality? Rather than beginning from news, commentary, or social media, I develop a fiscal epistemology of information grounded in public law, administrative data, and a geometric model of capital movement. The paper advances an X–Y coordinate framework in which the X-axis traces cross-border fiscal movement of pre-tax public capital and post-tax private capital across tax jurisdictions, while the Y-axis captures the downward transmission of intergenerational post-tax capacity. Within this plane, information is treated not as narrative text but as rule–capital events: eligibility rules, tax classifications, funding formulas, and boundary-linked requirements that can be located as movements or bottlenecks on the X–Y grid. Drawing on common-law doctrines of ministerial and collective responsibility, I argue that public administrative data—such as national statistics and officially reported fiscal aggregates— carry a qualitatively different accountability structure than profit-driven news media. This yields a hierarchy of evidence in which state-generated datasets, rather than journalism, form the primary substrate for institutional analysis. The paper concludes by proposing fiscal epistemology as a paradigm for re-reading social justice questions through legally accountable information and institutional geometry.

title: A Gym Bro, a Prepaid Scam, and a Digital City that Blue-Screened: Anatomy of a Governance Failure and Grey Ecosystems
affiliations: Nanyang Technological University (NTU)

detail.title: A Gym Bro, a Prepaid Scam, and a Digital City that Blue-Screened: Anatomy of a Governance Failure and Grey Ecosystems
detail.abstract:
This study starts from the J30 shadowing (institutional obfuscation) incident and traces a three-step path predator behavior model → grey ecosystem structure → digital governance OS to systematically analyze the diffusion mechanics of the Southeast-coast grey ecosystem after it landed in Hangzhou. It argues that the predator is not a one-off anomaly, but a script-based structure that can be replicated across industries; predatory organizations are simply the scale-up amplifiers of individual predation algorithms. By unpacking the  J30 grey boss skill set, the surrounding industry chain and the Capital Legitimacy Field, the paper presents the grey ecosystem as a three-layer recursive system of predatory cashflow → shell-layer chain-washing → white-layer capital amplification, and stresses that the real field-eye lies in the grey–white interface and the Capital Legitimacy Field, rather than in the street-front storefronts.

On the governance side, the paper contends that Hangzhou’s core problem in digital governance is not a lack of technology, but a syntax mismatch: a high-tech UI laid over an old-style human OS. In that configuration, “digital” is mobilized to accelerate shadowing rather than to render anything visible, causing responsibility chains to evaporate, risk signals to lag, and multi-department coordination to misfire in a systemic way. In this sense, J30 is not a one-off local incident; it is the system writing its own incident report under pressure, as long-accumulated grey ecosystem dynamics, institutional path dependence and base-layer OS flaws are forced into visibility.

The study proposes a three-layer “fact–pattern–responsibility” digital governance OS, advocating the use of a Script Pattern Engine, a Responsibility Graph Engine and grey–white interface management to build a governance cadence of high-frequency rendering to visibility, mid-frequency responsibility assignment, and low-frequency legislation. The core claim is simple, and mildly uncomfortable: real governance stability comes from rendering truth visible and from the system’s capacity for self-repair, not from suppressing risk or managing the narrative.

title: The Aggregate Production Function in the Age of AI
affiliations: Universidad de Alcalá

detail.title: The Aggregate Production Function in the Age of AI
detail.abstract: In modern economies with genuinely heterogeneous capital distinguishing between tangible capital (machinery, buildings), intangible capital (software, patents, organizational capital), and arti cial intelligence capital (trained models, data infrastructure) the neoclassical aggregate production function Y = F(K,L) constitutes a structural artifact. Using a combination of a static Sra an model with heterogeneous techniques and a dynamic agent-based model (ABM) with endogenous technological innovation, we demonstrate that: (i) reverse capital deepening is a systematic phenomenon under reasonable calibrations, not a pathological edge case, while classical reswitching can be constructed in benchmark examples but does not typically arise in random economies under our baseline parametrization; (ii) econometric estimates of Cobb-Douglas or translog production functions can achieve excellent statistical t (high R2) on simulated data generated by a model where the marginalist interpretation is structurally inconsistent; (iii) AI capital ampli es aggregation problems due to its distinctive properties (rapid obsolescence, partial non-rivalry, complementarity with skilled labor); (iv) capital precipitationthe abrupt transition of assets from rent-generating private capital to latent common capacity generates systematic divergences between physical productivity (which may rise) and monetary productiv-ity (which may fall), further undermining marginalist distribution theory. We argue that standard DSGE models function as parsimonious approximations that become fragile in the presence of heterogeneous, interacting, and precipitating capital, suggesting that agent-based models provide a necessary complementary methodology for analyzing AI-driven structural change. We propose an alternative framework based on the space of technique con gurations, where aggregate capital is recognized as a function of distribution especially the pro t rate rather than a primary factor of production with well-de ned marginal productivity.

title: The Insider-Outsider Theory Reconsidered: Labor Markets as Human Ecosystems
affiliations: University of Kiel - Institute for World Economics (IfW)

detail.title: The Insider-Outsider Theory Reconsidered: Labor Markets as Human Ecosystems
detail.abstract: Whereas labor markets are traditionally viewed as machine-like environments – where agents, coordinated by price signals, solve constrained optimization problems or adhere to established heuristics – this paper views labor markets as human ecosystems, containing living things, namely, the human beings who participate in these markets. Living things adapt to their environment and evolve across their domains of life. Consequently, activities in labor markets cannot be understood independently of their social and political foundations. Labor markets are embedded in social, economic, political and environmental systems, and their adaptiveness to their social and natural environments. In this context, the insider-outsider theory may be generalized by reconceptualizing insiders and outsiders in terms of their relative adaptive advantages and the structural barriers to adaptation. The functions and misfunctions of adaptively embedded labor markets can be specified in terms of the adaptiveness as systems or the adaptiveness of the components of these systems. The insider-outsider theory indicates why there is no “invisible hand” whereby agents that are individually adaptive will lead to a labor market that is systemically adaptive at the labor-market or economy-wide levels. The ecosystemic approach also involves a reconceptualization of agents operating in labor markets, implying a new theories of the firm and workers. The first- and second-best policy implications are briefly surveyed.

title: Fiscal Umbrellas in a Monetary Union: ECB Backstops and the Price of Integration
affiliations: Northwestern University, Kellogg School of Management

detail.title: Fiscal Umbrellas in a Monetary Union: ECB Backstops and the Price of Integration
detail.abstract: This paper develops a continuous-time asset-pricing model linking European Central Bank (ECB) backstops to sovereign and redenomination premia in the euro area. The credibility of common fiscal and liquidity support-the European fiscal umbrella-is a priced state variable u t that governs financial integration. When credibility falls (u t ↓), collateral quality and risk sharing deteriorate, widening periphery spreads and redenomination premia; when restored through ECB interventions (u t ↑), these wedges compress. Calibrated to event data, the model reproduces the 2012 OMT spread and risk-premium compressions, the shorter-lived 2020 PEPP stabilization, and the persistent fragmentation that would have occurred during COVID without the umbrella. The results show that ECB credibility operates as a priced fiscal asset-its valuation anchors integration and prevents self-reinforcing fragmentation within the monetary union.

title: The Dark Side of Escaping the Middle-Income Trap: A SAGE Study of Asian High-Income Countries
affiliations: Global Solutions Initiative Foundation GmbH and University of Kiel - Institute for World Economics (IfW)

detail.title: The Dark Side of Escaping the Middle-Income Trap: A SAGE Study of Asian High-Income Countries
detail.abstract: The experience of rapid economic growth and transition to high-income status in Asian countries has brought about significant improvements in material well-being and aggregate economic prosperity. This article examines the degree to which economic prosperity is the “great enabler” of social and environmental prosperity. We provide conceptual reasons why this is not necessarily the case and empirical evidence that the escape from the middle-income trap in three Asian high-income countries – Japan, Singapore and South Korea – was a mixed blessing, linked to challenges regarding social solidarity, personal and collective agency and environmental stewardship. Under these circumstances, traditional prescriptions for escaping the middle-income trap are insufficient. Without success in the social and environmental spheres, social fragmentation and environmental disruption is likely to occur, possibly leading to political instabilities, economic fragmentation and social conflict. This paper investigates this problem for the three Asian high-income countries, based on empirical measures of solidarity (S), agency (A), material gain (G) and environmental stewardship (E) that are consistent through time and across countries. On this foundation, policy recommendations are considered that are meant to run alongside the standard prescriptions to make the resulting package socially and environmentally acceptable.

title: High-Dependency Border Fractures and National 'Cascading Vulnerability': A Framework for Identifying Critical Vulnerabilities, Intelligence-Driven Simulation, and Early Warning in Cambodia Based on Structured Knowledge Graphs, with a Discussion on Thailand's Compliance Economic Action Portfolio Amidst Border Conflict Spillover
affiliations: Dhurakij Pundit University and Dhurakij Pundit University

detail.title: High-Dependency Border Fractures and National 'Cascading Vulnerability': A Framework for Identifying Critical Vulnerabilities, Intelligence-Driven Simulation, and Early Warning in Cambodia Based on Structured Knowledge Graphs, with a Discussion on Thailand's Compliance Economic Action Portfolio Amidst Border Conflict Spillover
detail.abstract: Against a backdrop of increasingly frequent external shocks and deepening cross-sectoral coupling, traditional national risk assessments centred on ‘industry/sector’ units often struggle to explain why seemingly localised disturbances rapidly evolve into systemic instability. This paper proposes an integrated ‘Dependency Network–Knowledge Graph (DN-KG)’ framework tailored for intelligence research and academic discourse. This framework abstracts Cambodia's macroeconomic, financial, real estate, fuel and power supply, border security, climate agriculture, tourism services, and governance regulatory systems into node sets. It integrates cross-system constraints and operationalises the DN-KG framework to: DN-KG)‘ framework for intelligence research and academic discourse. This framework abstracts Cambodia's macroeconomic, financial, real estate, fuel and power supply, border security, climate-agriculture, tourism services, and governance-regulation sectors into node sets, while cross-system constraints and transmission relationships are abstracted into edge sets. ’High-betweenness dependency edges" serve as the core indicator for identifying systemic vulnerabilities. detail.title: Economic Shocks, Opportunity Costs, and the Supply of Politicians
detail.abstract: Adverse economic shocks are known to reshape voter behavior – the demand side of politics. Much less is known about their consequences for the supply side: how such shocks affect who becomes a politician. This paper examines how job losses influence individuals' decisions to enter politics and the implications for political selection. Using administrative data linking political participation records to matched employer-employee data covering all formal workers in Brazil, and exploiting mass layoffs for causal identification, we find that job loss significantly increases the likelihood of joining a political party and running for local office. Layoff-induced candidates are positively selected on various competence measures, indicating that economic shocks can improve the quality of political entrants. The increase in candidacies is strongest among laid-off individuals with greater financial incentives from holding office and higher predicted income losses. A regression discontinuity design further shows that eligibility for unemployment benefits increases political entry. These results are consistent with a reduction in individuals' opportunity costs – both in terms of reduced private-sector income and increased time resources – facilitating greater political engagement.

detail.abstract: Ownership overlap-where two legally distinct firms share a common investor-has become a salient feature of modern capitalism, yet its implications for human capital remain largely unexplored. This paper examines whether such an overlap among legally distinct firms gives rise to cross-firm labor mobility analogous to internal labor markets within multi-unit firms. Using a novel panel of firm-pair × year observations with directed worker flows, I study mobility across firms that enter into a common investor ownership through private equity acquisitions. I find that cross-firm mobility increases sharply among rank-and-file employees and persists after ownership ends, indicating durable reductions in information and search frictions. Moreover, flows are more pronounced when investors are geographically proximate to destination firms, when workers move from less to more productive firms, or when departures originate from incumbent firms-consistent with investor-led redeployment that enhances allocative efficiency through two distinct channels: coordination at the hiring destination and informational advantages at the origin. Together, the results show that ownership overlap can induce mobility across legally distinct firms by facilitating information diffusion and selective coordination, with implications for the theory of the firm in which the allocation of human capital is shaped not only by formal firm boundaries but also by intermediary ownership-based coordination across firms.

Underdogs: Predicting Student Success at Abaarso School in Somaliland

Introduction

Ayana Mubarik closed the door of her office after ushering out a parent who had come to meet about her son's performance so far at Abaarso School of Science and Technology (Abaarso). Now in her third year as head of the lower school, and in charge of Abaarso's 7th and 8th graders, Mubarik anticipated that there would be at least a few of these meetings once the first school term ended. Having been a student here herself nearly a decade before, she knew that Abaarso was a pressure cooker—living at a boarding school that had an intense academic environment and taking classes taught in a foreign language was a lot to expect the 14-year-olds in her 7th-grade class to handle. Yet she had also seen students succeed time and time again over their six years at the school. She herself had arrived knowing only a few dozen words of English and remembered how much of a struggle those first few months had been. But she also remembered her surprise when a few of the students who seemed most advanced in their language skills during those early months had started to struggle after their first year. And while Mubarik had gone on to graduate from a top liberal arts college in the US state of Vermont, some of these other students had not even finished Abaarso.

Mubarik wondered if she could sense a pattern developing. She could tell that Abaarso's coheads of school, Ahmed Qaalib and Tomoki Sasaki, were noticing something as well. Qaalib—himself an Abaarso alum from the class of 2013—had called a meeting of the admissions team, of which Mubarik was the leading member, to discuss ways that Abaarso could update its admissions exam to ensure that it was selecting the students with the best chance to succeed at the school. In advance of the meeting, Mubarik wanted to dig into the data and see what observations she could make.

detail.abstract:
Entrepreneurship Through Acquisition (ETA)—where aspiring entrepreneurs search for, acquire, and scale established small-to-medium-sized businesses rather than launching start-ups—can benefit from a clear, robust industry thesis when entrepreneurs are searching for companies to purchase. Excerpt

Building an Industry Thesis in Entrepreneurship Through Acquisition (ETA)

Entrepreneurship Through Acquisition (ETA) represents a pragmatic pathway to business ownership, where aspiring entrepreneurs search for, acquire, and scale established small-to-medium-sized businesses rather than launching start-ups. This approach mitigates some of the risks inherent in new ventures by leveraging existing revenue streams, customer bases, and operational infrastructures. The development of a robust industry thesis is central to ETA success, particularly in the traditional search fund model, where a consortium of investors backs a searcher to identify and buy a company. This thesis serves as a strategic blueprint, guiding the searcher toward attractive industry niches with high acquisition potential, sustainable growth, and alignment with personal experience and expertise.

Understanding the diverse approaches to developing an industry thesis is critical for searchers analyzing potential business opportunities. For example, a traditional searcher with deep expertise in a specific industry often zeroes in on an in-depth niche analysis, a strategy that tends to appeal to investors seeking focused opportunities. Conversely, a traditional searcher lacking industry-specific knowledge, or often a self-funded searcher, typically casts a wider net and explores a broader range of industry targets, either across multiple sectors or within a select group, adopting an opportunistic stance that may span three or more industries.

Self-funded searchers with geographic preferences and armed with industry expertise may pursue a distinct path, conducting thorough research focused on an industry niche. This contrasts with their counterparts who don't have such constraints or expertise, and who maintain a flexible, broad-based approach to uncovering industry opportunities. Searchers may have diverse approaches to developing an industry thesis. It is crucial to consider this when determining the level of specificity for the industry target. title: Service Providers Who Use AI Receive Less Support from Consumers
affiliations: , Shandong University and University of Arizona

detail.title: Service Providers Who Use AI Receive Less Support from Consumers
detail.abstract: Generative AI promises to improve the performance of service providers and, consequently, has been adopted by a range of services. Although AI can help doctors diagnose patients, entrepreneurs build start-up charities, and providers across industries deliver more efficient and effective service, will consumers appreciate these benefits? We show that the answer is typically no. Consumers evaluate services less favorably when the provider uses AI, even when the consumer knows that the AI leads to better service. Specifically, five experiments (total N = 2,618) reveal that consumers are less likely to comply with, support, and intend to use services associated with providers who they know use AI. Consumers respond less favorably to services because they believe that providers who use AI are less warm and less competent. The pattern persists across different service categories, with different types of consumers, and even immediately after consumers read about how AI can help improve the performance of the service provider. Our research advances theory by highlighting a challenge faced by businesses and employees who use AI: even when it improves service quality, consumers may avoid using the service when they know that the provider uses AI.
