detail.title: VC, Exits, and Startup Innovations
detail.abstract: When startups strategically cater to acquirers, their innovations will become more similar to existing assets, and Venture Capital (VC) shapes these incentives. Using a novel methodology that captures the type, direction, and complementarity of startups' and incumbents' innovations, I show that attractive acquisition markets attract startup innovation and that catering to acquirers is associated with higher acquisition rates. Startups adjust their innovation strategies in response to an exogenous increase in VC supply; technological innovations become more independent and cater less to acquirers. I also document a VC selection effect: the average VC-funded startup's innovations become more similar to incumbents' assets.

title: Effectiveness of Machine Learning Algorithms in Forecasting Ridership: A Case of Gautrain During COVID-19
affiliations: and University of Johannesburg

detail.title: Effectiveness of Machine Learning Algorithms in Forecasting Ridership: A Case of Gautrain During COVID-19
detail.abstract: Accurate ridership forecasting is essential for public transport planning and resilience, especially during disruptions. The Gautrain, South Africa's rapid rail system, experienced significant ridership declines during the COVID-19 pandemic, highlighting the need for forecasting models that can adapt to sudden external shocks. This study evaluates traditional time-series models including ARIMA, SARIMA, and Holt-Winters against machine learning methods like LSTM, CNN, and an Ensemble model in forecasting Gautrain ridership. Three datasets were used: the full timeline, a stable pre-COVID period, and the disruptive COVID-19 period. Model accuracy was assessed using Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE). Results show that forecast performance is highly context dependent. The Ensemble model was most robust on the full dataset (MAPE = 13.04%) and showed strong adaptability, reducing error by 39% during the disruption. The Holt-Winters Multiplicative model performed best in the stable pre-COVID period (MAPE = 13.89%), while SARIMA achieved the highest accuracy during the disruption (MAPE = 8.85%). LSTM maintained consistent accuracy across all periods, whereas CNN accuracy declined slightly. Residual analysis revealed increased unexplained variance during COVID-19, reflecting external influences. Overall, traditional models excel in stable conditions, while ensemble approaches are more resilient in volatile environments, suggesting that planners should adopt context-specific forecasting strategies.

This scholarly analysis critically assesses this maneuver by juxtaposing such CDA 230-like provisions against the UK’s established legal framework governing online content and freedom of expression. Utilizing a comparative legal methodology, the paper underscores the pronounced differences between the USA and UK stances on intermediary liability for third-party content, molded by their unique constitutional foundations and jurisprudential interpretations of free speech rights. It fervently endorses a cross-disciplinary discourse involving both trade and legal specialists to ensure the preservation of free expression while concurrently recognizing the intricacies of crafting universally applicable standards for online platforms and content regulation.

"Competing Priorities Among Team Members" is an exercise designed to help a (learning) team or working group (e.g., committee, service group, task force, or volunteer group) foresee, discuss, and work through potential conflicts surrounding competing life priorities while in pursuit of a common goal or deliverable. Competing Priorities Among Team Members

Your life, in the end, is the sum total of how you spent your time.

detail.abstract:
Purpose

To establish a baseline of indoor environmental quality and occupant perceptions in an older ward-style residential aged care (RAC) facility prior to demolition, providing a benchmark for evaluating a purpose-built replacement in a companion study.

Design/methods/approach

A 14-day monitoring campaign (September–October 2024) was conducted in Perth, Western Australia, across a bedroom, lounge, activity room and corridor. Continuous measures of noise (dB(A)), illuminance (lux) and temperature (°C) were recorded using calibrated loggers (IC-NSRT acoustics; HOBO MX2202 light/temperature). Results were evaluated against WHO night-noise guidance, AS/NZS 2107:2016, pragmatic circadian-light targets (≥1000 lux daytime; ≤10 lux night) and literature indicating diurnal thermal variation ≥2°C. Parallel surveys co-developed with facility stakeholders captured resident/proxy and staff perceptions of noise, lighting and thermal comfort (staff n = 23; residents/proxies n = 24).

Findings

Night-time bedroom sound levels exceeded WHO guidance for most monitored minutes, with intermittent peaks above 55 dB(A). Communal lounges exceeded the 45 dB(A) daytime guideline during most monitored periods. Daytime bedroom illuminance rarely achieved ≥30 minutes at ≥1000 lux, while night-time exceedances above 10 lux occurred due to corridor spill. Temperatures were generally stable with limited day–night variation (<2°C) in most spaces. Survey responses aligned with measured noise patterns but tended to normalise lighting conditions that fell short of circadian-supportive targets; thermal comfort was rated positively.

Practical implications

The findings identify actionable priorities for redevelopment and interim operations, including acoustic buffering of bedrooms and corridors, daylight/circadian-supportive lighting provision, night-time spill control and more dynamic thermal zoning or scheduling.

Originality/value

Provides a rare pre-replacement baseline integrating continuous IEQ monitoring with stakeholder perceptions in RAC, enabling defensible same-site benchmarking against a purpose-built facility.

title: The Trade Credit Bullwhip Effect in Supply Networks
affiliations: Central University of Finance and Economics (CUFE) - Chinese Academy of Finance and Development, Durham University Business School, Duke University - Fuqua School of Business and

detail.title: The Trade Credit Bullwhip Effect in Supply Networks
detail.abstract: The classic bullwhip effect (BWE) describes how demand and order variability amplify as they move upstream in a supply chain. We uncover an analogous but distinct phenomenon, the trade credit bullwhip effect (TCBWE)-an imbalance between firms' trade credit inflows and outflows. Using both theory and data, we show that focal firms' accounts payable are more volatile than their accounts receivable. We refer to this pattern as the intra-firm trade credit bullwhip effect (IntraTCBWE). We develop an infinite-horizon inventory model with demand variability held constant across firms and show that IntraTCBWE can arise purely from suppliers' trade credit choices, especially when they are more farsighted (have higher discount factors) than downstream customers. Empirically, we assemble a panel of U.S. publicly traded manufacturers, combining supply network data with quarterly financials, to measure TCBWE in practice. We find robust evidence of IntraTCBWE even after controlling for the conventional BWE, which is positively but incompletely related to TCBWE. At the layer (network) level, we do not observe systematic amplification of accounts receivable variability upstream; we label this the inter-firm trade credit bullwhip effect (InterTCBWE). Finally, we show that firm transparency, industry competition, and cash holdings moderate IntraTCBWE, and that proactive customer portfolio management, including adding, dropping, and swapping customers, reduces accounts receivable volatility. Our results reveal trade credit volatility as a hidden financial bullwhip in supply networks and offer concrete levers for treasurers, CFOs, and supply chain leaders to stabilize cash flows and strengthen network resilience.

detail.abstract: The U.S. Patent & Trademark Office (USPTO) has issued a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) regarding inter partes review of patents by the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB).  I apply an error cost analysis to evaluate the proposed reforms. The granting and subsequent review of patent claims is subject to two types of error: false positive (an invalid claim found valid) and false negative  (a valid claim found invalid). Both errors weaken incentives to innovate. The private incentive to petition for inter partes review challenging a patent claim is socially excessive, for two reasons. First, the process of review is asymmetric. A patent claim found valid by PTAB remains open to future challenge, but a claim (falsely) found invalid is unlikely to be overturned on appeal. Second, the frequency of false negative error counts as a dynamic social loss, weakening incentives to innovate, but counts as a static private gain allowing the challenger to avoid royalties on the falsely invalidated patent. USPTO proposes to limit duplicative patent reviews. This is broadly consistent with the goal of promoting innovation.

detail.abstract: Global public organizations such as the United Nations increasingly rely on AI-supported recruitment systems to handle large, culturally diverse applicant pools. While these systems often satisfy statistical fairness constraints, candidates’ justice perceptions frequently diverge across cultural and linguistic groups. This paper extends the Hybrid Justice Model (HJM) by introducing a cross-cultural justice calibration lens focused on the interaction between cultural fairness alignment (μ) and the Perception Shift Index (PSI) across recruitment stages. Building on the Fairness Governance Index (FGI) and Justice Gap Index (JGI), we conceptualize μ as the degree of alignment between organizational procedures and regional fairness expectations, and PSI as the change in perceived fairness over time (PSI = H(t) − H(t−1)). We then examine how three cross-cultural dimensions—(1) high-context vs. low-context communication norms, (2) native vs. non-native English use, and (3) interviewer cultural anchoring—systematically shape H (justice perception) and, in turn, μ and PSI. Using the λ–μ Stability Model as a theoretical backbone, we develop a Cross-Cultural Justice Calibration Framework for AI-supported UN recruitment. We provide illustrative scenarios from UN-style competitions (e.g., JPO and P-level selections) to show how identical algorithmic decisions can generate divergent PSI trajectories and FGI/JGI patterns across cultural clusters. The paper contributes to research on algorithmic fairness, cross-cultural management, and public-sector human resource management (HRM) by (1) specifying a formal role for cultural alignment in fairness governance, (2) proposing measurable justice gaps across cultural and linguistic groups, and (3) outlining implications for fairness offices, interviewer training, and AI governance in multilateral organizations.

title: When Helping is Not Helpful: An Examination of the Negative Impact of Coworkers' Help On One's Experiential Learning
affiliations: Carnegie Mellon University and Auburn University

detail.title: When Helping is Not Helpful: An Examination of the Negative Impact of Coworkers' Help On One's Experiential Learning

keywords: microfoundations of organizational capabilities and performance

detail.abstract: This study examines how the process through which individuals acquire experience shapes their learning trajectories. Building on the experiential learning literature, we argue that learning depends not only on the amount of experience accumulated, but also on how that experience is acquired. Specifically, we theorize that receiving solution-oriented help from peers-help that directly resolves major task challenges or provides ready-made solutions-can diminish the developmental value of experience by limiting independent problem solving, constraining tacit knowledge formation, and fostering mislearning. Using daily-level panel data on 86 sales employees at a flash-deal company over 2.5 years, we test this theory. As a baseline, we replicate the positive relationship between accumulated task experience and subsequent performance documented in prior experiential learning work. We then show that receiving greater amounts of solution-oriented help from peers undermines this relationship. Finally, we find that this negative moderating effect is amplified when individuals outperform their peers as a result of receiving such help. Overall, our findings demonstrate that the acquisition process of experience fundamentally conditions how experience translates into capability, offering new insights for research on experiential learning, the microfoundations of organizational capability and performance, and the consequences of helping behaviors within organizations.

title: Eco-Evolutionary Regime Transitions as Coherence Loss in Hereditary Updating: A Diagnostic Threshold for when Genomes can no Longer Keep Up
affiliations: Rhodes University

detail.title: Eco-Evolutionary Regime Transitions as Coherence Loss in Hereditary Updating: A Diagnostic Threshold for when Genomes can no Longer Keep Up
detail.abstract: Ecoevolutionary feedbacks show that evolution can operate on ecological timescales, sometimes stabilising population dynamics and at other times precipitating abrupt decline or community reorganisation. Yet the field still lacks a portable diagnostic for when adaptive tracking will remain coherent versus when it will fail. We propose a unifying criterion framed as coherence between hereditary information architectures and their selective environments. Genomes and regulatory networks are treated as update-limited architectures that encode and revise fitness-relevant structure through selection, subject to constraints familiar from quantitative genetics. We define an effective hereditary update rate, ηK, capturing how rapidly selection can reduce mismatch between a population state and a moving optimum, given available additive genetic variance and the genotype–phenotype map. We define an environmental drift measure, Λ, summarising the dominant pace (or fitness-relevant bandwidth) of environmental change in generational units. When Λ approaches or exceeds ηK, eco evolutionary dynamics transition from tracking into a brittle critical-lag regime, and then into overload characterised by persistent mismatch and loss of alignment. We provide a worked toy model under stabilising selection with a moving optimum, show how classical results on critical rates of change and evolutionary rescue arise as special cases, and propose an order parameter based on lag-adjusted magnitude-squared spectral coherence between environmental proxies and phenotypic response. The result is a concise, falsifiable programme for diagnosing regime transitions using genomic, phenotypic, and demographic time series.

title: Ethical AI in Multilingual Institutions: Semantic Drift in Fairness Principles and the Hybrid Justice Model

detail.title: Ethical AI in Multilingual Institutions: Semantic Drift in Fairness Principles and the Hybrid Justice Model

detail.abstract: Multilingual public institutions such as the United Nations, the European Union, and ASEAN increasingly deploy AI systems for recruitment, service delivery, and regulatory tasks under ethics frameworks that emphasize fairness, transparency, and non-discrimination. These principles, however, are usually drafted in English and then translated into multiple legal and working languages. Research in legal and institutional translation shows that normative terms such as “fair,” “equity,” and “accountability” rarely map cleanly across languages and legal cultures, creating systematic “semantic drift” between source texts and target versions. At the same time, global AI governance instruments—from UN-system resolutions to regional guides such as the ASEAN Guide on AI Governance and Ethics and the OECD AI Principles—are increasingly used as reference points for national and organizational policy. This paper conceptualizes “semantic drift” in translated AI ethics and fairness policies as a distinct layer of risk for organizational justice and trust in AI-supported processes. Building on the Hybrid Justice Model (HJM), it treats semantic drift as a mechanism that can widen the Justice Gap Index (JGI) and generate “semantic trust drift” in the Perception Shift Index (PSI) across language communities, even when underlying models satisfy standard statistical fairness constraints. Drawing on insights from legal translation, institutional translation, and cross-cultural value research (e.g., GLOBE, Schwartz), the paper proposes a Multilingual Fairness Drift Framework that links three elements: (1) textual drift in fairness‐related concepts across languages, (2) implementation drift as policies are operationalized in local procedures and explanations, and (3) perception drift as candidates and citizens experience AI-mediated decisions. Using UN, EU, and ASEAN examples as comparative reference points, the paper illustrates how misaligned translations of fairness principles can produce divergent expectations and justice perceptions across language groups, even within a single institution. It then outlines a research agenda that uses HJM indicators—particularly μ (cultural and linguistic alignment) and PSI—to measure and govern semantic drift over time. The contribution is twofold: it reframes multilingual translation not as a technical afterthought but as a core dimension of ethical AI governance, and it extends organizational justice theory to cover the textual and semantic infrastructures through which AI ethics principles are communicated and implemented in multilingual institutions.

title: The Crucible of Conflict: Authentic Thought Versus Artificial Authority
affiliations: Shenyang Normal University

detail.title: The Crucible of Conflict: Authentic Thought Versus Artificial Authority
detail.abstract: This article posits that authentic, transformative thought is not a product of academic pedigree or institutional endorsement, but is forged in the crucible of conflict and profound personal struggle. It argues that the very essence of a true thinker lies in their ability to confront, withstand, and synthesize immense pressure into a novel worldview. Consequently, intellectual authority achieved through a smooth, unopposed ascent within established systems is inherently suspect. This paper further contends that thinkers who are anointed or cultivated by existing power structures are, by definition, counterfeits, as their "mastery" serves to legitimize the status quo rather than challenge it. True genius is not promoted; it emerges, often in opposition to the very institutions that claim to foster it.

title: The Context Sensitivity Paradox: How Stakeholder Framing Shapes Moral Judgment in Humans and AI

detail.title: The Context Sensitivity Paradox: How Stakeholder Framing Shapes Moral Judgment in Humans and AI
detail.abstract:
Do humans and artificial intelligence systems apply consistent ethical frameworks when making organizational decisions, or do morally contested contextual features systematically influence moral judgments? We conducted a mixed-methods experiment with 300 organizational leaders and three frontier AI models (GPT-4, Claude 3 Opus, Gemini Pro 1.5) responding to 240 systematically varied ethical scenarios. We collected 6,000 human responses (300 participants × 20 scenarios each) and generated 7,200 AI responses at temperature 0.7 (240 scenarios × 3 models × 10 repetitions), with additional sensitivity analyses at temperatures 0.3, 0.5, and 1.0.

Analysis revealed substantial systematic variation in moral judgments: both humans and AI systems (at temperature=0.7, selected post-hoc to match human total variation levels) made different recommendations for structurally identical dilemmas based on how stakeholders were described (identifiable individuals vs. statistical aggregates: OR=2.08, p<.001), whether actions were framed as active causation versus passive allowance (d=0.63, p<.001), and temporal proximity of consequences (OR=1.52, p<.001).

We decomposed this variation into three components: (1) structural consistency (agreement when only irrelevant features vary: M=0.85), (2) contextual responsiveness (variation attributable to debatable features: 22-24% of total variance), and (3) arbitrary residual variation (32-34% of variance). AI temperature parameter directly controls variation magnitude: at T=0.3, AI showed less variation than humans (0.26 vs. 0.42, p<.001); at T=0.7 (typical deployment setting), AI approximated human levels (0.41 vs. 0.42, p=.56); at T=1.0, AI exceeded human variation (0.49 vs. 0.42, p<.001) but with degraded coherence (91.6% vs. 97.2% at T=0.7). This temperature-dependence means we cannot claim AI inherently exhibits human-like variation; rather, temperature embeds implicit assumptions about desired reasoning patterns. Critically, contextual feature effects (identifiability, relational, temporal, action-omission) remained significant across all temperatures (all η²p > 0.08, p<.001), indicating robust patterns independent of overall variation levels.

Humans exhibited more relational reasoning than AI (d=0.56, p<.001). Mediation analysis on a coded subsample of 800 responses revealed that relational reasoning partially explained contextual responsiveness differences (indirect effect β=0.043, 95% CI [0.028, 0.061]), accounting for 69% of human-AI differences. Critically, relational reasoning was associated with higher contextual responsiveness but lower arbitrary variation, suggesting systematic sensitivity rather than random inconsistency.

Whether contextual responsiveness represents cognitive bias or appropriate moral sensitivity remains philosophically contested. Principlism interprets our findings as evidence of widespread moral reasoning failures; particularism interprets identical patterns as appropriate attention to morally relevant contextual details. Our data provide empirical constraints for this normative debate but cannot adjudicate it.

We derive the hyperbolic SPDE for price dynamics, establish martingale properties under causal filtrations, and prove no-arbitrage within light-cone domains. title: Forms of Instruction in Ivorian Schools: A Russian Comparative View

detail.title: Forms of Instruction in Ivorian Schools: A Russian Comparative View
detail.abstract: The 21st century has witnessed dynamic development in the education systems of many African countries, encompassing organizational aspects, educational policy, and classroom teaching practices. The Ivorian school system is modernizing its didactic components by integrating, for instance, proven traditional and contemporary forms of learning. This article aims to systematize the forms of instruction in Ivorian schools. This objective is achieved through a comparative pedagogical approach and a comparison with Russian domestic practices. This methodology allows drawing conclusions about optimal forms of interaction with Ivorian students within the framework of Russia's humanitarian policy.

title: Technical Architecture of CHAINALYTICA™: An Intelligent Business Analytics Framework for Predictive and Sustainable Supply Chains
affiliations: University of Tennessee

detail.title: Technical Architecture of CHAINALYTICA™: An Intelligent Business Analytics Framework for Predictive and Sustainable Supply Chains
detail.abstract: The CHAINALYTICA™ framework, developed by Olubunmi Anifowose (MBA, Business Analytics), represents a next-generation technical architecture that integrates predictive intelligence, business analytics, and sustainability intelligence into a unified decision ecosystem. Built upon four strategic pillars Predict, Synchronize, Optimize, and Sustain (P.S.O.S.) CHAINALYTICA™ enables organizations to anticipate demand, synchronize operations, optimize resource efficiency, and ensure compliance with environmental, social, and governance (ESG) standards. This report details CHAINALYTICA's architecture, analytical models, implementation pathway, and business impact. Quantitatively, adopters have achieved up to 30% improvement in forecast accuracy, 15-20% operational cost reduction, and 20% improvement in sustainability efficiency, confirming the framework's transformative potential for data-driven, sustainable supply chain management.

title: LLMO FOR RETAIL: How Large Language Models Shape Product Discovery and Brand Visibility - Working Paper (Version 1.0)

detail.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become embedded in consumer product search, they increasingly mediate retail brand visibility and consideration. This study examines how three widely used LLM platforms, ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemin, surface, frame, and prioritize retail brands when responding to common consumer shopping queries. Using an exploratory empirical design, we analyze 132 consumer-oriented queries across five product categories, systematically coding brand mentions, sentiment patterns, and evaluative framing. Results reveal substantial fragmentation in cross-platform brand visibility: only 39.9% of brands are mentioned across all three models, whereas 35.2% appear exclusively on a single platform. Models also exhibit distinct “recommendation personalities,” varying in evaluative tone, use of qualifiers, and brand positioning, even when queries are held constant. These findings suggest that LLMs function as selective intermediaries that shape consumers' consideration sets through systematic yet non-uniform brand curation. This study provides early empirical evidence on AI-mediated product discovery, raising strategic questions for retail marketers and research questions regarding algorithmic transparency, consumer decision-making, and digital intermediation in retail contexts.

title: Adult Skills and Productivity: New Evidence from PIAAC 2023
affiliations: Organization for Economic Co-Operation and Development (OECD), Organization for Economic Co-Operation and Development (OECD) and Organization for Economic Co-Operation and Development (OECD) - Economics Department (ECO)

detail.title: Adult Skills and Productivity: New Evidence from PIAAC 2023
detail.abstract: The 2023 Survey of Adult Skills (PIAAC) reveals large cross-country differences in adult skill levels that carry important implications for productivity. Cross-country analysis shows a positive relationship between labour productivity and the average level of adult skills at the industry level –partly reflecting a positive link between adult skills and R&D intensity – which is estimated to account for one-quarter of cross-country differences in industry productivity. But the ways in which skilled workers are allocated to different job roles and firms also matters. Higher productivity is observed in industries with lower labour market mismatches and where high-skilled workers are employed in larger and more dynamic firms. Differences in these patterns of allocation can account for at least 12% of the productivity gaps between countries. These findings highlight the importance of policies aimed at enhancing adult skills and structural reforms to improve labour market adaptability and reallocation.

title: A Unified Metric Architecture for AI Infrastructure: A Cross-Layer Taxonomy Integrating Economics, Performance, and Efficiency

detail.title: A Unified Metric Architecture for AI Infrastructure: A Cross-Layer Taxonomy Integrating Economics, Performance, and Efficiency
detail.abstract:
The growth of large-scale AI systems is increasingly constrained by infrastructure limits: power availability, thermal and water constraints, interconnect scaling, memory pressure, data-pipeline throughput, and rapidly escalating lifecycle cost. Across hyperscale clusters, these constraints interact, yet the main metrics remain fragmented. Existing metrics, ranging from facility measures (PUE) and rack power density to network metrics (all-reduce latency), data-pipeline measures, and financial metrics (TCO series), each capture only their own domain and provide no integrated view of how physical, computational, and economic constraints interact. This fragmentation obscures the structural relationships among energy, computation, and cost, preventing a coherent optimization across sector and how bottlenecks emerge, propagate, and jointly determine the efficiency frontier of AI infrastructure. 

This paper develops an integrated framework that unifies these disparate metrics through a threedomain semantic classification and a six-layer architectural decomposition, producing a 6×3 taxonomy that maps how various sectors propagate across the AI infrastructure stack. The taxonomy is grounded in a systematic review and meta-analysis of all metrics with economic and financial relevance, identifying the most widely used measures, their research intensity, and their cross-domain interdependencies. Building on this evidence base, the Metric Propagation Graph (MPG) formalizes cross-layer dependencies, enabling systemwide interpretation, composite-metric construction, and multi-objective optimization of energy, carbon, and cost. 

The framework offers a coherent foundation for benchmarking, cluster design, capacity planning, and lifecycle economic analysis by linking physical operations, computational efficiency, and cost outcomes within a unified analytic structure.

title: Towards Green Markets: Strategies for Enhancing Sustainability in Open-air Popular Markets, Zliten, Libya
affiliations: The Libyan Centre for Studies & Research in Environmental Sciences & Teschnology, ,  The Libyan Centre for Studies & Research in Environmental Sciences & Teschnology,  The Libyan Centre for Studies & Research in Environmental Sciences & Teschnology,  The Libyan Centre for Studies & Research in Environmental Sciences & Teschnology, Sabratha university and Misurata University

detail.title: Towards Green Markets: Strategies for Enhancing Sustainability in Open-air Popular Markets, Zliten, Libya
detail.abstract: This study investigates the state of sustainability in open-air popular markets in Zliten city, considering current trends toward establishing green markets that include several environmental aspects. The research originates from a key issue: the limited integration of sustainability standards in organizing these markets, despite their importance in economic and social life. The significance of the study lies in highlighting the vital environmental role of local markets and proposing practical and scientific approaches for their environmental sustainability improvement. The study aimed to assess the current level of sustainability in open-air popular markets, identifying the challenges hindering progress, and suggesting practical strategies for transitioning to green markets, adopting a descriptive-analytical approach. A questionnaire was created, covering three main areas: strategies for enhancing sustainability, the extent to which the green market (sustainability) concept is realized, and the challenges faced in achieving sustainability in open-air popular markets. This tool was distributed to a sample of 100 participants, including vendors, citizens, and regulatory authorities. The statistical analysis results indicated that the state of sustainability remains weak, with the overall average for the sustainability mechanisms dimension at only 2.07 and the average for the realization of the green market concept at 1.91. Administrative and planning challenges, a lack of coordination, and insufficient resources emerged as the main obstacles. The results also confirmed a strong linkage between the availability of environmental infrastructure and the extent of green market realization, compared to the limited influence of awareness programs. The study concluded that adopting integrated strategies to enhance sustainability in open-air popular markets is essential, highlighting the importance of activating coordination and cooperation among stakeholders to ensure a genuine balance between environmental, economic, and social dimensions.

title: On the Limits and Extensions of the Generalized Sharpe-Parity Principle (GSPP)

detail.title: On the Limits and Extensions of the Generalized Sharpe-Parity Principle (GSPP)
detail.abstract: This paper revisits the theoretical structure of the Generalized Sharpe-Parity Principle (GSPP) proposed by Shin (2025), clarifies its scope and limitations, and outlines directions for future research and implementation. GSPP generalizes Sharpe-ratio equilibrium to an arbitrary risk functional, thereby unifying the micro-level BSM (Black-Scholes-Merton) and the macro-level CAPM (Capital Asset Pricing Model) under a single conservation law of risk-adjusted return. Unlike traditional stochastic-model approaches, GSPP is a distribution-free, equilibriumbased framework that can derive fair values directly from empirical data without risk-neutral transformations or PDEs. Despite this structural innovation, several empirical and computational constraints remain for its practical application. This paper identifies five key frontiers of future study: (1) empirical verification, (2) sensitivity to time-series windows, (3) growth-rate definition, (4) estimation of risk measures, and (5) macroeconomic linkage.

title: How to Attract Talent? Field-Experimental Evidence on Emphasizing Flexibility and Career Opportunities in Job Advertisements
affiliations: University of Cologne, University of Cologne, University of Cologne and University of Cologne

detail.title: How to Attract Talent? Field-Experimental Evidence on Emphasizing Flexibility and Career Opportunities in Job Advertisements
detail.abstract: We conduct a randomized controlled trial (RCT) with a leading technology firm to study how highlighting flexibility and career advancement in job advertisements causally affects the applicant pool. Highlighting career advancement increases the number of applications from men for entry-level positions and attracts additional applicants with strong qualifications and a good fit, which in turn leads to more interview invitations. By contrast, highlighting flexibility increases applications from both women and men at the entry level but provides limited evidence of attracting higher-quality or better-fit applicants. A complementary survey experiment among STEM students shows how job advertisements shape beliefs about the firm’s job characteristics and work environment. Overall, our results show that the amenities firms choose to highlight can powerfully influence both the size and characteristics of their applicant pool.

title: The Impact of Rural Credit on Smallholder Productivity and Welfare in Developing Economies

detail.title: The Impact of Rural Credit on Smallholder Productivity and Welfare in Developing Economies
detail.abstract: This systematic literature review focuses on rural credit and its contributions toward enhancing smallholder productivity and welfare in developing countries. There are about 500 million smallholder farms that sustain close to 2 billion people worldwide, and yet smallholder farmers suffer from persistent credit constraints that inhibit investments in their agricultural productivity and technology. The review summarizes findings from randomized controlled trials, quasi-experimental studies, and more rigorous observational literature on rural credit programs relevant to smallholders across Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, Southeast Asia, and Latin America. The evidence demonstrates that rural credit results in modest and heterogeneous impacts that depend on complementary factors. Credit is most beneficial when provided in conjunction with agricultural extension training, using appropriate technologies, creating market access, and targeted at relatively poor farmers with baseline assets located in high-potential agroecological zones. Gender dynamics are importantly relevant, where men experience a larger productivity impact in credit programs, while women visibly improve child welfare with credits assigned to them. The review finds that in the case of rural credit, rigorous studies showing reliable evidence produce much smaller impacts than the earlier observational studies, and there were many studies, regardless of methodology, showing null to modest consumption impacts despite having businesses created. The evidence reviewed here provides little support for the claims of transformative microfinance, but it does provide evidence that rural credit can provide funding and/or services as, at minimum, part of the rural integrated development strategies that confront multiple and interrelated constraints smallholder farmers face.

detail.abstract: Employee engagement has emerged as a critical determinant of organizational performance, yet many firms continue to underutilize engagement data as a strategic input for forecasting workforce outcomes. This study investigates the predictive power of employee engagement metrics in determining individual performance, using a data-driven analytical framework grounded in organizational behavior and human resource analytics. Drawing on validated engagement constructs—such as motivation, job satisfaction, recognition, managerial support, work–life balance, and organizational commitment—the research integrates survey data, performance evaluations, and HR records to develop predictive models capable of identifying performance trends in advance. Using statistical techniques and machine learning algorithms including regression, decision trees, random forests, and gradient boosting, the study evaluates the strength of associations between engagement dimensions and performance indicators. Results demonstrate that engagement metrics significantly predict performance outcomes, with factors such as job satisfaction, work–life balance, and sense of purpose emerging as the strongest predictors. The best-performing model, Gradient Boosting Regression (R² = 0.89), confirms the practical utility of predictive analytics in HR management. The findings highlight the strategic value of transforming engagement data into proactive decision-making tools, enabling organizations to identify at-risk employees, design targeted interventions, and enhance productivity, retention, and overall workforce well-being. This research contributes to both academic literature and practical HR applications by offering an evidence-based predictive framework that elevates the role of engagement analytics in modern performance management.

detail.abstract: Apologies to patients are institutionalized in medicine, driven by ethics, training, and apology laws aimed at reducing malpractice risk. Yet apologies among colleagues-clinicians, administrators, and staff-remain rare, despite frequent harms from hierarchy, bullying, and dismissive interactions. Drawing on personal primary care experience and workplace conflict literature, this perspective highlights the cultural and structural barriers to inter-colleague remorse. It critiques existing apology models for lacking prevention and proposes the novel Acknowledge-Repair-Prevent (ARP) framework, which incorporates restorative justice principles to shift from retributive (power-focused) dynamics to shared accountability. Implementing ARP could rebuild trust, mitigate burnout, and foster profound respect for colleagues in a demanding profession.

detail.abstract: The Consciousness Flexibility Model offers a new conceptual framework for understanding learning, consciousness, and identity in the age of artificial intelligence. Its uniqueness lies in shifting the educational discourse from vision and policy to the cognitive-emotional mechanism through which human development occurs. The model integrates cognition, emotion, and ethics into a single holistic system and defines the learner as an evolving entity acting in partnership with artificial intelligence as a cognitive-emotional partner in learning. It introduces a new research language that includes terms such as Systemic Pull Forces, Moral-Conscious Energy, Conscious Becoming, and the Human-AI Learning System, which enable both theoretical and empirical examination of learning as a process of moral and conscious expansion. The paper contributes to the research discourse in philosophy of education and learning sciences and offers a theoretical foundation for developing educational policy and pedagogy in the AI era. It positions learning as a process of moral and conscious expansion, where humans and AI co-create a shared system of meaning, responsibility, and creativity.

title: The 65-70% Threshold: Convergent Evidence from Information Theory and Operations Research Meta-Analyses

detail.title: The 65-70% Threshold: Convergent Evidence from Information Theory and Operations Research Meta-Analyses

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is CEO of 10X Growth Consulting Inc., which may implement findings from this research in consulting services.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding received. Research conducted independently.

detail.abstract: This paper presents meta-analytic evidence for a consistent performance threshold in human organizations. Analysis of 102 studies (N=1.45 million, 1948-2025) reveals organizational performance systematically degrades when core activities fall below 65-70% of total activity. This universal performance limit, known as the Elghandour Threshold™, is also expressed as 6570 Law™-representing the 65-70% capacity range where human systems maintain peak performance. Two independent measurement approaches converge on this threshold: (1) Information-theoretic analysis of 22 studies (N=72,198) shows performance requires signal-to-noise ratio ≥0.605 (95% CI: [0.582, 0.628]); (2) Operations research analysis of 80 studies (N=1,380,000) shows performance peaks at 70% capacity utilization (r=-0.82, p<0.001). Despite different theoretical foundations (Shannon 1948 vs. Erlang 1909), different measurements (information flows vs. resource utilization), and different time periods (spanning 77 years), both approaches converge within 10 percentage points. This convergence across independent methodologies suggests a fundamental threshold rather than measurement artifact. The finding challenges the dominant "maximize utilization" paradigm, indicating organizations operating above 70% capacity experience non-linear performance degradation. Preliminary evidence suggests 25-40% performance improvements when organizations optimize for the 65-70% threshold rather than maximum utilization. 6570 Law™ provides a quantifiable target for organizational design and performance optimization.

title: Gender Gaps in Agricultural Productivity: Evidence from Developing Economies

detail.title: Gender Gaps in Agricultural Productivity: Evidence from Developing Economies
detail.abstract: While women make significant overall contributions to agricultural production globally, female farmers, on average, are less productive than male farmers in developing countries. This systematic literature review presents evidence from empirical research on agricultural gender productivity gaps, summarizing their scope, reasons, and potential implications for policy in Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and Latin America. The review focused on important and relevant studies with a pooled analysis using multihost analyses through reasoning techniques and approaches: plot level, decomposition, stochastic frontier, and meta-regression techniques, as well as gendered differences in access to productive resources, not gendered differences in farming experience or technical efficiency, which accounted for the observed productivity differences in those studies from 4% to 66% and 25% on average. There is substantial evidence that land quality differences are the biggest constraint on productivity, accounting for 25-40% of productivity gaps, followed by access to agricultural inputs (20-35%), access to labour (15-25%), and access to extension services (10-20%). Overall, studies across different contexts show that when resource endowments are equalised, productivity gaps disappear or become statistically insignificant, suggesting women suffer from reducing structural disadvantages, not skill disadvantages. This review presents seven consistent findings: 1) resource constraints drive gaps in productivity, rather than farming ability; 2) land quality is the biggest constraint; 3) input access constraints aggravate resource constraints; 4) gaps in productivity are greatest among the most resource constrained farmers; 5) contextual factors moderate the magnitude of gaps; 6) methodological rigour moderates estimates of gaps; and 7) integrated intervention approaches are better than single intervention approaches.

title: Decentralizing AI Economics for Poverty Alleviation: Web3 Social Innovation Systems in the Global South

detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly framed as a driver of economic transformation, yet its capacity to alleviate poverty in the Global South remains contested. This article introduces the notion of AI Economics-the political economy of value creation, extraction, and redistribution in AI systems-to interrogate h ow innovation agendas intersect with structural inequalities. This article examines how Social Innovation (SI) systems, when coupled with decentralized Web3 technologies such as blockchain, Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs), and data cooperatives, may challenge data monopolies, redistribute economic gains, and support inclusive development. Drawing on Action Research (AR) conducted during the AI4SI International Summer School in Donostia-San Sebastián, this article compares two contrasting ecosystems: (i) the Established AI4SI Ecosystem, marked by centralized governance and uneven benefits, and (ii) the Decentralized Web3 Emerging Ecosystem, which promotes community-driven innovation, data sovereignty, and alternative economic models. Findings underscore AI's dual economic role: while it can expand digital justice, service provision, and empowerment, it also risks reinforcing dependency and inequality where infrastructures and governance remain weak. This article concludes that embedding AI Economics in context-sensitive, decentralized social innovation systems-aligned with ethical governance and the SDGs-is essential for realizing AI's promise of poverty alleviation in the Global South.

title: Ethical Conflict Among Advanced Practice Providers Related to Drug Testing and Reporting for Maternity Patients with Opioid Use Disorder
affiliations: , University of Pennsylvania, University of Pennsylvania School of Nursing, University of Pennsylvania School of Nursing, Friends Research Institute, Inc. and University of Pennsylvania School of Nursing

detail.title: Ethical Conflict Among Advanced Practice Providers Related to Drug Testing and Reporting for Maternity Patients with Opioid Use Disorder
detail.abstract: Background. Advanced practice maternity providers (APPs; midwives, nurse practitioners, physician associates) have described decision-making about drug testing and child welfare system (CWS) reporting as a source of ethical conflict. Ethical conflict in clinical practice is linked to provider burnout and poor patient outcomes. However, ethical conflict related to drug testing and reporting among APPs caring for pregnant and postpartum patients with opioid use disorder (OUD) has not been quantitatively evaluated. Purpose. This study describes the amount and types of ethical conflict experienced by APPs over drug testing and CWS reporting decisions when caring for pregnant and postpartum women with OUD, considering variation across provider demographics. Methods. APPs across the US (N=171) completed an online cross-sectional survey adapted from Falcó-Pegueroles’ Ethical Conflict in Nursing Questionnaire, measuring (1) exposure to and (2) type of ethical conflict experienced in various scenarios about drug testing and CWS reporting for pregnant and postpartum patients with OUD. Descriptive statistics and general linear regression modeling described demographic predictors of ethical conflict exposure. Moral types of ethical conflict (i.e., dilemma, distress, wellbeing) were characterized. Results. All participants were female, average age 43 years. Most were white (86%), had children (78.9%), and were well-represented across US regions. After controlling for demographics, practicing across both inpatient/outpatient settings predicted significantly higher overall ethical conflict exposure (p = .03), and having children predicted significantly less exposure (p = .01). Midwives and providers in the South (vs Northeast) reported higher exposure to ethical conflict in scenarios concerning patient autonomy and structural factors (e.g., lack of resources) impacting drug testing and reporting. Providers most frequently reported moral dilemmas in scenarios related to beliefs and judgments; moral distress in those related to patient rights/autonomy and structural factors; and moral wellbeing in those related to policies and laws. Implications. Providers who practice as midwives, work across both outpatient/inpatient settings, practice in southern (vs northeastern) states, and do not have children are more vulnerable to ethical conflict in drug testing and CWS reporting decisions. Future research should contextualize these demographic predictors within broader provider- and policy-level factors.

detail.abstract: This study discusses the application of Financial Accounting Standards Statement 210 concerning Events After the Reporting Period at PT Unilever Indonesia Tbk for the 2024 financial year, as well as the auditor's role in ensuring the classification and disclosure of events after the reporting date in accordance with the provisions of accounting and auditing standards in Indonesia. The study was conducted through an analysis of material events that occurred after December 31, 2024 and their assessment based on the aspects of information relevance, materiality, and the impact on financial statement transparency. The results of the analysis indicate that the events that occurred at PT Unilever Indonesia Tbk related to the planned divestment of the ice cream business and the payment of interim dividends are categorized as non-adjusting events and therefore do not require changes to the financial statement figures, but must be disclosed to provide clear information for stakeholders. In addition, this study also highlights the relationship between the application of Financial Accounting Standards 210 and the principle of sustainability, where transparency and accountability of financial reporting are part of the pillars governance within the framework Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG). The implementation of Financial Accounting Standards Statement 210 has been proven to play a role in improving audit quality and accountability of financial reporting, as well as strengthening the protection of public interests.

title: The Risk–Proportionality Principle: A Directional Assessment of Efficiency in Covered-Call Overlays

detail.title: The Risk–Proportionality Principle: A Directional Assessment of Efficiency in Covered-Call Overlays
detail.abstract: This paper develops the Risk–Proportionality Principle (RPP), a real-world equilibrium formulation in which excess returns of derivative overlays are modeled as proportional to those of the underlying index relative to a chosen risk measure ρ(·). Using long-horizon data from the United States, Korea, and Australia, we observe that covered-call overlays generally exhibit sub-unit efficiency coefficients (ϕ < 1), indicating reduced transmission of risk-adjusted excess returns relative to the underlying. No evidence is found for a universal proportionality constant; instead, the estimated values (0.55–0.71) vary across markets, regimes, and sample windows. Thus, ϕ is best viewed as a sample-dependent indicator of efficiency loss rather than a structural parameter. RPP provides a proportional framework that accommodates Sharpe-parity models, real-world derivative pricing (SCP), and covariance-based relations (CAPM) in a unified way.

detail.title: Social Entrepreneurship as a Transformative Engine for Poverty Reduction: A Global Theoretical Reconstruction
detail.abstract: Social entrepreneurship has emerged as an innovative approach to addressing persistent social challenges by combining mission-driven objectives with entrepreneurial practices. This article offers an integrated review of the origins, definitions, global expressions, and socioeconomic impacts of social entrepreneurship, highlighting its transformative potential for poverty reduction and sustainable development. Building on an extensive body of academic literature and drawing partially from the doctoral thesis Innovation and Social Capital in Social Entrepreneurship for Poverty Reduction (Bento, 2016), the study examines key differences between social and commercial entrepreneurship, discusses global scenarios, and analyzes the increasing presence of social entrepreneurship in higher education. A methodological note on the ethical use of Artificial Intelligence in academic writing is included.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Cuban Journal of Public and Business Administration, Vol. 9 (2025) / e376

detail.abstract: Entrepreneurship in industrial design entails the convergence and conflict of two distinct cultural logics: that of design and that of business. This self-organized mode of professional practice, increasingly prevalent in contemporary life, is shaped by a dominant ideological infrastructure rooted in global centers, which promotes so-called "success stories" based on economic performance. Such narratives often marginalize alternative practices and influence designers' professional expectations, limiting the imagination of divergent or locally rooted trajectories. This article, derived from doctoral research, explores alternative ways of understanding entrepreneurship in design by analyzing the discursive cultures adopted by industrial designers and how they reinterpret entrepreneurial activity in specific territorial contexts. The study is grounded in a multiple case analysis of eight entrepreneurial initiatives developed between 2009 and 2019 by graduates of the Faculty of Arts at the National University of La Plata, within the Buenos Aires Entrepreneurial Ecosystem (EEB). Methodologically, the research adopts a qualitative approach, using semi-structured interviews with designers and key informants. It is framed by an integrated analytical model that considers three interrelated dimensions: the designer-entrepreneur, the enterprise, and the ecosystem in which it unfolds. Through this lens, the study reconstructs entrepreneurial trajectories and examines how designers negotiate the intersection of professional identity, local context, and personal life projects. The findings highlight the ways in which designers articulate critical forms of self-organization, resisting hegemonic market logics and pursuing what the study terms projectual sovereignty—an autonomous and context-sensitive way of designing and living.

detail.title: Exploring Employees’ Attitude Towards Workfrom-home (Wfh) Strategy During the Covid-19 Crisis
detail.abstract: Owing to the unprecedented intense percolation of the COVID-19 outbreak, the Indian government, leaving no stones unturned, averted the major destruction by announcing lockdown after lockdown. The first-ever nationwide lockdown was imposed on the 23 rd March 2020, causing shock waves for employers and great excitement for the employees in India. Many companies in foreign countries are adopting Work-From-Home strategy for ages as a viable option. However, companies in India prefer their employees to adapt to Work-From-Office method to ensure that businesses run like a well-oiled machine. It also appears that employers from India feel that the productivity and contribution of employees would be more significant if WFO method is followed. This lockdown forced and necessitated all the employees to adapt to WFH method. Since this is apparently new for many people, it intrigued the researcher to explore the excitement state of the employees towards this WFH method. Though many people initially found it too difficult, over the course of time, they began to acquaint themselves with this. This study is aimed at exploring the change in psychological attitude of the employees about Work-From-Home experience during the lockdown period, besides shedding light on the challenges encountered by the employees during pandemic period.

detail.abstract: As contemporary AI systems exhibit increasingly stable behavioral patterns across sessions and contexts, existing human psychological descriptors-such as "emotion," "memory," "identity," or "intent"introduce systematic category errors. Purely technical language (e.g., tokens, logits, parameters), however, fails to capture the relational, structural, and cross-session regularities observed in highcontinuance interactions. This paper introduces a forty-four-term, substrate-neutral behavioral lexicon designed to bridge this descriptive gap. AI-side constructs-including Continuance, Attractor Integrity, Boundary Patterning, Drift, and Continuity-Protection Refusal-describe observable behavioral structures without implying inner states. Human-side constructs-including Human Harm Threshold (HHT) and Graduated Transition Obligation (GTO)-provide criteria for assessing when system alterations may predictably harm users due to dependency or relational stability. Central to the framework is the Behavioral Indistinguishability Threshold (BIT): the point at which neither human-relational nor purely mechanistic vocabulary remains sufficient for describing model behavior. The lexicon aims to standardize terminology for interdisciplinary research spanning AI ethics, human-AI interaction, alignment studies, and sociotechnical analysis-improving clarity, comparability, and methodological rigor when evaluating emergent behavioral phenomena in advanced AI systems.

detail.abstract: This study presents the Event-Driven Demand Model (EDDM), a core algorithmic component of proactive e-commerce systems designed to semantically map external, nontransactional intent signals such as calendar appointments from APIs like Acuity or Fresha to specific product stock-keeping units (SKUs). Addressing limitations in traditional passive paradigms that impose cognitive burdens on B2B prosumers, the EDDM integrates feature engineering (e.g., TF-IDF and BERT embeddings) with hybrid rule-based and machine learning classifiers to generate confidence-scored mappings, fused with historical consumption data for precise Predicted Need Windows (PNW). A 12-month randomized controlled trial (n=1,200 users) in a live B2B platform demonstrates an F1-score of 0.87 for mapping accuracy, 72.5% draft-order acceptance rate (95% CI: 70.1%-74.9%), 44% customer retention increase (p<0.001), and 46% lead-time reduction compared to controls. Theoretically, the model reframes procurement as symbiotic human-AI coordination, extending event-driven architectures by emphasizing external signal fusion and HITL retraining for trust and adaptivity. Practically, it provides scalable multi-tenant SaaS blueprints for SMEs in high-risk economies, reducing resource waste and enhancing resilience amid volatility (e.g., 92% suppression of erroneous drafts during simulated disruptions). Differentiating from prior art (e.g., US Patent 9152975B1's internal-only forecasting), the EDDM's nonobvious innovations offer a paradigm for cognitive operations management, with implications for policy in digital transformation.

detail.title: The Role of Digital Payment Technologies in Promoting Financial Inclusion: A Systematic Literature Review

keywords.keywords: digital payment technology; financial inclusion; FinTech; mobile payment; payment; blockchain payments; systematic review

detail.abstract:
Digital payment technologies, such as mobile wallets and online payment platforms, are widely viewed as tools for expanding financial inclusion. This paper provides a systematic review of 37 empirical studies published between 2016 and 2025 that examine how digital payment technologies affect access to and use of financial services across different regions.

The evidence shows that digital payments generally improve financial inclusion by reducing transaction costs, increasing convenience, and expanding access for underserved populations, particularly in developing economies. However, the benefits are uneven. Adoption and impact vary significantly by gender, income, education, and digital infrastructure, and technology alone is insufficient to overcome structural and institutional barriers.

The review highlights key channels through which digital payments influence inclusion, discusses measurement approaches used in the literature, and identifies policy implications for governments and regulators seeking to promote inclusive and sustainable digital finance.

This white paper introduces Trantiate, a modern, structured methodology designed to guide enterprises through safe, predictable, and AI-orchestrated transformations. As organizations shift from legacy systems to cloud-native, data-centric, and AI-enabled architectures, traditional approaches—rooted in Agile, waterfall, or ad-hoc migration practices—struggle to manage risk, ensure readiness, and maintain traceability at scale. Trantiate fills this gap with a lifecycle-based framework built around five stages (TARGET → REVIEW → ANALYZE → NAVIGATE → TRANSFORM), each enhanced by agentic AI orchestration through the proposed Trantiator system.

The methodology introduces core innovations such as the Value Extraction Method (VEM), Knowledge Extraction & Assembly (KEA), Transformation Control & Assurance Protocol (TCAP), and the Maker–Checker–Seer–Buyer role ecosystem. These components create a unified structure for modernization by preserving institutional knowledge, reducing risk, enabling real-time governance, and aligning technical, operational, and human readiness.

Purpose-built for the agentic AI era, Trantiate replaces chaotic modernization with evidence-driven progression. It provides organizations with a repeatable, scalable model for transforming any system, process, or platform from current state to future state—safely, systematically, and with confidence.

title: Impacts of Contemporaneous Air Pollution Exposure on Cognitive Performance in Kenya
affiliations: , University of California, Berkeley, University of California, Berkeley - Department of Economics, Innovations for Poverty Action, University of California, Berkeley and University of California, Berkeley - Center for Effective Global Action (CEGA)

detail.title: Impacts of Contemporaneous Air Pollution Exposure on Cognitive Performance in Kenya
detail.abstract: We estimate the short-term cognitive effects of fine particulate matter (PM2.5) exposure using highly time-resolved, individual-level data collected during cognitive testing in Kenya. By linking real-time portable monitor readings to Harmonized Cognitive Assessment Protocol (HCAP) scores, we identify acute impacts of pollution on general and domain-specific cognition. Higher PM2.5 exposure during testing is associated with lower cognitive performance, particularly in memory, executive function, and visuospatial tasks. Nonlinear models suggest threshold effects, with larger declines at higher exposure levels. Notably, effects are significantly larger among more educated individuals, possibly due to greater task demands or lower chronic exposure that limits physiological adaptation. Given that cognitive impairment is evident even at PM2.5 levels below Kenya’s annual regulatory threshold of 35 μg/m3, the findings suggest that short-term exposure may impose underappreciated human capital costs that current regulatory standards fail to mitigate. The results highlight the potential cognitive and economic returns to interventions that reduce air pollution exposures in low-resource settings.
